# 1-0-0.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/updates/release-notes/1-0-0.mdx

title: 1.0.0
description: Anchor release notes for 1.0.0.

`1.0.0` is the first stable major release of Anchor. It ships a large number of breaking changes designed to clean up long-standing technical debt, modernize the toolchain, and establish a stable foundation going forward. These notes cover the most significant changes. The full list lives in the [`CHANGELOG.md{:file}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/v1.0.0/CHANGELOG.md#100---2026-04-02).

## How to upgrade

### Using AVM (recommended)

1. Update `avm` itself before installing the new CLI. Existing `avm` installs that already support `self-update` can update in place:

   ```bash
   $ <blue>avm</blue> self-update
   ```

   Older installs need a fresh `cargo install` first to pick up the new binary:

   ```bash
   $ <blue>cargo</blue> install avm <dim>--git</dim> https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor <dim>--locked</dim>
   ```

2. Update `anchor-cli`:

   ```bash
   <blue>avm</blue> install 1.0.0
   ```

### Without AVM

Install `anchor-cli` directly:

```console
$ <blue>cargo</blue> install <dim>--git</dim> https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor <dim>--tag</dim> v1.0.0 anchor-cli <dim>--locked</dim>
```

### Common steps

3. Update Anchor crate(s) to `1.0.0`.

4. Update TS package(s). The package has been renamed in this release. See [TypeScript package rename](#typescript-package-rename) for the new import path.

## Recommended Solana version

The recommended Solana version is `3.1.10`. Install the new tooling with:

```console
$ <blue>sh</blue> <dim>-c</dim> "$(curl <dim>-sSfL</dim> https://release.anza.xyz/v3.1.10/install)"
```

## Breaking changes

### TypeScript package rename

The TypeScript package has been moved from `@coral-xyz/anchor` to `@anchor-lang/core`:

```console
$ <blue>npm</blue> install @anchor-lang/core
```

Every import in the project needs the new package name:

```ts title="example.ts" showLineNumbers=false del={1-2} add={3-4}
import * as anchor from '@coral-xyz/anchor'
import { Program } from '@coral-xyz/anchor'
import * as anchor from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { Program } from '@anchor-lang/core'
```

IDL types that were previously imported from `@coral-xyz/anchor/dist/cjs/idl` are now exported directly from `@anchor-lang/core`:

```ts title="example.ts" showLineNumbers=false del={1} add={2}
import { Idl } from '@coral-xyz/anchor/dist/cjs/idl'
import { Idl } from '@anchor-lang/core'
```

### Solana 3.0

Anchor `1.0.0` targets Solana `3.x`. Workspaces still on Solana `2.x` must upgrade their toolchain before installing the new CLI.

### Solana CLI dependency removed

The `anchor` CLI no longer depends on the external `solana` CLI binary. Native implementations are now provided for the most common subcommands, including `balance`, `airdrop`, `address`, and `deploy`. The `solana` binary no longer needs to be on `PATH` for any `anchor` command to function.

### `<blue>anchor</blue> test` and `<blue>anchor</blue> localnet` use Surfpool by default

[Surfpool](https://github.com/solana-foundation/surfpool) replaces `solana-test-validator` as the default local backend for `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` and `$ <blue>anchor</blue> localnet`. Pass `<dim>--validator legacy</dim>` to keep using `solana-test-validator`.

Surfpool must be installed for the default `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` and `$ <blue>anchor</blue> localnet` flow. Verify the installation with `$ <blue>surfpool</blue> <dim>--version</dim>`. The minimum recommended Surfpool version for use with Anchor is [`v1.1.2`](https://github.com/solana-foundation/surfpool/releases/tag/v1.1.2). For installation, follow the [Surfpool installation instructions](https://github.com/solana-foundation/surfpool?tab=readme-ov-file#installation).

### Duplicate mutable accounts disallowed by default

Passing the same mutable account twice in an instruction now produces a runtime error by default. The `dup{:rs}` constraint opts back into duplicate mutable accounts when they are intentional:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct MyIx<'info> {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub account_a: Account<'info, MyData>,
    #[account(mut, dup)]
    pub account_b: Account<'info, MyData>,
}
```

### Legacy IDL instructions replaced by Program Metadata

The on-chain IDL management instructions that Anchor has used since the beginning have been removed and replaced with the new [Program Metadata Program (PMP)](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/pull/3798). IDL uploads through `$ <blue>anchor</blue> deploy` and `$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl` commands work as before. Only the underlying storage mechanism has changed.

The `program-id` argument of `$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl init` and `$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl upgrade` is now optional. When omitted, the program ID is read from the `address` field of the IDL file itself.

Existing deployed programs with IDLs require migration. The legacy IDL accounts must be closed before deploying the v1 program, since the v1 binary no longer carries the IDL management instructions. The closure step itself requires the previous `v0.32.1` CLI.

### Remove program account info from CPI context

The `program` field in `CpiContext{:rs}` previously held a redundant copy of the program's `AccountInfo{:rs}`. The constructor now takes the program ID directly:

```rust showLineNumbers=false del={1} add={2}
CpiContext::new(ctx.accounts.token_program.to_account_info(), cpi_accounts)
CpiContext::new(Token::id(), cpi_accounts)
```

### `interface-instructions` feature removed

The `interface-instructions` feature flag and the `#[interface]{:rs}` attribute have been removed. Use `#[instruction(discriminator = <EXPR>)]{:rs}` to specify custom discriminators.

### `Anchor.toml{:file}` cleanup

- The `[registry]` section is no longer recognized. Remove it from `Anchor.toml{:file}`.
- The program `arch` build options have been removed from the CLI.

### `#[error_code]` may only appear once per program

Having more than one `#[error_code]{:rs}` block in a single program is now a compile-time error.

### Client tx signing error no longer panics

`RequestBuilder::send(){:rs}` (and its variants) previously panicked when signing failed. It now returns an `Err{:rs}` instead.

## AVM

### `<blue>avm</blue> self-update`

A v1-capable `avm` can update itself without going back through `cargo install`:

```console
$ <blue>avm</blue> self-update
```

Bootstrapping to a version that supports the command requires a one-off `cargo` install first:

```console
$ <blue>cargo</blue> install avm <dim>--git</dim> https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor <dim>--tag</dim> v1.0.0 <dim>--locked</dim>
```

`avm` also passively warns when it detects that a newer version of itself is available.

### Pre-release support

All three `avm` commands (`install`, `list`, `update`) now recognize pre-release version labels:

```console
$ <blue>avm</blue> install latest-pre-release
$ <blue>avm</blue> list <dim>--pre-release</dim>
$ <blue>avm</blue> update <dim>--pre-release</dim>
```

## CLI

### Lifecycle hooks

Shell commands can now run at key points in the build, test, and deploy lifecycle through a `[hooks]` section in `Anchor.toml{:file}`:

```toml
[hooks]
pre_build  = "echo building..."
post_build = ["echo done", "echo done again"]
pre_test   = "some-setup-script"
post_deploy = "some-notify-script"
```

Supported hooks: `pre_build`, `post_build`, `pre_test`, `post_test`, `pre_deploy`, `post_deploy`.

### LiteSVM test template is now the default

`$ <blue>anchor</blue> init` now generates a [LiteSVM](https://github.com/LiteSVM/litesvm) test template by default, replacing the previous TypeScript-based default. A different template can be selected explicitly:

```console
$ <blue>anchor</blue> init my-program <dim>--test-template</dim> mollusk
$ <blue>anchor</blue> init my-program <dim>--test-template</dim> mocha
```

### Program ID mismatch check

`$ <blue>anchor</blue> build` now checks that the program ID declared in source matches the public key in the program's keypair file and emits an error when they differ. The check is skipped during `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` where ephemeral keypairs are common. Pass `<dim>--ignore-keys</dim>` to suppress the check on builds.

### `<dim>--install-agent-skills</dim>`

Pass `<dim>--install-agent-skills</dim>` to `$ <blue>anchor</blue> init` to install Solana agent-AI skills into the new workspace automatically.

### `<blue>anchor</blue> login` removed

`$ <blue>anchor</blue> login` has been removed alongside the `[registry]` section of `Anchor.toml{:file}`.

## Lang

### `Migration<'info, From, To>{:rs}` account type

The new `Migration{:rs}` type migrates an account between two different data layouts in a single instruction:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct MigrateMyAccount<'info> {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub my_account: Migration<'info, OldAccount, NewAccount>,
}
```

The account is deserialized as `From{:rs}` and serialized back as `To{:rs}` on instruction exit.

### `declare_program!(){:rs}` improvements

Several renames apply to the code generated by `declare_program!(){:rs}`. The `utils` module is now `parsers`, and the deserialization methods are now named `parse` instead of `try_from_bytes`:

```rust showLineNumbers=false del={1,4} add={2,5}
my_program::utils::Account::try_from_bytes(&data)?;
my_program::parsers::Account::parse(&data)?;

my_program::utils::Event::try_from_bytes(&data)?;
my_program::parsers::Event::parse(&data)?;
```

The `errors` module is now `error` (singular), and `ProgramError{:rs}` has been renamed to `<ProgramName>Error{:rs}`, where `<ProgramName>` is the PascalCase name of the declared program:

```rust showLineNumbers=false del={1} add={2}
my_program::errors::ProgramError
my_program::error::MyProgramError
```

A typed instruction parser is now generated alongside the CPI helpers. Call `my_program::parsers::Instruction::parse(){:rs}` with a `solana_instruction::Instruction{:rs}` to decode any instruction belonging to the program.

Composite (non-instruction) account structs used more than once in a program previously caused duplicate definitions or incorrect instruction-name derivation in the generated code. Each composite account definition is now guaranteed to be unique, and colliding instruction names have a numeric suffix appended until uniqueness is reached.

Error generation has also been improved. `declare_program!(){:rs}` previously interfered with the IDL error module of the declaring program. Programs that use `declare_program!(){:rs}` alongside their own `#[error_code]{:rs}` block now produce correct error code definitions.

### Use `declare_program!(){:rs}` with only `anchor-client`

`declare_program!(){:rs}` no longer requires `anchor-lang` in client-side contexts. Adding `anchor-client` as a dependency is sufficient.

### Remove lifetime definitions from `Context`

Three redundant lifetime parameters have been removed from `Context{:rs}`. Most programs are unaffected. Programs that referenced the removed lifetimes explicitly need to update their annotations:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
// Before (v0.32)
pub fn my_handler<'a, 'b, 'c, 'info>(
    ctx: Context<'a, 'b, 'c, 'info, MyAccounts<'info>>,
) -> Result<()> { ... }

// After (v1)
pub fn my_handler<'info>(ctx: Context<'info, MyAccounts<'info>>) -> Result<()> { ... }
// or simply (when the lifetime is inferred)
pub fn my_handler(ctx: Context<MyAccounts>) -> Result<()> { ... }
```

### Deprecate `AccountInfo` in `Accounts` macro

Using `AccountInfo{:rs}` directly inside a `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` struct now emits a compile-time warning. Prefer `UncheckedAccount{:rs}` or a more specific account type.

### Relaxed PDA seed syntax

Seed expressions inside `seeds = [...]{:rs}` constraints accept a broader set of Rust expressions. More complex seed expressions reduce the likelihood that the seeds can be represented in the IDL and resolved automatically by the client.

### Owner check on account reload

`Account::reload(){:rs}` now re-validates the account's owner, matching the behavior of the initial load.

### Generic `Program` type

`Program<'info>{:rs}` can now be used without a generic type argument for executable-only validation when the concrete program type isn't known statically:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
pub program: Program<'info>,
```

### `Owners` exported from `prelude`

`anchor_lang::Owners{:rs}` is now re-exported from `anchor_lang::prelude{:rs}`, removing the need for a separate `use{:rs}` statement.

### Borsh upgraded to 1.5.7

Both the Rust and TypeScript Borsh implementations have been updated to `1.5.7`. The `borsh` dependency in `Cargo.toml{:file}` must be compatible with that version.

### `#[instruction(..)]{:rs}` argument validation

The compiler now enforces that the types and count of arguments declared in `#[instruction(..)]{:rs}` match the corresponding instruction handler's signature, catching mismatches that were previously silent.

## IDL

### Unsupported field types produce a hard error

Defined types that contained unsupported fields (such as tuple types) were previously omitted from the generated IDL silently. They now produce a compile-time error:

```text
error: Unsupported type
  --> programs/name/src/lib.rs:37:8
   |
37 |     x: (u32, u32),
   |        ^^^^^^^^^^
```

Programs that previously relied on silent omission must refactor those fields into supported types before building.

### Full path account names supported in IDL generation

The IDL builder previously rejected account types that shared a short name with another type in a different module (for example, `program::module::Account{:rs}` conflicting with `other::Account{:rs}`). The duplicate-name check has been removed, so fully qualified account paths now resolve without error.

### `address` constraint resolves constants with numbers in their names

The `address{:rs}` constraint previously failed to resolve constants whose identifiers contained numbers, such as `MY_PROGRAM_V2_ID{:rs}`. The resolver now handles them correctly.

### `serde_json` is now optional

The `serde_json` dependency of `anchor-lang-idl` is now behind an opt-in feature flag. Disabling it reduces compile time when JSON serialization isn't needed.

### External accounts excluded from IDL

Accounts defined in external programs (such as SPL token accounts referenced through CPI) are no longer included in the generated IDL's `accounts` array, keeping the IDL scoped to the declaring program's own types.

### Custom error offset respected

The `offset = N{:rs}` argument in `#[error_code]{:rs}` is now reflected in the generated IDL, so IDL error codes match the values emitted at runtime.

## TypeScript

### IDL fetching uses Program Metadata Program

The TypeScript client now fetches IDLs from the new Program Metadata Program storage. Existing code calling `Program.fetchIdl(){:ts}` continues to work without changes.

## Rust client

### `FnMut{:rs}` closures for event subscriptions

`program.on::<Event>(|event, slot| { ... }){:rs}` now accepts `FnMut{:rs}` closures, so the callback can capture and mutate state from the surrounding scope.

### Reduced re-exports from `anchor-client`

`anchor-client` previously re-exported the entirety of `solana-sdk`, which made types easy to discover but pulled in a large transitive dependency. It now only re-exports the types that are part of its own public API. Programs that depended on transitive `solana-sdk` types through `anchor-client` must now add the underlying crates (`solana-account`, `solana-pubkey`, and so on) as direct dependencies.

See the full list of notable changes in the [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/v1.0.0/CHANGELOG.md).

---

# 1-0-1.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/updates/release-notes/1-0-1.mdx

title: 1.0.1
description: Anchor release notes for 1.0.1.

`1.0.1` is a patch release that fixes a regression in `AnchorSerialize{:rs}` and `AnchorDeserialize{:rs}` when user-supplied `#[borsh(...)]{:rs}` attributes are present (see [user-provided `borsh` attributes fix](#fix-user-provided-borsh-attributes-in-derives)).

## How to upgrade

To bump only the affected crate in an existing `1.0.0` workspace:

```console
$ <blue>cargo</blue> update anchor-derive-serde
```

Otherwise, install the new `anchor-cli` via AVM:

```console
$ <blue>avm</blue> install 1.0.1
```

Or directly from the repository:

```console
$ <blue>cargo</blue> install <dim>--git</dim> https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor <dim>--tag</dim> v1.0.1 anchor-cli <dim>--locked</dim>
```

Then update Anchor crate(s) and TS package(s) to `1.0.1`.

## Recommended Solana version

The recommended Solana version is `3.1.10`, the same as [v1.0.0's recommended Solana version](./1-0-0#recommended-solana-version).

## Lang

### Fix user-provided `borsh` attributes in derives

Structs and enums carrying custom `#[borsh(...)]{:rs}` attributes (for example, `#[borsh(skip)]{:rs}` or `#[borsh(use_discriminant = true)]{:rs}`) now compile correctly under `#[derive(AnchorSerialize, AnchorDeserialize)]{:rs}`:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(AnchorSerialize, AnchorDeserialize)]
#[borsh(use_discriminant = true)]
pub enum MyEnum {
    A = 0,
    B = 5,
}
```

Previously, the derive macros emitted their own item-level `#[borsh]{:rs}` attribute alongside any user-supplied one. Only a single item-level `#[borsh]{:rs}` attribute is permitted, so the duplicate produced a compile error. The macros now extract user-provided attributes and merge them with the generated ones.

The `#[borsh]{:rs}` attribute is not supported when the `lazy-account` feature is enabled. The only accepted form under `lazy-account` is `#[borsh(use_discriminant = false)]{:rs}`.

See the full list of notable changes in the [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/v1.0.1/CHANGELOG.md#101---2026-04-16).

---

# 1-0-2.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/updates/release-notes/1-0-2.mdx

title: 1.0.2
description: Anchor release notes for 1.0.2.

`1.0.2` is a patch release with fixes across `anchor-cli`, `anchor-lang`, and `anchor-client`. The most user-visible change is the localnet bind default that unblocks `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` against `solana-test-validator` `3.1.10` (see [bind localnet to `127.0.0.1` by default](#bind-localnet-to-127001-by-default)).

## How to upgrade

To install the new `anchor-cli` via AVM:

```console
$ <blue>avm</blue> install 1.0.2
```

Or directly from the repository:

```console
$ <blue>cargo</blue> install <dim>--git</dim> https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor <dim>--tag</dim> v1.0.2 anchor-cli <dim>--locked</dim>
```

Then update Anchor crate(s) and TS package(s) to `1.0.2`.

## Recommended Solana version

The recommended Solana version is `3.1.10`, the same as [v1.0.0's recommended Solana version](./1-0-0#recommended-solana-version).

## CLI

### Bind localnet to `127.0.0.1` by default

`$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` now defaults the localnet bind address to `127.0.0.1` rather than `0.0.0.0`. The previous `0.0.0.0` default caused `solana-test-validator` `3.1.10` to panic on startup, which broke the localnet test loop on the recommended Solana toolchain. The `bind_address` field in `Anchor.toml{:file}` still overrides the default for workspaces that need a different value.

### Fall back to a priority fee of `0` on localnet

`$ <blue>anchor</blue> deploy` and related commands no longer surface a fee-lookup error when targeting a local cluster. The recent-priority-fee RPC method may either fail or return an empty list against localnet, so the CLI now falls back to a priority fee of `0` in both cases and prints a warning. This matches the assumption that localnet does not need fee competition.

## Lang

### Faster IDL builds via cached `CrateContext`

The IDL build pipeline now caches the parsed crate context inside a `OnceLock{:rs}` shared across `gen_idl_type{:rs}` invocations within a single compilation. Previously, each emitted type re-parsed `lib.rs{:file}` through `CrateContext::parse{:rs}`, which made IDL generation scale poorly with the number of account, instruction, and event types in a program. Workspaces with many defined types see materially shorter IDL build times.

### Fix compile error with `init` and a runtime seeds expression

`#[account(init, ..., seeds = <runtime expression>, bump)]{:rs}` now compiles when the seed list is computed at runtime rather than spelled out as a literal array:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Open<'info> {
    #[account(
        init,
        payer = user,
        space = 8,
        seeds = pda_seeds(user.key()),
        bump,
    )]
    pub pda: Account<'info, Dummy>,
    #[account(mut)]
    pub user: Signer<'info>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}
```

Previously, the generated code pushed a borrowed temporary array (`&[__bump][..]{:rs}`) into the runtime signer-seeds vector. The borrow checker rejected this when the rest of the seed list came from a runtime expression because the temporary did not outlive the enclosing block. The fix binds the bump byte to a named local so the borrow lives long enough.

## Client

### Replace `solana-program` with `solana-hash`

`anchor-client` previously depended on `solana-program` solely to re-export `solana_program::hash::Hash{:rs}`. The dependency is now `solana-hash`, which trims the client's transitive surface and reduces compile time for downstream Rust SDKs that consume `anchor-client`.

See the full list of notable changes in the [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/v1.0.2/CHANGELOG.md#102---2026-05-02).

---

# declare-program.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/clients/declare-program.mdx

title: Dependency free composability
description: "Use Anchor's `declare_program` macro to interact with programs without additional dependencies."

import Code from '@/components/code.astro'
import callee from './_declare-program/callee.rs?raw'
import caller from './_declare-program/caller.rs?raw'
import callerTest from './_declare-program/caller.test.ts?raw'
import idl from './_declare-program/example.json?raw'
import client from './_declare-program/client.rs?raw'
import cargo from './_declare-program/Cargo.toml?raw'

The [`declare_program!(){:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/macro.declare_program.html) macro generates Rust modules from a program's IDL, letting on-chain and off-chain code interact with an Anchor program without depending on its source crate. A reference example lives in the [Anchor repository](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/tree/master/tests/declare-program).

The macro generates the following modules:

| Module | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [`cpi{:rs}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/program/src/declare_program/mods/cpi.rs) | Helper functions for making cross-program invocations (CPIs) to the program from other on-chain programs |
| [`client{:rs}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/program/src/declare_program/mods/client.rs) | Accounts and arguments required to build program instructions to add to client-side transactions |
| [`account{:rs}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/program/src/declare_program/mods/accounts.rs) | Account data types (program state) defined in the program |
| [`program{:rs}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/program/src/declare_program/mods/program.rs) | Program ID constant used to identify the program |
| [`constants{:rs}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/program/src/declare_program/mods/constants.rs) | Program constants defined in the program |
| [`events{:rs}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/program/src/declare_program/mods/events.rs) | Program events defined in the program |
| [`types{:rs}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/program/src/declare_program/mods/types.rs) | Program types defined in the program |
| [`error{:rs}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/program/src/declare_program/mods/error.rs) | Program errors defined in the program |
| [`parsers{:rs}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/program/src/declare_program/mods/parsers.rs) | Parsers for program accounts, instructions and events |

## Examples

The following examples demonstrate two scenarios for `declare_program!(){:rs}`:

1. Making cross program invocations (CPIs) from one program to another.
2. Building client-side transactions to invoke a program's instructions.

Both scenarios show how the generated modules simplify program interactions, whether the calling code is on-chain or off-chain.

### On-chain CPI

The macro reads its IDL from a directory named `idls/{:dir}` placed anywhere in the project. A typical layout for a CPI between two programs:

<FileTree>

    <File name="example.json" />
  </Dir>
  <Dir name="programs" open={true}>
    <Dir name="example-cpi" open={true}>
      <Dir name="src" open={true}>
        <File name="lib.rs" />
      </Dir>
      <File name="Cargo.toml" />
    </Dir>
  </Dir>
</FileTree>

The callee program defines the instructions the caller will invoke. Its IDL (produced by `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build`) is the input to `declare_program!(){:rs}` in the caller:

# rust.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/clients/rust.mdx

title: Rust
description: Learn how to use Anchor's Rust client library to interact with Solana programs.

import Code from '@/components/code.astro'
import lib from './_rust/lib.rs?raw'
import idl from './_rust/example.json?raw'
import main from './_rust/main.rs?raw'

The [`anchor-client`](https://docs.rs/anchor-client/latest/anchor_client/) crate is the Rust client library for interacting with Anchor programs.

## Example

The following example uses the `anchor-client` crate to interact with a simple Anchor program. The `declare_program!{:rs}` macro generates dependency-free client modules from the program's IDL, exposing typed builders for the program's instructions and accounts.

The program below exposes two instructions: `initialize{:rs}` creates and initializes a counter account that stores a value, and `increment{:rs}` increments the stored value.

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" />

# typescript.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/clients/typescript.mdx

title: TypeScript
description: Learn how to use Anchor's TypeScript client library to interact with Solana programs.

import Code from '@/components/code.astro'
import methodsChain from './_typescript/methods_chain.ts?raw'
import lib from './_typescript/lib.rs?raw'
import exampleJson from './_typescript/example.json?raw'
import exampleTs from './_typescript/example.ts?raw'
import exampleClient from './_typescript/example_client.ts?raw'

Anchor provides a TypeScript client library, [`@anchor-lang/core`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/tree/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/ts/packages/anchor), that simplifies interacting with Solana programs from JavaScript or TypeScript clients.

<Callout variant="important" title="`@solana/web3.js` v1 only">
  `@anchor-lang/core` is only compatible with the legacy version (v1) of `@solana/web3.js` and
  `@solana/spl-token`. It is not compatible with the new (v2) version of `@solana/web3.js`.
</Callout>

## Client program

Interacting with an Anchor program through `@anchor-lang/core` requires a [`Program{:ts}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/ts/packages/anchor/src/program/index.ts#L58) instance built from the program's [IDL file](/docs/v1/fundamentals/idl/).

A `Program{:ts}` is constructed from the IDL and an `AnchorProvider{:ts}`, which bundles a `Connection{:ts}` to a Solana cluster (localhost, devnet, mainnet) with an optional default `Wallet{:ts}` used to pay for and sign transactions.

<Tabs items={['Frontend/Node', 'Test File']}>
<Tab>

A frontend integration with the [Solana wallet adapter](https://github.com/anza-xyz/wallet-adapter) wires the `AnchorProvider{:ts}` and `Program{:ts}` together:

```ts title="example.ts" showLineNumbers=false {9-10,12-14}
import { Program, AnchorProvider, setProvider } from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { useAnchorWallet, useConnection } from '@solana/wallet-adapter-react'
import type { HelloAnchor } from './idlType'
import idl from './idl.json'

const { connection } = useConnection()
const wallet = useAnchorWallet()

const provider = new AnchorProvider(connection, wallet, {})
setProvider(provider)

export const program = new Program(idl as HelloAnchor, {
  connection,
})
```

The snippet imports two files Anchor generates at `anchor build`: `idl.json{:file}` (written to `/target/idl/<program-name>.json{:file}`) and `idlType.ts{:file}` (the corresponding TypeScript type definition, written to `/target/types/<program-name>.ts{:file}`).

A `Program{:ts}` can also be created from the IDL and a `Connection{:ts}` alone. There is no default `Wallet{:ts}`, so the instance can fetch accounts and build instructions without a connected wallet:

```ts title="example.ts" showLineNumbers=false {8-10}
import { clusterApiUrl, Connection, PublicKey } from '@solana/web3.js'
import { Program } from '@anchor-lang/core'
import type { HelloAnchor } from './idlType'
import idl from './idl.json'

const connection = new Connection(clusterApiUrl('devnet'), 'confirmed')

export const program = new Program(idl as HelloAnchor, {
  connection,
})
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

A new Anchor project ships with a default test file that already includes a `Program{:ts}` instance. Applications outside the Anchor workspace, such as React or Node.js apps, must construct the `Program{:ts}` manually:

```ts title="hello_anchor.ts" showLineNumbers=false {9}
import * as anchor from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { Program } from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { HelloAnchor } from '../target/types/hello_anchor'

describe('hello_anchor', () => {
  // Configure the client to use the local cluster.
  anchor.setProvider(anchor.AnchorProvider.env())

  const program = anchor.workspace.helloAnchor as Program<HelloAnchor>

  it('Is initialized!', async () => {
    // Add your test here.
    const tx = await program.methods.initialize().rpc()
    console.log('Your transaction signature', tx)
  })
})
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Invoke instructions

Once the `Program{:ts}` is set up, Anchor's [`MethodsBuilder{:ts}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/ts/packages/anchor/src/program/namespace/methods.ts#L155) builds and sends instructions. The builder supports building individual instructions, building transactions, and building and sending transactions in one call.

The basic chain looks like this:

<Tabs items={['.methods{:ts}', '.instructionName(){:ts}', '.accounts(){:ts}', '.signers([]){:ts}']}>
<Tab>

`program.methods{:ts}` is the builder API for creating instruction calls from the program's IDL:

<Code code={methodsChain} lang="ts" meta="{1} showLineNumbers=false" />

</Tab>
<Tab>

After `.methods`, name an instruction from the IDL and pass any required arguments as comma-separated values:

<Code code={methodsChain} lang="ts" meta="{2} showLineNumbers=false" />

</Tab>
<Tab>

`.accounts(){:ts}` takes the addresses of the accounts the instruction requires, as specified in the IDL:

<Code code={methodsChain} lang="ts" meta="{3} showLineNumbers=false" />

Some account addresses do not need to be supplied explicitly because Anchor resolves them from the IDL. These typically include common accounts such as the System Program, and accounts whose address is a Program Derived Address (PDA).

</Tab>
<Tab>

`.signers([]){:ts}` optionally takes an array of keypairs that must sign the instruction in addition to the provider wallet. This is most often used when creating a new account whose address is the public key of a freshly generated keypair:

<Code code={methodsChain} lang="ts" meta="{4} showLineNumbers=false" />

<Callout variant="note">
  `.signers([]){:ts}` should only be used with `.rpc(){:ts}`. When using `.transaction(){:ts}` or `.instruction(){:ts}`, signers should be added to the transaction before sending.
</Callout>

</Tab>
</Tabs>

Anchor offers three terminal methods for completing the builder chain:

<Tabs items={['.rpc(){:ts}', '.transaction(){:ts}', '.instruction(){:ts}']}>
<Tab>

`.rpc(){:ts}` sends a signed transaction with the specified instruction and returns a `TransactionSignature{:ts}`. The `Wallet{:ts}` from the `Provider{:ts}` is automatically included as a signer:

```ts showLineNumbers=false {12}
// Generate keypair for the new account
const newAccountKp = new Keypair()

const data = new BN(42)
const transactionSignature = await program.methods
  .initialize(data)
  .accounts({
    newAccount: newAccountKp.publicKey,
    signer: wallet.publicKey,
    systemProgram: SystemProgram.programId,
  })
  .signers([newAccountKp])
  .rpc()
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

`.transaction(){:ts}` builds a `Transaction{:ts}` containing the specified instruction without sending it:

```ts showLineNumbers=false {11}
// Generate keypair for the new account
const newAccountKp = new Keypair()

const data = new BN(42)
const transaction = await program.methods
  .initialize(data)
  .accounts({
    newAccount: newAccountKp.publicKey,
    signer: wallet.publicKey,
    systemProgram: SystemProgram.programId,
  })
  .transaction()

const transactionSignature = await connection.sendTransaction(transaction, [
  wallet.payer,
  newAccountKp,
])
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

`.instruction(){:ts}` builds a `TransactionInstruction{:ts}`, useful when manually composing a transaction from multiple instructions:

```ts showLineNumbers=false {11}
// Generate keypair for the new account
const newAccountKp = new Keypair()

const data = new BN(42)
const instruction = await program.methods
  .initialize(data)
  .accounts({
    newAccount: newAccountKp.publicKey,
    signer: wallet.publicKey,
    systemProgram: SystemProgram.programId,
  })
  .instruction()

const transaction = new Transaction().add(instruction)

const transactionSignature = await connection.sendTransaction(transaction, [
  wallet.payer,
  newAccountKp,
])
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Fetch accounts

The `Program{:ts}` client also fetches and deserializes accounts created by the program. Use `program.account{:ts}` followed by the name of the account type defined in the IDL.

<Tabs items={['.all(){:ts}', 'memcmp{:ts}', '.fetch(){:ts}', '.fetchMultiple(){:ts}']}>
<Tab>

`program.account.newAccount.all(){:ts}` fetches every existing account of a given type:

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const accounts = await program.account.newAccount.all()
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

`memcmp{:ts}` (memory compare) filters for account data that matches a specific value at a specific offset. Using `memcmp{:ts}` requires knowing the byte layout of the account's data field.

The first 8 bytes of any Anchor account are reserved for the discriminator, so offsets into the account's own fields start at 8:

```ts showLineNumbers=false {3-6}
const accounts = await program.account.newAccount.all([
  {
    memcmp: {
      offset: 8,
      bytes: '',
    },
  },
])
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

`program.account.newAccount.fetch(){:ts}` fetches and deserializes a single account by address:

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const account = await program.account.newAccount.fetch(ACCOUNT_ADDRESS)
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

`program.account.newAccount.fetchMultiple(){:ts}` fetches and deserializes multiple accounts at once, taking an array of addresses:

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const accounts = await program.account.newAccount.fetchMultiple([
  ACCOUNT_ADDRESS_ONE,
  ACCOUNT_ADDRESS_TWO,
])
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

# cpi.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/fundamentals/cpi.mdx

title: Cross program invocation
description: Learn how to implement Cross Program Invocations (CPIs) in Anchor programs to enable composability between different Solana programs.

import Code from '@/components/code.astro'
import lib from './_cpi/lib.rs?raw'
import libPda from './_cpi/lib_pda.rs?raw'

A Cross Program Invocation (CPI) is one program calling an instruction on another program. This is how composability works on Solana: programs build on top of each other rather than reimplementing the same logic. The example below uses a SOL transfer to illustrate the mechanics, but the same pattern applies to any instruction on any program.

## Cross program invocations

The `lib.rs{:file}` file below defines a single `sol_transfer(){:rs}` instruction. When invoked, it issues a CPI to the System Program's `transfer(){:rs}` instruction:

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="{10,22}" />

The `cpi.test.ts{:file}` file invokes `sol_transfer(){:rs}` and logs a link to the transaction details on SolanaFM:

```ts title="cpi.test.ts" showLineNumbers=false
it('SOL Transfer Anchor', async () => {
  const transactionSignature = await program.methods
    .solTransfer(new BN(transferAmount))
    .accounts({
      sender: sender.publicKey,
      recipient: recipient.publicKey,
    })
    .rpc()

  console.log(
    `\nTransaction Signature:` +
      `https://solana.fm/tx/${transactionSignature}?cluster=devnet-solana`,
  )
})
```

The transaction details show the Anchor program invoked first (instruction 1), which then invokes the System Program (instruction 1.1):

![Transaction details](/docs/basics/cpi/transaction-details.png)

### Example explanation

A CPI is constructed the same way as any other Solana instruction. The caller must specify:

1. The program ID of the program being called.
2. The accounts required by the instruction.
3. Any instruction data required as arguments.

The System Program's `transfer(){:rs}` instruction requires a `from{:rs}` account that sends the SOL and a `to{:rs}` account that receives it. The `SolTransfer{:rs}` struct declares both accounts plus the System Program itself, since the CPI invokes that program:

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="collapse={1-26}" />

The tabs below present three approaches to implementing the same CPI, each at a different level of abstraction:

<Tabs groupId="language" items={['CpiContext{:rs}', 'invoke(){:rs}', 'Manual']}>
<Tab>

The first approach uses Anchor's [`CpiContext{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/context/struct.CpiContext.html), which bundles the `program_id{:rs}` and accounts required by the instruction. The `cpi_context{:rs}` is then passed to the `transfer(){:rs}` helper to invoke the instruction:

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="{15-22} collapse={1-9, 24-34}" />

The `cpi_context{:rs}` variable specifies the program ID (System Program) and the accounts (sender and recipient) required by the `transfer(){:rs}` instruction. The `cpi_context{:rs}` and `amount{:rs}` are then passed into `transfer(){:rs}` to execute the CPI.

</Tab>
<Tab>

The next approach uses `invoke(){:rs}` directly with `system_instruction::transfer(){:rs}`, the pattern typically seen in native Rust programs. The first approach is an abstraction over this one:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {8-9,11}
use anchor_lang::solana_program::{program::invoke, system_instruction};

pub fn sol_transfer(ctx: Context<SolTransfer>, amount: u64) -> Result<()> {
    let from_pubkey = ctx.accounts.sender.to_account_info();
    let to_pubkey = ctx.accounts.recipient.to_account_info();
    let program_id = ctx.accounts.system_program.to_account_info();

    let instruction =
        &system_instruction::transfer(&from_pubkey.key(), &to_pubkey.key(), amount);

    invoke(instruction, &[from_pubkey, to_pubkey, program_id])?;
    Ok(())
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

The instruction can also be built manually and passed into `invoke(){:rs}`. This is useful when no helper crate exists for the target program. The caller must specify the `AccountMeta{:rs}` entries and construct the instruction data buffer:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {21-25,28}
pub fn sol_transfer(ctx: Context<SolTransfer>, amount: u64) -> Result<()> {
    let from_pubkey = ctx.accounts.sender.to_account_info();
    let to_pubkey = ctx.accounts.recipient.to_account_info();
    let program_id = ctx.accounts.system_program.to_account_info();

    // Prepare instruction AccountMetas
    let account_metas = vec![
        AccountMeta::new(from_pubkey.key(), true),
        AccountMeta::new(to_pubkey.key(), false),
    ];

    // SOL transfer instruction discriminator
    let instruction_discriminator: u32 = 2;

    // Prepare instruction data
    let mut instruction_data = Vec::with_capacity(4 + 8);
    instruction_data.extend_from_slice(&instruction_discriminator.to_le_bytes());
    instruction_data.extend_from_slice(&amount.to_le_bytes());

    // Create instruction
    let instruction = Instruction {
        program_id: program_id.key(),
        accounts: account_metas,
        data: instruction_data,
    };

    // Invoke instruction
    invoke(&instruction, &[from_pubkey, to_pubkey, program_id])?;
    Ok(())
}
```

When building an instruction in Rust, use the following syntax to specify the `AccountMeta{:rs}` for each account:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
AccountMeta::new(account1_pubkey, true),           // writable, signer
AccountMeta::new(account2_pubkey, false),          // writable, not signer
AccountMeta::new_readonly(account3_pubkey, false), // not writable, not signer
AccountMeta::new_readonly(account4_pubkey, true),  // not writable, signer
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

A reference program containing all three approaches is available on [Solana Playground](https://beta.solpg.io/github.com/ZYJLiu/doc-examples/tree/main/cpi).

## Cross program invocations with PDA signers

A program can sign a CPI for a Program Derived Address (PDA) derived from its own program ID. The example below transfers SOL from a PDA to a recipient by passing the PDA's seeds into the CPI.

The `lib.rs{:file}` file declares a single `sol_transfer(){:rs}` instruction. The sender is a `pda_account{:rs}` derived from the seeds `b"pda"{:rs}` and the recipient's address:

<Code code={libPda} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="{10,17,26}" />

The `cpi.test.ts{:file}` file derives the PDA on the client, funds it, then invokes `sol_transfer(){:rs}` to move SOL back to the wallet via a CPI signed by the program:

```ts title="cpi.test.ts" showLineNumbers=false {1-4}
const [PDA] = PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync(
  [Buffer.from('pda'), wallet.publicKey.toBuffer()],
  program.programId,
)

it('Fund PDA with SOL', async () => {
  const transferInstruction = SystemProgram.transfer({
    fromPubkey: wallet.publicKey,
    toPubkey: PDA,
    lamports: transferAmount,
  })

  const transaction = new Transaction().add(transferInstruction)

  const transactionSignature = await sendAndConfirmTransaction(
    connection,
    transaction,
    [wallet.payer], // signer
  )

  console.log(
    `\nTransaction Signature:` +
      `https://solana.fm/tx/${transactionSignature}?cluster=devnet-solana`,
  )
})

it('SOL Transfer with PDA signer', async () => {
  const transactionSignature = await program.methods
    .solTransfer(new BN(transferAmount))
    .accounts({
      pdaAccount: PDA,
      recipient: wallet.publicKey,
    })
    .rpc()

  console.log(
    `\nTransaction Signature: https://solana.fm/tx/${transactionSignature}?cluster=devnet-solana`,
  )
})
```

The transaction details show the custom program invoked first (instruction 1), which then invokes the System Program (instruction 1.1):

![Transaction details](/docs/basics/cpi/transaction-details-pda.png)

### Example explanation

The sender is a PDA the program signs for. The seeds for the `pda_account{:rs}` are the hardcoded string `b"pda"{:rs}` and the address of the `recipient{:rs}`, so each recipient gets a unique PDA:

<Code code={libPda} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="{37} collapse={1-32}" />

The tabs below present two approaches to implementing the same PDA-signed CPI:

<Tabs groupId="language" items={['CpiContext{:rs}', 'invoke_signed(){:rs}']}>
<Tab>

The first approach uses [`CpiContext{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/context/struct.CpiContext.html), then attaches the signer seeds via `with_signer(){:rs}`:

<Code code={libPda} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="{15-17,26,28} collapse={1-9, 30-44}" />

The `signer_seeds{:rs}` slice contains the seeds plus the `bump_seed{:rs}`. The bump seed for a PDA validated by the `seeds{:rs}` constraint is available via `ctx.bumps{:rs}` followed by the field name.

When the CPI executes, the Solana runtime validates that the supplied seeds and the caller program ID derive a valid PDA, then adds that PDA as a signer on the invocation. This is the mechanism programs use to sign for PDAs derived from their program ID.

</Tab>
<Tab>

The first approach is a wrapper around `invoke_signed(){:rs}` paired with `system_instruction::transfer(){:rs}`. Calling `invoke_signed(){:rs}` directly produces an equivalent CPI:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {11,16}
use anchor_lang::solana_program::{program::invoke_signed, system_instruction};

pub fn sol_transfer(ctx: Context<SolTransfer>, amount: u64) -> Result<()> {
    let from_pubkey = ctx.accounts.pda_account.to_account_info();
    let to_pubkey = ctx.accounts.recipient.to_account_info();
    let program_id = ctx.accounts.system_program.to_account_info();

    let seed = to_pubkey.key();
    let bump_seed = ctx.bumps.pda_account;

    let signer_seeds: &[&[&[u8]]] = &[&[b"pda", seed.as_ref(), &[bump_seed]]];

    let instruction =
        &system_instruction::transfer(&from_pubkey.key(), &to_pubkey.key(), amount);

    invoke_signed(instruction, &[from_pubkey, to_pubkey, program_id], signer_seeds)?;
    Ok(())
}
```

The `signer_seeds{:rs}` are passed into `invoke_signed(){:rs}` as the third argument.

</Tab>
</Tabs>

A reference program containing both approaches is available on [Solana Playground](https://beta.solpg.io/github.com/ZYJLiu/doc-examples/tree/main/cpi-pda).

# idl.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/fundamentals/idl.mdx

title: Program IDL file
description: Learn about the Interface Description Language (IDL) file in Anchor, its purpose, benefits, and how it simplifies program-client interactions.

import Code from '@/components/code.astro'
import lib from './_idl/lib.rs?raw'
import idl from './_idl/idl.json?raw'
import client from './_idl/test.ts?raw'

An Interface Description Language (IDL) file for an Anchor program is a standardized JSON file describing the program's instructions and accounts. It gives client code generators a consistent format to consume so they can produce typed bindings for the program without reading its Rust source.

<Callout variant="tip" title="Where the IDL lives">
  The `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build` command writes the IDL to `/target/idl/<program-name>.json{:file}`.
</Callout>

The sections below show how the same program corresponds to its IDL and to a generated client.

## Program instructions

The `instructions` array in the IDL maps directly to the public functions inside the `#[program]{:rs}` module. Each entry records the accounts and arguments the instruction requires.

<Tabs items={['Program', 'IDL', 'Client']}>
<Tab>

The program below exposes a single `initialize(){:rs}` instruction along with the `Initialize{:rs}` accounts struct it expects:

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="{8-12,15-22} collapse={23-27}" />

</Tab>
<Tab>

The IDL captures that instruction in JSON, including its name, 8-byte discriminator, account list, and argument list:

<Code code={idl} lang="json" title="idl.json" meta="{11-12,14-27,30-33} collapse={3-8,37-56}" />

</Tab>
<Tab>

A generated client uses the IDL to build and send the transaction. The fluent builder mirrors the IDL fields, with `.initialize(data){:ts}` carrying the args and `.accounts({...}){:ts}` supplying the account list:

<Code code={client} lang="ts" title="test.ts" meta="{19-26}" />

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Program accounts

The `accounts` array in the IDL maps to every struct annotated with `#[account]{:rs}`. These structs define the data layout for accounts created and owned by the program.

<Tabs items={['Program', 'IDL', 'Client']}>
<Tab>

The program defines a `NewAccount{:rs}` struct with a single `data: u64{:rs}` field:

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="{24-27} collapse={4-23}" />

</Tab>
<Tab>

The IDL records the account's name and 8-byte discriminator under `accounts`, and its field layout under `types`:

<Code code={idl} lang="json" title="idl.json" meta="{39-40,44-55} collapse={3-36}" />

</Tab>
<Tab>

The client fetches the account by public key and deserializes it into the typed shape declared in the IDL:

<Code code={client} lang="ts" title="test.ts" meta="{29}" />

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Discriminators

Anchor assigns a unique 8-byte discriminator to every instruction and every account type. These bytes act as runtime identifiers so the program can dispatch the right instruction handler and so deserialization can verify the right account type.

A discriminator is the first 8 bytes of `SHA256("<prefix>:<name>"){:rs}`. The prefix is `global{:rs}` for instructions and `account{:rs}` for accounts. Since Anchor v0.30, every discriminator is included in the generated IDL.

<Callout variant="remark">
  You won't normally interact with discriminators directly. Anchor inserts them on the wire and
  verifies them on read. This section is here for reference.
</Callout>

<Tabs items={['Instructions', 'Accounts']}>
<Tab>

The instruction discriminator tells the program which handler to invoke. The Anchor client prepends it as the first 8 bytes of the instruction data:

```json title="idl.json"
"instructions": [
  {
    "name": "initialize",
    "discriminator": [175, 175, 109, 31, 13, 152, 155, 237],
     ...
  }
]
```

The discriminator is the first 8 bytes of `SHA256("global:<InstructionName>"){:rs}`. For `initialize{:rs}`:

```text
sha256("global:initialize")
```

The full hash, in hex:

```text
af af 6d 1f 0d 98 9b ed d4 6a 95 07 32 81 ad c2 1b b5 e0 e1 d7 73 b2 fb bd 7a b5 04 cd d4 aa 30
```

The leading 8 bytes become the discriminator:

```text
af = 175
af = 175
6d = 109
1f = 31
0d = 13
98 = 152
9b = 155
ed = 237
```

See the `gen_discriminator{:rs}` [source](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/syn/src/codegen/program/common.rs#L5-L22) for the implementation.

</Tab>
<Tab>

The account discriminator identifies the account type during deserialization. Anchor writes it to the first 8 bytes of account data when the account is created and checks it on every read:

```json title="idl.json"
"accounts": [
  {
    "name": "NewAccount",
    "discriminator": [176, 95, 4, 118, 91, 177, 125, 232]
  }
]
```

The discriminator is the first 8 bytes of `SHA256("account:<StructName>"){:rs}`. For `NewAccount{:rs}`:

```text
sha256("account:NewAccount")
```

The full hash, in hex:

```text
b0 5f 04 76 5b b1 7d e8 a1 93 57 2a d3 5e b1 ae e5 f0 69 e2 09 7e 5c d2 64 56 55 2a cb 4a e9 57
```

The leading 8 bytes become the discriminator:

```text
b0 = 176
5f = 95
04 = 4
76 = 118
5b = 91
b1 = 177
7d = 125
e8 = 232
```

See the [account discriminator source](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/account/src/lib.rs#L113-L125) for the implementation.

<Callout variant="note">
  Two programs that define accounts with the same struct name produce identical discriminators.
  Anchor avoids confusion at deserialization time by also verifying that the account is owned by the
  expected program.
</Callout>

</Tab>
</Tabs>

# pdas.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/fundamentals/pdas.mdx

title: Program derived address
description: Learn how to use Program Derived Addresses (PDAs) in Anchor programs to create deterministic account addresses.

import Code from '@/components/code.astro'
import lib from './_pda/lib.rs?raw'
import idl from './_pda/idl.json?raw'
import client from './_pda/test.ts?raw'
import logs from './_pda/logs.txt?raw'

<Callout variant="definition" title="Program Derived Address">
  A Program Derived Address (PDA) is a Solana account address derived deterministically from a list of seeds and a program ID. PDAs are off the Ed25519 curve so they have no associated private key, which is what allows the owning program to sign for them through `invoke_signed{:rs}` rather than a user-provided keypair.
</Callout>

Program Derived Addresses give programs a way to create accounts whose addresses are predictable from program-defined inputs.

## Anchor PDA constraints

PDA derivation in Anchor is expressed through account constraints. These constraints serve as security checks that ensure the correct address is derived.

The `seeds{:rs}` constraint takes an array of optional seeds used to derive the PDA, which can be static values or dynamic references to account data. The `bump{:rs}` constraint provides the bump seed that pushes the address off the Ed25519 curve so it's a valid PDA. The optional `seeds::program{:rs}` constraint specifies the program ID used for derivation and is only needed when deriving a PDA for a program other than the current one.

<Callout variant="note">
  The `seeds{:rs}` and `bump{:rs}` constraints are required to be used together.
</Callout>

### Usage examples

<Tabs items={['seeds{:rs}', 'bump{:rs}', 'seeds::program{:rs}', 'init{:rs}']}>
<Tab>

The `seeds{:rs}` constraint specifies the optional values used to derive the PDA.

#### No optional seeds

Use an empty array `[]{:rs}` to define a PDA without optional seeds:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {4}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    #[account(
        seeds = [],
        bump,
    )]
    pub pda_account: SystemAccount<'info>,
}
```

#### Single static seed

Pass a single byte literal to derive a PDA from a fixed value:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {4}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    #[account(
        seeds = [b"hello_world"],
        bump,
    )]
    pub pda_account: SystemAccount<'info>,
}
```

#### Multiple seeds and account references

The `seeds{:rs}` constraint accepts multiple values and can reference other account addresses or account data:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {5}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub signer: Signer<'info>,
    #[account(
        seeds = [b"hello_world", signer.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
    )]
    pub pda_account: SystemAccount<'info>,
}
```

The example above uses both a static seed (`b"hello_world"{:rs}`) and a dynamic seed (the signer's public key).

</Tab>
<Tab>

The `bump{:rs}` constraint specifies the bump seed used to derive the PDA.

#### Automatic bump calculation

When `bump{:rs}` is used without a value, the bump is automatically calculated each time the instruction is invoked:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {5}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    #[account(
        seeds = [b"hello_world"],
        bump,
    )]
    pub pda_account: SystemAccount<'info>,
}
```

#### Specify bump value

The bump value can be provided explicitly, which is useful for optimizing compute unit usage. This assumes that the PDA account has been created and the bump seed is stored as a field on an existing account:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {5}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    #[account(
        seeds = [b"hello_world"],
        bump = pda_account.bump_seed,
    )]
    pub pda_account: Account<'info, CustomAccount>,
}

#[account]
pub struct CustomAccount {
    pub bump_seed: u8,
}
```

By storing the bump value in the account's data, the program doesn't need to recalculate it, saving compute units. The saved bump value can live on the account itself or on another account.

</Tab>
<Tab>

The `seeds::program{:rs}` constraint specifies the program ID used to derive the PDA. Use it when an instruction needs to interact with PDA accounts created by another program:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {6}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    #[account(
        seeds = [b"hello_world"],
        bump,
        seeds::program = other_program.key(),
    )]
    pub pda_account: SystemAccount<'info>,
    pub other_program: Program<'info, OtherProgram>,
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

The `init{:rs}` constraint is commonly used with `seeds{:rs}` and `bump{:rs}` to create a new account whose address is a PDA. Under the hood, `init{:rs}` invokes the System Program to create the account:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {5-7}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub signer: Signer<'info>,
    #[account(
        init,
        payer = signer,
        space = 8 + 1,
        seeds = [b"hello_world", signer.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
    )]
    pub pda_account: Account<'info, CustomAccount>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}

#[account]
pub struct CustomAccount {
    pub bump_seed: u8,
}
```

<Callout variant="note">
  The `init{:rs}` constraint must be used with `payer{:rs}` and `space{:rs}`. The `payer{:rs}` specifies the account that will pay for the account creation. The `space{:rs}` specifies the bytes to allocate for the account (including the 8-byte discriminator).
</Callout>

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## PDA seeds in the IDL

PDA seeds defined in the `seeds{:rs}` constraint are included in the program's IDL file. This allows the Anchor client to automatically resolve account addresses using these seeds when constructing instructions.

<Tabs items={['Program', 'IDL', 'Client']}>
<Tab>

The program below defines a `pda_account{:rs}` using a static seed (`b"hello_world"{:rs}`) and the signer's public key as a dynamic seed:

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="{18}" />

</Tab>
<Tab>

The IDL records the PDA seeds declared on the account. The static seed `b"hello_world"{:rs}` is converted to byte values, and the dynamic seed is included as a reference to the signer account:

<Code code={idl} lang="json" title="idl.json" meta="{16-17,20-21} collapse={3-8}" />

</Tab>
<Tab>

The Anchor client uses the IDL to automatically resolve the PDA address. The provider wallet acts as the signer, and its public key becomes the dynamic seed for derivation, so the client can call the instruction without explicitly deriving the PDA:

<Code code={client} lang="ts" title="test.ts" meta="{13}" />

When the instruction is invoked, the PDA is printed to program logs:

<Code code={logs} lang="text" meta="{3}" />

</Tab>
</Tabs>

# program-structure.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/fundamentals/program-structure.mdx

title: Program structure
description: Learn about the structure of Anchor programs, including key macros and their roles in simplifying Solana program development.

import Code from '@/components/code.astro'
import lib from './_lib.rs?raw'

The Anchor framework uses [Rust macros](https://rust-book.cs.brown.edu/ch20-05-macros.html) to reduce boilerplate and enforce the security checks every Solana program needs. Four macros form the backbone of any Anchor program.

- [`declare_id!(){:rs}`](#declare_id) sets the program's on-chain address.
- [`#[program]{:rs}`](#program) annotates the module containing the program's instruction handlers.
- [`#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}`](#deriveaccounts) declares the accounts an instruction requires.
- [`#[account]{:rs}`](#account) defines a custom account data type owned by the program.

## Example program

The following program exposes a single `initialize(){:rs}` instruction that creates a `NewAccount{:rs}` and stores a `u64{:rs}` value in it. Every macro discussed in this page appears in the file:

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" />

## `declare_id!(){:rs}`

The [`declare_id!(){:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/macro.declare_id.html) macro embeds the program's on-chain address, known as the program ID, into the compiled binary:

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="{3} collapse={4-27}" />

By default, the program ID is the public key of the keypair at `/target/deploy/<program_name>-keypair.json{:file}`. To rewrite the `declare_id!(){:rs}` string to match the on-disk keypair, run `$ <blue>anchor</blue> keys sync`.

<Callout variant="tip" title="When to run anchor keys sync">
  Run `$ <blue>anchor</blue> keys sync` after cloning a repository. The committed program ID will
  not match the keypair generated by `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build` on your machine, so syncing
  prevents a mismatch between the declared ID and the deployed binary.
</Callout>

## `#[program]{:rs}`

The [`#[program]{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/attr.program.html) attribute annotates the module that contains the program's instruction handlers. Every public function inside this module becomes an instruction callable from clients:

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="collapse={1-4, 14-27}" />

### Instruction context

The first parameter of every instruction handler is a [`Context<T>{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/context/struct.Context.html), where `T{:rs}` is a struct that implements the [`Accounts{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/trait.Accounts.html) trait. The context exposes everything the handler needs from the runtime beyond its own arguments:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
pub struct Context<'a, 'b, 'c, 'info, T: Bumps> {
    /// Currently executing program id.
    pub program_id: &'a Pubkey,
    /// Deserialized accounts.
    pub accounts: &'b mut T,
    /// Remaining accounts given but not deserialized or validated.
    /// Be very careful when using this directly.
    pub remaining_accounts: &'c [AccountInfo<'info>],
    /// Bump seeds found during constraint validation.
    pub bumps: T::Bumps,
}
```

Access each field on the `ctx{:rs}` parameter using dot notation:

- `ctx.accounts{:rs}` contains the deserialized, validated accounts declared by `T{:rs}`.
- `ctx.program_id{:rs}` is the public key of the currently executing program.
- `ctx.remaining_accounts{:rs}` holds any accounts passed beyond the `Accounts{:rs}` struct. These are neither deserialized nor validated, so use with caution.
- `ctx.bumps{:rs}` exposes bump seeds discovered during PDA constraint validation.

Any additional parameters on the handler function become instruction arguments supplied by the client at invocation time. In the example, `data: u64{:rs}` is an argument:

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="collapse={1-7, 13-27}" />

## `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}`

The [`#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/derive.Accounts.html) macro generates the `Accounts{:rs}` trait implementation for a struct, letting Anchor deserialize and validate every account passed into an instruction:

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="collapse={1-14, 23-27}" />

Each field maps to one account the instruction requires. Field names are arbitrary but should describe the role the account plays in the instruction.

### Account validation

Account validation is the first line of defense against malicious input. Anchor enforces two complementary mechanisms, typically used together.

- **[Account constraints](/docs/v1/reference/account-constraints/)** declared in the `#[account(...)]{:rs}` attribute enforce runtime conditions on each account. Common constraints include `init{:rs}`, `mut{:rs}`, `has_one{:rs}`, `seeds{:rs}`, and `constraint{:rs}`.
- **[Account types](/docs/v1/programs/account-types/)** specified in the field's type enforce static expectations about what kind of account the client must pass. Examples include `Account<T>{:rs}`, `Signer{:rs}`, `Program<T>{:rs}`, and `UncheckedAccount{:rs}`.

Once validation succeeds, the handler accesses accounts through `ctx<cyan>.</cyan>accounts<cyan>.</cyan><dim><field_name></dim>`.

## `#[account]{:rs}`

The [`#[account]{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/attr.account.html) attribute turns a plain struct into an Anchor-managed account type. The macro derives implementations for several traits, summarized in the [full reference](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/attr.account.html):

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="collapse={1-23}" />

Accounts created with this type are owned by the program identified in `declare_id!(){:rs}`. Anchor writes an 8-byte discriminator to the front of the account at initialization and checks it on every read, and serializes and deserializes the account's data through Borsh.

### Account discriminator

The discriminator is the first 8 bytes of `SHA256("account:<StructName>"){:rs}`, stored as the leading 8 bytes of every account created with this type ([source](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/account/src/lib.rs#L113-L130)). It serves two purposes.

- On **initialization**, Anchor writes the discriminator as the first 8 bytes of the account's data.
- On **deserialization**, Anchor compares the stored discriminator against the one expected by the target type. A mismatch fails the instruction before the handler runs, preventing the client from substituting an account of the wrong type.

<Callout variant="important" title="Reserving discriminator space">
  Every `init{:rs}` constraint must allocate 8 extra bytes of space for the discriminator in addition to the account's own fields. In the example below, `space = 8 + 8{:rs}` covers 8 bytes for the discriminator plus 8 bytes for the `data: u64{:rs}` field.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(init, payer = signer, space = 8 + 8)]
pub new_account: Account<'info, NewAccount>,
```

</Callout>

# installation.mdx

title: Installation

## Quick installation

A single script installs Rust, the Solana CLI, the Anchor CLI, Surfpool, Node.js, and Yarn in one go.

<Tabs groupId="os" items={["Mac/Linux", "Windows"]}>

</Tab>
<Tab>

</Callout>

Install WSL from PowerShell with `$ <blue>wsl</blue> <dim>--install</dim>`, restart your machine, and create a default Ubuntu user when prompted. Then open the Ubuntu terminal and run:

```console
$ <blue>curl</blue> <dim>--proto</dim> '=https' <dim>--tlsv1.2</dim> <dim>-sSfL</dim> https://solana-install.solana.workers.dev | <blue>bash</blue>
```

</Tab>

```console
Installation complete. Please restart your terminal to apply all changes.
```

## Manual installation

The walkthroughs below install each dependency individually.

<Tabs groupId="os" items={["Mac", "Linux", "Windows"]}>

<Tab>

<Steps>

<Step title="Install Rust">

Solana programs are written in [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/). The recommended installer is [rustup](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install):

```console
$ <blue>curl</blue> <dim>--proto</dim> '=https' <dim>--tlsv1.2</dim> <dim>-sSf</dim> https://sh.rustup.rs | <blue>sh</blue> <dim>-s</dim> -- <dim>-y</dim>
```

A successful install prints:

```console
<bold>Rust is installed now. Great!</bold>

To get started you may need to restart your current shell.
This would reload your <bold>PATH</bold> environment variable to include
Cargo's bin directory ($HOME/.cargo/bin).
```

Reload your `PATH` to pick up the `~/.cargo/bin/{:dir}` directory:

```console
$ . "$HOME/.cargo/env"
```

Verify the install with `$ <blue>rustc</blue> <dim>--version</dim>`:

```console
$ <blue>rustc</blue> <dim>--version</dim>
rustc 1.95.0 (59807616e 2026-04-14)
```

</Step>

<Step title="Install Solana CLI">

The Solana CLI ships the tools required to build and deploy Solana programs. Install with the official script:

```console
$ <blue>sh</blue> <dim>-c</dim> "$(curl <dim>-sSfL</dim> https://release.anza.xyz/stable/install)"
```

<Callout variant="tip" title="Pinning a version">
  Replace `stable` with a release tag (e.g. `v2.0.3{:bash}`) or one of `beta` / `edge`. All available releases are listed on the [Agave GitHub repo](https://github.com/anza-xyz/agave/releases).
</Callout>

On macOS with `zsh`, append the `PATH` export to `~/.zshrc{:file}` so it persists between shell sessions:

```console
$ <blue>echo</blue> 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/solana/install/active_release/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
```

Reload the shell with `$ <blue>source</blue> ~/.zshrc`, then verify with `$ <blue>solana</blue> <dim>--version</dim>`:

```console
$ <blue>solana</blue> <dim>--version</dim>
solana-cli 3.1.14 (src:ca2c682f; feat:534737035, client:Agave)
```

<Callout>
  Agave is the validator client from [Anza](https://www.anza.xyz/), formerly known as the Solana
  Labs validator client.
</Callout>

To update the Solana CLI later, run `$ <blue>agave-install</blue> update`.

</Step>

<Step title="Install Anchor CLI">

[Anchor](https://www.anchor-lang.com/) is a framework for developing Solana programs that uses Rust macros to reduce boilerplate. The recommended install path is the Anchor Version Manager (AVM), which tracks multiple Anchor versions and simplifies upgrades.

<Tabs groupId="anchor" items={["AVM", "Without AVM"]}>

```console
avm 1.0.1
```

```console

$ <blue>avm</blue> use latest
```

<Callout variant="tip" title="Pinning a version">
  To install a specific version, pass the version number:

```bash
$ <blue>avm</blue> install 1.0.1
$ <blue>avm</blue> use 1.0.1
```

</Callout>

<Callout variant="note">
  `$ <blue>avm</blue> use` is required after every `$ <blue>avm</blue> install` to activate the
  version on your system.
</Callout>

</Tab>
<Tab>

```console
$ <blue>cargo</blue> install <dim>--git</dim> https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor <dim>--tag</dim> v1.0.1 anchor-cli <dim>--locked</dim>
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

Verify with `$ <blue>anchor</blue> <dim>--version</dim>`:

```console

anchor-cli 1.0.1
```

</Step>

<Step title="Install Node.js and Yarn (optional)">

Node.js and Yarn are required for `$ <blue>anchor</blue> init` and the TypeScript-based test templates (`mocha`, `jest`). The default `litesvm` template runs entirely in Rust, so Node and Yarn are not needed for day-to-day work once a project is initialized.

<Tabs groupId="node-yarn" items={["Node", "Yarn"]}>

Install [Node Version Manager (nvm)](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm):


Restart your terminal, then verify nvm is on your `PATH` with `$ <blue>command</blue> <dim>-v</dim> nvm`. Install Node and verify with `$ <blue>node</blue> <dim>--version</dim>`:

```console
v23.7.0
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

Install Yarn globally via npm:


Verify with `$ <blue>yarn</blue> <dim>--version</dim>`:

```console

1.22.1
```
