<Callout variant="warning" title="Common build errors">
  These errors can surface on any OS when running `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build` or `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test`.

  <Callout variant="problem" title='"error: not a directory"' defaultOpen={false}>
    ```bash
    error: not a directory: '.../solana-release/bin/sdk/sbf/dependencies/platform-tools/rust/lib'
    ```

    Try these solutions in order:

    1. Force install platform tools:

        ```bash
        $ <blue>cargo</blue> build-sbf <dim>--force-tools-install</dim>
        ```

    2. If that doesn't work, clear the Solana cache:

        ```bash
        $ <blue>rm</blue> <dim>-rf</dim> ~/.cache/solana/*
        ```

  </Callout>

  <Callout variant="problem" title="lock file version 4 requires -Znext-lockfile-bump" defaultOpen={false}>
    Change the `version` field of `Cargo.lock{:file}` from `4` to `3`:

    ```yml title="Cargo.lock" showLineNumbers={false} add={2} del={1}
    version = 4
    version = 3
    ```

    Then retry `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build`. See [anchor#3392](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/issues/3392) for background.

  </Callout>

  <Callout variant="problem" title='"Permission denied" or "No such file or directory"' defaultOpen={false}>
    On Linux or WSL, `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` may fail with `Permission denied (os error 13)` or `No such file or directory (os error 2)` when Node.js or Yarn are not installed. Install both using the steps above and retry.
  </Callout>
</Callout>

## Solana CLI basics

The following steps cover the most common Solana CLI commands. These work identically on every operating system.

<Steps>
<Step>

### Solana config

Inspect the current config with `$ <blue>solana</blue> config get`:

```console
$ <blue>solana</blue> config get
<bold>Config File:</bold> /Users/test/.config/solana/cli/config.yml
<bold>RPC URL:</bold> https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com <italic></italic>
<bold>WebSocket URL:</bold> wss://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com/ <italic>(computed)</italic>
<bold>Keypair Path:</bold> /Users/test/.config/solana/id.json <italic></italic>
<bold>Commitment:</bold> confirmed <italic></italic>
```

`RPC URL` and `WebSocket URL` identify the cluster the CLI targets. The default is `mainnet-beta`. To switch clusters, use either the long (`--url`) or short (`-u<letter>`) form:

| Cluster | Long | Short |
| --- | --- | --- |
| mainnet-beta | `$ <blue>solana</blue> config set <dim>--url</dim> mainnet-beta` | `$ <blue>solana</blue> config set <dim>-um</dim>` |
| devnet | `$ <blue>solana</blue> config set <dim>--url</dim> devnet` | `$ <blue>solana</blue> config set <dim>-ud</dim>` |
| localhost | `$ <blue>solana</blue> config set <dim>--url</dim> localhost` | `$ <blue>solana</blue> config set <dim>-ul</dim>` |
| testnet | `$ <blue>solana</blue> config set <dim>--url</dim> testnet` | `$ <blue>solana</blue> config set <dim>-ut</dim>` |

`Keypair Path` points at the default wallet used to sign transactions and pay fees, located at `~/.config/solana/id.json{:file}`. The next step generates a keypair at that location.

</Step>
<Step>

### Create wallet

The Solana CLI requires a keypair wallet funded with SOL to interact with the network. Generate one at the default keypair path:

```console
$ <blue>solana-keygen</blue> new
Generating a new keypair

For added security, enter a BIP39 passphrase

NOTE! This passphrase improves security of the recovery seed phrase NOT the
keypair file itself, which is stored as insecure plain text

BIP39 Passphrase (empty for none):

Wrote new keypair to /Users/test/.config/solana/id.json
===========================================================================
pubkey: 8dBTPrjnkXyuQK3KDt9wrZBfizEZijmmUQXVHpFbVwGT
===========================================================================
Save this seed phrase and your BIP39 passphrase to recover your new keypair:
cream bleak tortoise ocean nasty game gift forget fancy salon mimic amazing
===========================================================================
```

<Callout variant="note">
  If a wallet already exists at the default path, `$ <blue>solana-keygen</blue> new` will not
  overwrite it unless you pass `<dim>--force</dim>`.
</Callout>

Print the public key of the wallet with `$ <blue>solana</blue> address`:

```console
$ <blue>solana</blue> address
8dBTPrjnkXyuQK3KDt9wrZBfizEZijmmUQXVHpFbVwGT
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Airdrop SOL

Your wallet needs SOL to pay transaction fees and deployment costs. Point the CLI at devnet:

```console {3,4}
$ <blue>solana</blue> config set <dim>-ud</dim>
<bold>Config File:</bold> /Users/test/.config/solana/cli/config.yml
<bold>RPC URL:</bold> https://api.devnet.solana.com <italic></italic>
<bold>WebSocket URL:</bold> wss://api.devnet.solana.com/ <italic>(computed)</italic>
<bold>Keypair Path:</bold> /Users/test/.config/solana/id.json <italic></italic>
<bold>Commitment:</bold> confirmed <italic></italic>
```

Then request an airdrop with `$ <blue>solana</blue> airdrop 2`.

<Callout variant="important" title="Rate limits">
  The public faucet rate-limits airdrops per IP. If you see this error, use the [Solana Web Faucet](https://faucet.solana.com) instead.

```bash
$ <blue>solana</blue> airdrop 2
Requesting airdrop of 2 SOL
Error: airdrop request failed. This can happen when the rate limit is reached.
```

</Callout>

Check the wallet balance with `$ <blue>solana</blue> balance`:

```console
$ <blue>solana</blue> balance
2 SOL
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Run local validator

The Solana CLI ships with a built-in [test validator](https://docs.anza.xyz/cli/examples/test-validator) for local development.

<Callout variant="tip" title="localhost cluster">
  Point the CLI at the local validator before sending commands with `$ <blue>solana</blue> config
  set <dim>-ul</dim>`.
</Callout>

In a separate terminal, start the validator with `$ <blue>solana-test-validator</blue>`.

</Step>
</Steps>

## Anchor CLI basics

The following steps cover the most common Anchor CLI commands. For full reference documentation, see the [Anchor docs](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs).

<Steps>
<Step>

### Initialize project

Create a new Anchor project with `$ <blue>anchor</blue> init <dim><project-name></dim>`.

This creates a directory named `<dim><project-name></dim>` and scaffolds a modular Rust program. Tests default to the [LiteSVM](https://github.com/LiteSVM/litesvm) crate. To choose a different test template (`mollusk`, `mocha`, `jest`, etc.), pass `<dim>--test-template</dim>`:

```console
$ <blue>anchor</blue> init <dim><project-name></dim> <dim>--test-template</dim> mollusk
```

<Callout variant="note">
  The default modular layout separates instructions, state, constants, and errors into distinct
  files. This structure is recommended for any codebase you plan to maintain. See the [project file
  structure](/docs/v1/get-started/local-development/#project-file-structure) for details.
</Callout>

Navigate into the new directory with `$ <blue>cd</blue> <dim><project-name></dim>`.

</Step>

<Step>

### Build program

Compile the program with `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build`. The compiled artifact is written to `target/deploy/`.

</Step>
<Step>

### Deploy program

Deploy the program to the cluster specified in [`Anchor.toml`](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/references/anchor-toml) with `$ <blue>anchor</blue> deploy`.

</Step>
<Step>

### Test program

Run the project's test suite with `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test`.

<Callout>
  `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` builds, deploys, and runs the tests. When `cluster = "Localnet"{:toml}` in `Anchor.toml`, it also starts a local validator, runs the tests against it, and shuts it down afterward.
</Callout>

</Step>
</Steps>

## Shell completions

`anchor` and `avm` can generate completions for `bash`, `fish`, and `zsh`.

<Tabs groupId="shell-completions" items={["bash", "fish", "zsh"]}>
  <Tab>
    ```bash
    $ <blue>mkdir</blue> <dim>-p</dim> $HOME/.local/share/bash-completion/completions
    $ <blue>anchor</blue> completions bash > $HOME/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/anchor
    $ <blue>avm</blue> completions bash > $HOME/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/avm
    $ <blue>exec</blue> bash
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab>
    ```bash
    $ <blue>mkdir</blue> <dim>-p</dim> $HOME/.config/fish/completions
    $ <blue>anchor</blue> completions fish > $HOME/.config/fish/completions/anchor.fish
    $ <blue>avm</blue> completions fish > $HOME/.config/fish/completions/avm.fish
    $ <blue>source</blue> $HOME/.config/fish/config.fish
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab>
    First ensure the following is in your `~/.zshrc{:file}` (skip this if using `oh-my-zsh`):

    ```bash
    autoload <dim>-U</dim> compinit
    compinit <dim>-i</dim>
    ```

    Then generate the completions:

    ```bash
    $ <blue>anchor</blue> completions zsh | <blue>sudo</blue> tee /usr/local/share/zsh/site-functions/_anchor
    $ <blue>avm</blue> completions zsh | <blue>sudo</blue> tee /usr/local/share/zsh/site-functions/_avm
    $ <blue>exec</blue> zsh
    ```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

# local-development.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/get-started/local-development.mdx

title: Local development
description: Learn how to build Solana programs using the Anchor framework on your local machine.

The Anchor framework streamlines the process of writing, testing, and deploying Solana programs. This guide walks through creating a new project, iterating on it locally, and deploying it to a public cluster.

## Prerequisites

Before you begin, ensure you have Rust, the Solana CLI, and the Anchor CLI installed. See the [Installation](/docs/v1/get-started/installation/) page for step-by-step instructions.

## Getting started

<Steps>

<Step>

### Create a new project

To start a new project, use the `$ anchor init <dim><project-name></dim>` (for our examples, we will use `my-project` for `<dim><project-name></dim>`). This creates a new directory with the specified name and scaffolds a default program and test file. By default, Anchor generates a modular program structure to promote better code organization and maintainability:

<FileTree>
  <Dir name="programs">
    <Dir name="my-project">
      <Dir name="src">
        <Dir name="instructions" comment="Instruction handler implementations">
          <File name="initialize.rs" />
        </Dir>
        <File name="constants.rs" comment="Program constants" />
        <File name="error.rs" comment="Custom error definitions" />
        <File name="instructions.rs" comment="Instructions module root" />
        <File name="lib.rs" comment="Main entry point" highlight />
        <File name="state.rs" comment="Account state module root" />
      </Dir>
    </Dir>
  </Dir>
</FileTree>

`lib.rs{:file}` is the program's entry point. It declares each submodule and wires instruction handlers into the `#[program]{:rs}` block. The `declare_id!(){:rs}` value is your program's on-chain address (by default, the public key of the keypair at `/target/deploy/my_project-keypair.json{:file}`).

<Tabs items={["lib.rs", "instructions/initialize.rs"]}>
<Tab>
```rust
pub mod constants;
pub mod error;
pub mod instructions;
pub mod state;

use anchor_lang::prelude::\*;

pub use constants::_; pub use instructions::_; pub use state::\*;

declare_id!("3ynNB373Q3VAzKp7m4x238po36hjAGFXFJB4ybN2iTyg");

#[program] pub mod my_project { use super::\*;

    pub fn initialize(ctx: Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
        initialize::handler(ctx)
    }

}

````
</Tab>
<Tab>
```rust
use anchor_lang::prelude::*;

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize {}

pub fn handler(ctx: Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
    msg!("Greetings from: {:?}", ctx.program_id);
    Ok(())
}
````

</Tab>
</Tabs>

<Callout variant="tip" title="Single-file template">
  For quick prototypes, skip the module split with `$ anchor init <dim>--template</dim> single`. The
  modular layout is recommended for anything you plan to maintain.
</Callout>

### Test file

Anchor generates a test file alongside the program. TypeScript is the default. To get a Rust test instead, pass `<dim>--test-template</dim> rust` ([Rust client](/docs/v1/clients/rust/)) or `<dim>--test-template</dim> mollusk` ([Mollusk](/docs/v1/testing/mollusk/)).

<Tabs items={["TypeScript", "Rust"]}>
<Tab>
Located at `/tests/my-project.ts{:file}`. Invokes the `initialize(){:ts}` instruction via the generated client:

```ts title="tests/my-project.ts"
import * as anchor from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { Program } from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { MyProject } from '../target/types/my_project'

describe('my-project', () => {
  anchor.setProvider(anchor.AnchorProvider.env())
  const program = anchor.workspace.myProject as Program<MyProject>

  it('Is initialized!', async () => {
    const tx = await program.methods.initialize().rpc()
    console.log('Your transaction signature', tx)
  })
})
```

</Tab>
<Tab>
Located at `/tests/src/test_initialize.rs{:file}`. Uses `<yellow>anchor_client</yellow>` to call the program against localnet:

```rust title="tests/src/test_initialize.rs"
use std::str::FromStr;

use anchor_client::{
    solana_sdk::{
        commitment_config::CommitmentConfig, pubkey::Pubkey, signature::read_keypair_file,
    },
    Client, Cluster,
};

#[test]
fn test_initialize() {
    let program_id = "3ynNB373Q3VAzKp7m4x238po36hjAGFXFJB4ybN2iTyg";
    let anchor_wallet = std::env::var("ANCHOR_WALLET").unwrap();
    let payer = read_keypair_file(&anchor_wallet).unwrap();

    let client = Client::new_with_options(Cluster::Localnet, &payer, CommitmentConfig::confirmed());
    let program_id = Pubkey::from_str(program_id).unwrap();
    let program = client.program(program_id).unwrap();

    let tx = program
        .request()
        .accounts(my_program::accounts::Initialize {})
        .args(my_program::instruction::Initialize {})
        .send()
        .expect("");

    println!("Your transaction signature {}", tx);
}
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

</Step>
<Step>

### Build the program

Run `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build` to compile the program. The compiled artifact is written to `/target/deploy/my_project.so{:file}`. This binary is the executable bytecode uploaded to the chain during deployment.

</Step>
<Step>

### Test the program

Run `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` to execute the test suite against a local cluster.

With the default `Anchor.toml{:file}` targeting `localnet`, this starts a local validator, builds and deploys the program, runs the tests in `/tests{:dir}`, then shuts the validator down.

<Callout variant="tip" title="Persistent validator for debugging">
  To keep the validator running between iterations so you can inspect accounts and transaction logs
  on the [Solana Explorer](https://explorer.solana.com/?cluster=custom) while developing, start `${' '}
  <blue>solana-test-validator</blue>` in a separate terminal. From there, pass `
  <dim>--skip-local-validator</dim>` to `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test{' '}
  <dim>--skip-local-validator</dim>` so tests attach to the running instance instead of spawning
  their own.
</Callout>

</Step>
<Step>

### Deploy to Devnet

By default, the `Anchor.toml{:file}` config file in an Anchor project specifies the localnet cluster. To deploy your program to devnet, change the `cluster{:toml}` value to `"Devnet"{:js}`:

```toml title="Anchor.toml" showLineNumbers add={12} del={11}
[toolchain]

[features]
resolution = true
skip-lint = false

[programs.localnet]
my_program = "3ynNB373Q3VAzKp7m4x238po36hjAGFXFJB4ybN2iTyg"

[provider]
cluster = "Localnet"
cluster = "Devnet"
wallet = "~/.config/solana/id.json"

[scripts]
test = "yarn run ts-mocha -p ./tsconfig.json -t 1000000 tests/**/*.ts"
```

<Callout variant="important" title="Funding the deploy wallet">
  Deploying to devnet requires your wallet to have enough SOL to cover the deployment cost. You can
  get devnet SOL using the [Web Faucet](https://faucet.solana.com/).
</Callout>

Run `$ <blue>anchor</blue> deploy` to push the program to the cluster specified in `Anchor.toml{:file}`. The `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` command also respects this setting.

To deploy to mainnet, update the `Anchor.toml{:file}` file to specify the mainnet cluster:

```toml title="Anchor.toml" add={3} del={2}
[provider]
cluster = "Devnet"
cluster = "Mainnet"
wallet = "~/.config/solana/id.json"
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Update the program

Solana programs are updated in place by redeploying a new build to the same program ID. After making code changes, run `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build` to produce an updated `.so{:file}` artifact, then `$ <blue>anchor</blue> deploy` to upload it.

</Step>
<Step>

### Close the program

Closing a program reclaims the SOL allocated to its on-chain account. Run `$ solana program close <dim><program-id></dim>` to retire it:

```console
$ <blue>solana</blue> program close <dim><program-id></dim> --bypass-warning
```

The program ID is permanently retired once closed. You cannot redeploy to the same address.

</Step>

</Steps>

## Project file structure

A default Anchor workspace contains the following top-level files and directories. A single workspace may host multiple programs under `programs/{:dir}`, though `$ <blue>anchor</blue> init` generates one by default.

{/* cspell:disable */}

<FileTree>
  <Dir name=".anchor" open={false}>
    <File name="program-logs" comment="Transaction logs from the last test run" />
  </Dir>
  <Dir name="app" comment="Frontend code (empty by default)" />
  <Dir name="migrations" comment="Deployment scripts (optional)" />
  <Dir name="programs" comment="Anchor programs">
    <Dir name="[project-name]">
      <Dir name="src">
        <Dir name="instructions">
          <File name="initialize.rs" />
        </Dir>
        <File name="constants.rs" />
        <File name="error.rs" />
        <File name="instructions.rs" comment="Instructions module root" />
        <File name="lib.rs" comment="Program entry point and #[program] module" />
        <File name="state.rs" comment="Account state module root" />
      </Dir>
      <File name="Cargo.toml" />
    </Dir>
  </Dir>
  <Dir name="target" comment="Build outputs">
    <Dir name="deploy" comment="Program binary (.so) and keypair" />
    <Dir name="idl" comment="JSON IDL generated from the program" />
    <Dir name="types" comment="TypeScript types derived from the IDL" />
  </Dir>
  <Dir name="tests" comment="Integration tests (TypeScript by default)">
    <File name="[project-name].ts" />
  </Dir>
  <File name="Anchor.toml" comment="Workspace config (clusters, wallet, scripts)" />
  <File name="Cargo.toml" comment="Rust workspace manifest" />
  <File name="package.json" comment="Node dependencies for TypeScript tests" />
</FileTree>

{/* cspell:enable */}

# solana-playground.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/get-started/solana-playground.mdx

title: Solana Playground
description: Learn how to build your first Solana program using the Anchor framework directly in your browser.

In this section, we'll build, deploy, and test a simple Solana program using the Anchor framework. By the end, you'll have deployed your first program to the Solana blockchain!

Solana Playground (Solpg) is a browser-based development environment that lets you develop, deploy, and test Solana programs without installing anything locally.

## Getting started

Open a new tab in your web browser and navigate to https://beta.solpg.io/.

<Steps>

<Step>
### Create Playground wallet

If you're new to Solana Playground, the first step is to create your Playground wallet. This wallet lets you interact with the Solana network right from your browser.

Click the "Not connected" button at the bottom left of the screen.

![Not Connected](/docs/quickstart/pg-not-connected.png)

You'll see an option to save your wallet's keypair. Optionally save it for backup, then click "Continue".

![Create Playground Wallet](/docs/quickstart/pg-create-wallet.png)

You should now see your wallet's address, SOL balance, and connected cluster (Devnet by default) at the bottom of the window.

![Connected](/docs/quickstart/pg-connected.png)

<Callout>
  Your Playground wallet is saved in your browser's local storage. Clearing your browser cache will
  remove it.
</Callout>

Some useful terms:

<Callout variant="definition" title="Wallet address">
  A public key that serves as your unique identity on the Solana blockchain. Just like an email
  address is used to receive emails, your wallet address is used to receive SOL.
</Callout>

<Callout variant="definition" title="Connection cluster">
  A network of Solana nodes (computers running the Solana validator client). Devnet is the cluster
  used for developer testing.
</Callout>

</Step>
<Step>

### Get Devnet SOL

Before we start building, we need some devnet SOL. SOL is required to create accounts on the network and to pay transaction fees.

In the Playground terminal, run `$ <blue>solana</blue> airdrop 5`. If the airdrop command doesn't work (due to rate limits), use the [Web Faucet](https://faucet.solana.com/). Enter your wallet address (found at the bottom of the Playground screen), select an amount, and click "Confirm Airdrop".

![Faucet Airdrop](/docs/quickstart/faucet-airdrop.gif)

</Step>

<Step>

### Create Anchor project

Open https://beta.solpg.io in a new browser tab. Click "Create a new project", enter a project name, select Anchor as the framework, then click "Create".

![New Project](/docs/quickstart/pg-new-project.gif)

You'll see a new project with the program code in `src/lib.rs{:file}`:

```rust title="lib.rs"
use anchor_lang::prelude::*;

// This is your program's public key and it will update
// automatically when you build the project.
declare_id!("11111111111111111111111111111111");

#[program]
mod hello_anchor {
    use super::*;
    pub fn initialize(ctx: Context<Initialize>, data: u64) -> Result<()> {
        ctx.accounts.new_account.data = data;
        msg!("Changed data to: {}!", data); // Message will show up in the tx logs
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize<'info> {
    // We must specify the space in order to initialize an account.
    // First 8 bytes are default account discriminator,
    // next 8 bytes come from NewAccount.data being type u64.
    // (u64 = 64 bits unsigned integer = 8 bytes)
    #[account(init, payer = signer, space = 8 + 8)]
    pub new_account: Account<'info, NewAccount>,
    #[account(mut)]
    pub signer: Signer<'info>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}

#[account]
pub struct NewAccount {
    data: u64
}
```

<Callout variant="explanation" title="Code explanation" defaultOpen={false}>

- `declare_id!(){:rs}` specifies the on-chain address of your program. It will be automatically updated when you build.

  ```rust startLineNumber={5}
  declare_id!("11111111111111111111111111111111");
  ```

- `#[program]{:rs}` annotates a module containing the program's instruction handlers.

  ```rust startLineNumber={7}
  #[program]
  mod hello_anchor {
      use super::*;
      pub fn initialize(ctx: Context<Initialize>, data: u64) -> Result<()> {
          ctx.accounts.new_account.data = data;
          msg!("Changed data to: {}!", data);
          Ok(())
      }
  }
  ```

  The `initialize(){:rs}` instruction takes a `Context<Initialize>{:rs}` (the required accounts) and a `data: u64{:rs}` parameter. It stores the value and logs it.

- `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` annotates a struct that declares the accounts required by an instruction. Field types and constraints let Anchor auto-generate security checks.

  ```rust startLineNumber={16}
  #[derive(Accounts)]
  pub struct Initialize<'info> {
      #[account(init, payer = signer, space = 8 + 8)]
      pub new_account: Account<'info, NewAccount>,
      #[account(mut)]
      pub signer: Signer<'info>,
      pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
  }
  ```

- `#[account]{:rs}` annotates a struct that defines the data layout of an account owned by this program.

  ```rust startLineNumber={30}
  #[account]
  pub struct NewAccount {
    data: u64
  }
  ```

</Callout>

</Step>
<Step>
### Build and deploy program

To build the program, run `$ <blue>build</blue>` in the terminal:

```console title="Terminal"
$ <blue>build</blue>
<bold><blue>Building...</blue></bold>
<bold><green>Build successful.</green></bold> Completed in 1.46s.
```

Notice that the address in `declare_id!(){:rs}` has been updated. This is your program's on-chain address.

Once built, run `$ <blue>deploy</blue>` to deploy to the network (devnet by default). Make sure you have enough SOL first:

```console title="Terminal"
$ <blue>deploy</blue>
<bold><blue>Deploying...</blue></bold> This could take a while depending on the program size and network conditions.
<bold><yellow>Warning</yellow></bold>: 8 transactions not confirmed, retrying...
<bold><green>Deployment successful.</green></bold> Completed in 18s.
```

You can also use the `Build` and `Deploy` buttons on the left-side panel.

![Build and Deploy](/docs/quickstart/pg-build-deploy.png)

</Step>
<Step>
### Test program

The starter code includes a test file at `tests/anchor.test.ts{:file}` that shows how to invoke the `initialize(){:ts}` instruction from the client:

```ts title="anchor.test.ts"
// No imports needed: web3, anchor, pg and more are globally available

describe('Test', () => {
  it('initialize', async () => {
    // Generate keypair for the new account
    const newAccountKp = new web3.Keypair()

    // Send transaction
    const data = new BN(42)
    const txHash = await pg.program.methods
      .initialize(data)
      .accounts({
        newAccount: newAccountKp.publicKey,
        signer: pg.wallet.publicKey,
        systemProgram: web3.SystemProgram.programId,
      })
      .signers([newAccountKp])
      .rpc()
    console.log(`Use 'solana confirm -v ${txHash}' to see the logs`)

    // Confirm transaction
    await pg.connection.confirmTransaction(txHash)

    // Fetch the created account
    const newAccount = await pg.program.account.newAccount.fetch(newAccountKp.publicKey)

    console.log('On-chain data is:', newAccount.data.toString())

    // Check whether the data on-chain is equal to local 'data'
    assert(data.eq(newAccount.data))
  })
})
```

Run the tests with `$ <blue>test</blue>`:

```console title="Terminal"
$ <blue>test</blue>
<bold><blue>Running tests...</blue></bold>
  <bold>anchor.test.ts:</bold>
  Test
    Use 'solana confirm -v h6JV2E4HKiFMHLVQaFDRma9h8K3RBHKTb7vMiT8cLBsVQoyBnZmF6wD5cSrEG1ai6Bu7x7ibJakAyqXE45BJti' to see the logs
    On-chain data is: 42
    <green>✓</green> initialize <dim>(2139ms)</dim>
  <bold><green>1 passing</green></bold> <dim>(2s)</dim>
```

You can also click the `Test` button on the left-side panel.

![Run Test](/docs/quickstart/pg-test.png)

# index.mdx

title: Anchor v1
description: Anchor is a development framework for building secure Solana programs (smart contracts).
autoCards: false

Anchor v1 is the stable, published Anchor framework for building Solana programs and clients. It simplifies the process of writing, testing, deploying, and interacting with Solana programs.

The Anchor framework helps developers build production-ready applications faster while reducing potential vulnerabilities through built-in security features.

<Callout variant="note" title="Anchor v2 alpha">
  Anchor v2 (`anchor-lang-v2`) is in alpha on the [`anchor-next`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/tree/anchor-next) branch. v2 is built on pinocchio and `#![no_std]{:rs}`, producing up to 95% smaller binaries and 3.0 to 50.4 times fewer CU per instruction in checked-in benchmarks. The v1 path documented here remains the stable, published path. See the [v2 docs](/docs/v2/) for the alpha reference.
</Callout>

# account-space-and-realloc.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/programs/account-space-and-realloc.mdx

title: Account space
description: Reference for calculating account data size requirements by Rust type.

The `space{:rs}` constraint on an [`init{:rs}`](/docs/v1/programs/account-types/) account must reserve enough bytes for the account's serialized data plus an 8-byte Anchor discriminator. The table below lists the byte size of each Rust type Anchor supports.

This applies to accounts that use Borsh serialization. Accounts annotated with `#[account(zero_copy)]{:rs}` use `repr(C){:rs}` with a pointer cast, so the C layout rules apply instead.

## Type chart

| Type | Space in bytes | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bool{:rs}` | 1 | One byte even though only 1 bit is meaningful |
| `u8{:rs}` / `i8{:rs}` | 1 |  |
| `u16{:rs}` / `i16{:rs}` | 2 |  |
| `u32{:rs}` / `i32{:rs}` | 4 |  |
| `u64{:rs}` / `i64{:rs}` | 8 |  |
| `u128{:rs}` / `i128{:rs}` | 16 |  |
| `f32{:rs}` | 4 | Serialization fails for `NaN{:rs}` |
| `f64{:rs}` | 8 | Serialization fails for `NaN{:rs}` |
| `[T; N]{:rs}` | `space(T) * N{:rs}` | e.g. `[u16; 32]{:rs}` is `2 * 32 = 64{:rs}` |
| `Pubkey{:rs}` | 32 |  |
| `Vec<T>{:rs}` | `4 + space(T) * length{:rs}` | 4-byte length prefix plus elements |
| `String{:rs}` | `4 + len{:rs}` | 4-byte length prefix plus UTF-8 bytes |
| `Option<T>{:rs}` | `1 + space(T){:rs}` | 1-byte tag plus the inner value |
| `enum{:rs}` | `1 + largest variant{:rs}` | e.g. `enum E { A, B { val: u8 }, C { val: u16 } }{:rs}` is `1 + 2 = 3{:rs}` |

## Manual calculation

Add up the field sizes and store the total as a `MAX_SIZE{:rs}` constant on the struct, then reference it in the `space{:rs}` constraint along with 8 bytes for the discriminator:

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false {"up to 10 players":5-6}
#[account]
pub struct MyData {
    pub val: u16,
    pub state: GameState,

    pub players: Vec<Pubkey>,
}

impl MyData {
    pub const MAX_SIZE: usize = 2 + (1 + 32) + (4 + 10 * 32);
}

#[derive(AnchorSerialize, AnchorDeserialize, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum GameState {
    Active,
    Tie,
    Won { winner: Pubkey },
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InitializeMyData<'info> {
    #[account(init, payer = signer, space = 8 + MyData::MAX_SIZE)]
    pub acc: Account<'info, MyData>,
    #[account(mut)]
    pub signer: Signer<'info>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}
```

## `#[derive(InitSpace)]{:rs}`

The [`InitSpace{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/derive.InitSpace.html) derive macro generates an `INIT_SPACE{:rs}` associated constant that holds the struct's serialized size. The struct does not need `#[account]{:rs}` for the derive to work:

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
#[account]
#[derive(InitSpace)]
pub struct ExampleAccount {
    pub data: u64,
    #[max_len(50)]
    pub string_one: String,
    #[max_len(10, 5)]
    pub nested: Vec<Vec<u8>>,
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize<'info> {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer<'info>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
    #[account(init, payer = payer, space = 8 + ExampleAccount::INIT_SPACE)]
    pub data: Account<'info, ExampleAccount>,
}
```

`InitSpace{:rs}` follows three rules:

- Always add 8 bytes to `space{:rs}` for the discriminator. The macro does not include it.
- `#[max_len]{:rs}` declares the maximum number of _elements_, not bytes. On `Vec<u32>{:rs}`, `#[max_len(10)]{:rs}` reserves 10 elements × 4 bytes plus a 4-byte length prefix for 44 bytes total.
- Nested vectors take one length per dimension. `#[max_len(10, 5)]{:rs}` on `Vec<Vec<u8>>{:rs}` allows up to 10 outer elements, each holding up to 5 inner.

---

# account-types.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/programs/account-types.mdx

title: Account types
description: 'Reference for the Anchor account types used in the `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` struct.'

Anchor's [account types](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/accounts/index.html) are the type wrappers used in fields of a `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` struct. Each type performs a specific runtime check on the account before the instruction handler runs, complementing the [account constraints](/docs/v1/reference/account-constraints/) declared in the `#[account(...)]{:rs}` attribute.

For background on how account types fit into instruction validation, see [account validation](/docs/v1/fundamentals/program-structure/#deriveaccounts).

## `Account<'info, T>{:rs}`

[`Account<'info, T>{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/accounts/account/struct.Account.html) wraps an `AccountInfo{:rs}`, deserializes its data into the type `T{:rs}`, and verifies that the account is owned by the program declared in `declare_id!(){:rs}`:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {3}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub account: Account<'info, CustomAccountType>,
}

#[account]
pub struct CustomAccountType {
    data: u64,
}
```

## `Signer<'info>{:rs}`

[`Signer<'info>{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/accounts/signer/struct.Signer.html) verifies that the account signed the transaction. Use it when the handler needs proof of authorization but does not read or write the account's data:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {3}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub signer: Signer<'info>,
}
```

## `SystemAccount<'info>{:rs}`

[`SystemAccount<'info>{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/accounts/system_account/struct.SystemAccount.html) verifies that the account is owned by the System Program:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {3}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub account: SystemAccount<'info>,
}
```

## `Program<'info, T>{:rs}`

[`Program<'info, T>{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/accounts/program/struct.Program.html) verifies that the account is the executable program identified by `T{:rs}`. Use it for any program invoked through CPI:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {5-6}
use anchor_spl::token::Token;

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
    pub token_program: Program<'info, Token>,
}
```

## `Interface<'info, T>{:rs}`

[`Interface<'info, T>{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/accounts/interface/struct.Interface.html) verifies that the account is one of a known set of programs sharing an interface. The canonical use is accepting either the SPL Token program or Token-2022:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {6}
// Token program or Token2022 program
use anchor_spl::token_interface::TokenInterface;

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub program: Interface<'info, TokenInterface>,
}
```

## `InterfaceAccount<'info, T>{:rs}`

[`InterfaceAccount<'info, T>{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/accounts/interface_account/struct.InterfaceAccount.html) deserializes account data into `T{:rs}` and verifies ownership against any program in the interface set. Use it for token accounts and mints that may be owned by either SPL Token or Token-2022:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {6-8}
// Token program or Token2022 program Mint/TokenAccount
use anchor_spl::token_interface::{Mint, TokenAccount, TokenInterface};

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub mint: InterfaceAccount<'info, Mint>,
    pub token: InterfaceAccount<'info, TokenAccount>,
    pub program: Interface<'info, TokenInterface>,
}
```

## `Sysvar<'info, T>{:rs}`

[`Sysvar<'info, T>{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/accounts/sysvar/struct.Sysvar.html) verifies that the account is the Solana sysvar identified by `T{:rs}` and deserializes its data:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {4-5}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub rent: Sysvar<'info, Rent>,
    pub clock: Sysvar<'info, Clock>,
}
```

## `UncheckedAccount<'info>{:rs}`

[`UncheckedAccount<'info>{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/accounts/unchecked_account/struct.UncheckedAccount.html) is an explicit wrapper around `AccountInfo{:rs}` that performs no checks. Every field of this type requires a `/// CHECK:{:rs}` doc comment explaining why the lack of validation is safe:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {4}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    /// CHECK: No checks are performed
    pub account: UncheckedAccount<'info>,
}
```

## `AccountInfo<'info>{:rs}`

[`AccountInfo<'info>{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/solana-program/latest/solana_program/account_info/struct.AccountInfo.html) is the raw Solana account type and performs no checks. Prefer `UncheckedAccount{:rs}` instead, which makes the lack of validation explicit and requires a `/// CHECK:{:rs}` comment:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {4}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    /// CHECK: AccountInfo is an unchecked account
    pub unchecked_account: AccountInfo<'info>,
}
```

## `Box<Account<'info, T>>{:rs}`

`Box{:rs}` moves an account to the heap, freeing space on the BPF stack. Use it when the wrapped type is large enough to risk a stack overflow during instruction execution:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {3}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub account: Box<Account<'info, AccountType>>,
}
```

## `Option<Account<'info, T>>{:rs}`

Wrapping an account type in `Option{:rs}` marks it as optional. Clients pass `None{:rs}` to omit the account, and the handler accesses it as `Option<T>{:rs}`:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {3}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub account: Option<Account<'info, AccountType>>,
}
```

## `AccountLoader<'info, T>{:rs}`

[`AccountLoader<'info, T>{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/accounts/account_loader/struct.AccountLoader.html) provides on-demand zero-copy deserialization for accounts marked with `#[account(zero_copy)]{:rs}`. The handler calls `load(){:rs}` or `load_mut(){:rs}` to obtain a reference into the account's bytes without copying:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {3}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub account: AccountLoader<'info, ZeroCopyAccountType>,
}

#[account(zero_copy)]
pub struct ZeroCopyAccountType {
    data: u64,
}
```

## `Migration<'info, From, To>{:rs}`

`Migration<'info, From, To>{:rs}` handles schema migrations between two account types. The account must deserialize as `From{:rs}` on entry and is migrated to `To{:rs}` before serialization on exit. Pair it with the `realloc{:rs}` constraint to resize the account when the new schema is larger.

The type performs three checks: ownership matches `From::owner(){:rs}`, the account is initialized (not a zero-lamport System Program account), and its data deserializes as `From{:rs}`:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {16-22}
use anchor_lang::prelude::*;

#[account]
pub struct AccountV1 {
    pub data: u64,
}

#[account]
pub struct AccountV2 {
    pub data: u64,
    pub new_field: u64,
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct MigrateAccount<'info> {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer<'info>,
    #[account(
        mut,
        realloc = 8 + AccountV2::INIT_SPACE,
        realloc::payer = payer,
        realloc::zero = false
    )]
    pub my_account: Migration<'info, AccountV1, AccountV2>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}
```

### Usage patterns

Call `migrate(){:rs}` for an explicit one-shot migration. Old fields remain accessible through `Deref{:rs}` until the call:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
let old_data = ctx.accounts.my_account.data;

ctx.accounts.my_account.migrate(AccountV2 {
    data: old_data,
    new_field: 42,
})?;
```

Call `into_inner(){:rs}` for an idempotent migration that returns a reference to the new data, migrating only if needed:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
let migrated = ctx.accounts.my_account.into_inner(AccountV2 {
    data: ctx.accounts.my_account.data,
    new_field: ctx.accounts.my_account.data * 2,
});
msg!("New field: {}", migrated.new_field);
```

Call `into_inner_mut(){:rs}` for the same idempotent migration with a mutable reference:

```rust
let migrated = ctx.accounts.my_account.into_inner_mut(AccountV2 {
    data: ctx.accounts.my_account.data,
    new_field: 0,
});
migrated.new_field = 42;
```

---

# errors.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/programs/errors.mdx

title: Custom errors
description: Learn how to implement custom error handling in Anchor programs.

import Code from '@/components/code.astro'
import lib from './_errors/lib.rs?raw'
import client from './_errors/test.ts?raw'
import errorResponse from './_errors/error-response.txt?raw'

All instruction handlers in Anchor programs return a custom `Result<T>{:rs}` type that allows handling successful execution with `Ok(T){:rs}` and error cases with `Err(Error){:rs}`:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
pub fn custom_instruction(ctx: Context<CustomInstruction>) -> Result<()> {
    // --snip--
    Ok(())
}
```

The `Result<T>{:rs}` type in Anchor programs is a type alias that wraps the standard Rust `Result<T, E>{:rs}`. `T{:rs}` represents the successful return type, while `E{:rs}` is Anchor's custom `Error{:rs}` type:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
pub type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, error::Error>;
```

## Anchor error

When an error occurs in an Anchor program, it returns a custom [`Error{:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/error/enum.Error.html) type defined as:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Error {
    AnchorError(Box<AnchorError>),
    ProgramError(Box<ProgramErrorWithOrigin>),
}
```

The `Error{:rs}` type has two variants.

`ProgramErrorWithOrigin{:rs}` wraps a standard Solana `ProgramError{:rs}` from the `solana_program` crate:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct ProgramErrorWithOrigin {
    pub program_error: ProgramError,
    pub error_origin: Option<ErrorOrigin>,
    pub compared_values: Option<ComparedValues>,
}
```

`AnchorError{:rs}` represents errors defined by the Anchor framework:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct AnchorError {
    pub error_name: String,
    pub error_code_number: u32,
    pub error_msg: String,
    pub error_origin: Option<ErrorOrigin>,
    pub compared_values: Option<ComparedValues>,
}
```

An `AnchorError{:rs}` falls into one of two categories. Internal Anchor errors are built into the framework and defined in the `ErrorCode{:rs}` enum. Custom program errors are program-specific errors that developers define for their own validation logic.

The `error_code_number{:rs}` from an `AnchorError{:rs}` follows this numbering scheme:

| Error code | Description                           |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------- |
| >= 100     | Instruction error codes               |
| >= 1000    | IDL error codes                       |
| >= 2000    | Constraint error codes                |
| >= 3000    | Account error codes                   |
| >= 4100    | Misc error codes                      |
| = 5000     | Deprecated error code                 |
| >= 6000    | Starting point for custom user errors |

## Usage

Anchor provides a convenient way to define custom errors through the `#[error_code]{:rs}` attribute. When an enum is annotated with `#[error_code]{:rs}`, Anchor assigns each variant an error code starting from 6000, generates the error-handling boilerplate, and enables custom error messages via the `#[msg(...)]{:rs}` attribute:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[error_code]
pub enum MyError {
    #[msg("My custom error message")]
    MyCustomError,
    #[msg("My second custom error message")]
    MySecondCustomError,
}
```

### `err!(){:rs}`

To throw an error, use the [`err!(){:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/macro.err.html) macro. Under the hood, `err!(){:rs}` uses the `error!(){:rs}` macro to construct an `AnchorError{:rs}`:

```rust title="lib.rs" {5} showLineNumbers=false
#[program]
mod hello_anchor {
    use super::*;
    pub fn set_data(ctx: Context<SetData>, data: MyAccount) -> Result<()> {
        if data.data >= 100 {
            return err!(MyError::DataTooLarge);
        }
        ctx.accounts.my_account.set_inner(data);
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[error_code]
pub enum MyError {
    #[msg("MyAccount may only hold data below 100")]
    DataTooLarge
}
```

### `require!(){:rs}`

The [`require!(){:rs}`](https://docs.rs/anchor-lang/latest/anchor_lang/macro.require.html) macro provides a more concise way to handle error conditions. It combines a condition check with returning an error if the condition is false:

```rust title="lib.rs" {5} showLineNumbers=false
#[program]
mod hello_anchor {
    use super::*;
    pub fn set_data(ctx: Context<SetData>, data: MyAccount) -> Result<()> {
        require!(data.data < 100, MyError::DataTooLarge);
        ctx.accounts.my_account.set_inner(data);
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[error_code]
pub enum MyError {
    #[msg("MyAccount may only hold data below 100")]
    DataTooLarge
}
```

Anchor provides several `require{:rs}` macros for different validation needs:

- `require!(){:rs}` ensures a condition is true, otherwise returns the given error.
- `require_eq!(){:rs}` ensures two non-pubkey values are equal.
- `require_neq!(){:rs}` ensures two non-pubkey values are not equal.
- `require_keys_eq!(){:rs}` ensures two pubkeys are equal.
- `require_keys_neq!(){:rs}` ensures two pubkeys are not equal.
- `require_gt!(){:rs}` ensures the first non-pubkey value is greater than the second.
- `require_gte!(){:rs}` ensures the first non-pubkey value is greater than or equal to the second.

## Example

The program below validates that an input amount falls within an acceptable range. It defines two custom error variants with messages and uses `require!(){:rs}` to enforce the bounds:

<Tabs items={['Program', 'Client']}>
<Tab>

<Code code={lib} lang="rust" title="lib.rs" meta="{10-11,21-25}" />

</Tab>
<Tab>

<Code code={client} lang="ts" title="test.ts" />

</Tab>
</Tabs>

When a program error occurs, Anchor's TypeScript client SDK returns a detailed [error response](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/ts/packages/anchor/src/error.ts#L51-L71) containing information about the error:

<Code code={errorResponse} lang="text" />

For a more comprehensive example, see the [errors test program](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/master/tests/errors/programs/errors/src/lib.rs) in the Anchor repository.

# events.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/programs/events.mdx

title: Emit events
description: 'Learn how to emit events in Anchor programs using `emit!(){:rs}` and `emit_cpi!(){:rs}` macros.'

Anchor exposes two macros for emitting events from a program. The `emit!(){:rs}` macro writes events to program logs, which is the simpler path but can be truncated by some data providers. The `emit_cpi!(){:rs}` macro emits events through a Cross Program Invocation (CPI) by including the event data in the inner instruction's data, which is less likely to be truncated.

<Callout variant="remark" title="Why two macros exist">
  `emit_cpi!(){:rs}` was introduced as an alternative to program logs, which can sometimes be truncated by data providers. CPI instruction data is less likely to be truncated, but this approach incurs additional compute costs from the Cross Program Invocation.
</Callout>

<Callout variant="tip" title="Geyser gRPC for production">
  For more robust event delivery, consider geyser gRPC services from
  [Triton](https://docs.triton.one/project-yellowstone/dragons-mouth-grpc-subscriptions) or
  [Helius](https://docs.helius.dev/data-streaming/geyser-yellowstone).
</Callout>

## `emit!(){:rs}`

The `emit!(){:rs}` macro emits events through program logs. When called, it:

1. Uses the [`sol_log_data(){:rs}`](https://github.com/anza-xyz/agave/blob/c2b350023ba849d1b33142592264aaa51fcb7f1e/sdk/program/src/log.rs#L115-L124) syscall to write the data to program logs.
2. Encodes the event data as a base64 string prefixed with `Program data:`.

To receive emitted events in a client application, use the `addEventListener(){:ts}` method on the `Program{:ts}` instance. It parses and decodes event data from the program logs automatically.

Example usage:

<Tabs items={["Program", "Client"]}>
<Tab>

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_lang::prelude::*;

declare_id!("8T7MsCZyzxboviPJg5Rc7d8iqEcDReYR2pkQKrmbg7dy");

#[program]
pub mod event {
    use super::*;

    pub fn emit_event(_ctx: Context<EmitEvent>, input: String) -> Result<()> {
        emit!(CustomEvent { message: input });
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct EmitEvent {}

#[event]
pub struct CustomEvent {
    pub message: String,
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

```ts title="test.ts" showLineNumbers=false
import * as anchor from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { Program } from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { Event } from '../target/types/event'

describe('event', () => {
  // Configure the client to use the local cluster.
  anchor.setProvider(anchor.AnchorProvider.env())

  const program = anchor.workspace.event as Program<Event>

  it('Emits custom event', async () => {
    // Set up listener before sending transaction
    const listenerId = program.addEventListener('customEvent', (event) => {
      // Do something with the event data
      console.log('Event Data:', event)
    })

    // Message to be emitted in the event
    const message = 'Hello, Solana!'
    // Send transaction
    await program.methods.emitEvent(message).rpc()

    // Remove listener
    await program.removeEventListener(listenerId)
  })
})
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

{/* cspell:disable */}

The program logs below show the emitted event data, base64-encoded as `Zb1eU3aiYdwOAAAASGVsbG8sIFNvbGFuYSE=`:

```text
Log Messages:
  Program 8T7MsCZyzxboviPJg5Rc7d8iqEcDReYR2pkQKrmbg7dy invoke [1]
  Program log: Instruction: EmitEvent
  Program data: Zb1eU3aiYdwOAAAASGVsbG8sIFNvbGFuYSE=
  Program 8T7MsCZyzxboviPJg5Rc7d8iqEcDReYR2pkQKrmbg7dy consumed 1012 of 200000 compute units
  Program 8T7MsCZyzxboviPJg5Rc7d8iqEcDReYR2pkQKrmbg7dy success
```

{/* cspell:enable */}

<Callout variant="danger" title="RPC providers may truncate program logs">
  Ensure the RPC provider you use does not truncate program logs from the transaction data. A silent
  truncation will drop emitted events on the floor without surfacing an error to the listener.
</Callout>

## `emit_cpi!(){:rs}`

The `emit_cpi!(){:rs}` macro emits events through Cross Program Invocations to the program itself. The event data is encoded and included in the CPI's instruction data instead of the program logs.

To emit events through CPIs, enable the `event-cpi` feature in `Cargo.toml{:file}`:

```toml title="Cargo.toml"
[dependencies]
anchor-lang = { version = "1.0.1", features = ["event-cpi"] }
```

Example usage:

<Tabs items={["Program", "Client"]}>
<Tab>

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_lang::prelude::*;

declare_id!("2cDQ2LxKwQ8fnFUz4LLrZ157QzBnhPNeQrTSmWcpVin1");

#[program]
pub mod event_cpi {
    use super::*;

    pub fn emit_event(ctx: Context<EmitEvent>, input: String) -> Result<()> {
        emit_cpi!(CustomEvent { message: input });
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[event_cpi]
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct EmitEvent {}

#[event]
pub struct CustomEvent {
    pub message: String,
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

```ts title="test.ts" showLineNumbers=false
import * as anchor from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { Program } from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { EventCpi } from '../target/types/event_cpi'

describe('event-cpi', () => {
  // Configure the client to use the local cluster.
  anchor.setProvider(anchor.AnchorProvider.env())
  const program = anchor.workspace.eventCpi as Program<EventCpi>

  it('Emits custom event', async () => {
    const message = 'Hello, Solana!'
    const transactionSignature = await program.methods.emitEvent(message).rpc()

    // Wait for the transaction to be confirmed
    await program.provider.connection.confirmTransaction(transactionSignature, 'confirmed')

    // Fetch the transaction data
    const transactionData = await program.provider.connection.getTransaction(transactionSignature, {
      commitment: 'confirmed',
    })

    // Decode the event data from the CPI instruction data
    const eventIx = transactionData.meta.innerInstructions[0].instructions[0]
    const rawData = anchor.utils.bytes.bs58.decode(eventIx.data)
    const base64Data = anchor.utils.bytes.base64.encode(rawData.subarray(8))
    const event = program.coder.events.decode(base64Data)
    console.log(event)
  })
})
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

The `#[event_cpi]{:rs}` attribute must be added to the `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` struct for any instruction that emits events with `emit_cpi!(){:rs}`. The attribute injects the additional accounts required for the self-CPI:

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
#[event_cpi]
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct RequiredAccounts {
  // --snip--
}
```

To get the emitted event data in a client application, fetch the transaction by signature and parse the event data from the CPI instruction data:

```ts title="test.ts" showLineNumbers=false
// 1. Fetch the full transaction data using the transaction signature
const transactionData = await program.provider.connection.getTransaction(transactionSignature, {
  commitment: 'confirmed',
})

// 2. Extract the CPI (inner instruction) that contains the event data
const eventIx = transactionData.meta.innerInstructions[0].instructions[0]

// 3. Decode the event data
const rawData = anchor.utils.bytes.bs58.decode(eventIx.data)
const base64Data = anchor.utils.bytes.base64.encode(rawData.subarray(8))
const event = program.coder.events.decode(base64Data)
console.log(event)
```

In the example, the encoded event data is `"data": "6AJcBqZP8afBKheoif1oA6UAiLAcqYr2RaR33pFnEY1taQp"` inside the `innerInstructions` array.

# zero-copy.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v1/programs/zero-copy.mdx

title: Zero copy
description: Use Anchor's zero-copy deserialization to handle large account data in Solana programs.

## Overview

Zero-copy deserialization lets programs read and write account data directly from memory without copying or deserializing it. This approach is the practical way to handle large accounts on Solana.

### Why use zero-copy?

Traditional account deserialization with `Account<T>{:rs}` copies the account data into a heap-allocated struct. The copied struct is constrained by Solana's 4KB stack and 32KB heap limits, the deserialization step consumes significant compute units, and the same data ends up duplicated in memory.

`AccountLoader<T>{:rs}` casts the raw account bytes directly to the struct type without copying, supports accounts up to 10MB (10,485,760 bytes), reduces compute usage by roughly 90% for large accounts, and modifies account data in place.

<Callout variant="intuition" title="Why the cast is sound">
  The struct annotated with `#[account(zero_copy)]{:rs}` is `#[repr(C)]{:rs}` and `Pod{:rs}`, so its in-memory layout matches the raw bytes byte-for-byte. The "deserialize" step that `Account<T>{:rs}` performs is therefore unnecessary work; the bytes already are the struct, and `AccountLoader<T>{:rs}` exposes that fact through a checked pointer cast.
</Callout>

### Performance comparison

| Account Size | `Account<T>{:rs}` | `AccountLoader<T>{:rs}` | Improvement |
| ------------ | ----------------- | ----------------------- | ----------- |
| 1 KB         | ~8,000 CU         | ~1,500 CU               | 81% faster  |
| 10 KB        | ~50,000 CU        | ~5,000 CU               | 90% faster  |
| 100 KB       | Too large         | ~12,000 CU              | Possible    |
| 1 MB         | Impossible        | ~25,000 CU              | Possible    |

### When to use zero-copy

Reach for zero-copy when accounts exceed roughly 1KB, when fields are large fixed-size arrays such as orderbooks or event queues, when instructions run at high frequency, or when the program is compute-sensitive.

A regular `Account<T>{:rs}` is the better choice for small accounts under 1KB, dynamic data structures (`Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, `HashMap{:rs}`), schemas that change frequently, and simple state that does not require optimization.

## Usage

Add the `bytemuck` crate to the program's dependencies. The `min_const_generics` feature lets zero-copy types contain arrays of any size:

```toml title="Cargo.toml" showLineNumbers=false
[dependencies]
bytemuck = { version = "1.20.0", features = ["min_const_generics"] }
anchor-lang = "1.0.1"
```

### Define a zero-copy account

To define an account type that uses zero-copy, annotate the struct with [`#[account(zero_copy)]{:rs}`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/62865c636aecc6974fc9cfebfc6cf08ca4f0bb72/lang/attribute/account/src/lib.rs#L419):

```rust showLineNumbers=false {1}
#[account(zero_copy)]
pub struct Data {
    // 10240 bytes - 8 bytes account discriminator
    pub data: [u8; 10232],
}
```

The `#[account(zero_copy)]{:rs}` attribute automatically implements the traits required for zero-copy deserialization:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {1-4}
#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
#[derive(bytemuck::Zeroable)]
#[derive(bytemuck::Pod)]
#[repr(C)]
struct Data {
  // --snip--
}
```

### Use `AccountLoader<'info, T>{:rs}` for zero-copy accounts

To deserialize a zero-copy account, use `AccountLoader<'info, T>{:rs}`, where `T` is the zero-copy account type defined with the `#[account(zero_copy)]{:rs}` attribute:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {3}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct InstructionAccounts<'info> {
    pub zero_copy_account: AccountLoader<'info, Data>,
}
```

#### Initialize a zero-copy account

The `init{:rs}` constraint can be used with `AccountLoader{:rs}` to create a zero-copy account:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {4-7}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize<'info> {
    #[account(
        init,
        // 10240 bytes is max space to allocate with init constraint
        space = 8 + 10232,
        payer = payer,
    )]
    pub data_account: AccountLoader<'info, Data>,
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer<'info>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}
```

<Callout variant="note">
  The `init{:rs}` constraint is limited to allocating a maximum of 10240 bytes due to CPI limitations. Under the hood, `init{:rs}` invokes the System Program to create the account.
</Callout>

When initializing a zero-copy account for the first time, use `load_init(){:rs}` to get a mutable reference to the account data. The `load_init(){:rs}` method also sets the account discriminator:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {2}
pub fn initialize(ctx: Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
    let account = &mut ctx.accounts.data_account.load_init()?;
    account.data = [1; 10232];
    Ok(())
}
```

For accounts that require more than 10240 bytes, use the `zero{:rs}` constraint instead of `init{:rs}`. The `zero{:rs}` constraint verifies the account has not been initialized by checking that its discriminator has not been set:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {3}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize<'info> {
    #[account(zero)]
    pub data_account: AccountLoader<'info, Data>,
}
```

With the `zero{:rs}` constraint, the account must first be created in a separate instruction by directly calling the System Program. This bypasses the CPI allocation limit and supports accounts up to Solana's maximum size of 10MB (10_485_760 bytes).

Just as before, `load_init(){:rs}` returns a mutable reference and sets the account discriminator. Since 8 bytes are reserved for the discriminator, the maximum data size is 10_485_752 bytes (10MB - 8 bytes):

```rust showLineNumbers=false {2}
pub fn initialize(ctx: Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
    let account = &mut ctx.accounts.data_account.load_init()?;
    account.data = [1; 10_485_752];
    Ok(())
}
```

#### Update a zero-copy account

Use `load_mut(){:rs}` to obtain mutable access to an existing zero-copy account:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {3}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Update<'info> {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub data_account: AccountLoader<'info, Data>,
}
```

```rust showLineNumbers=false {2}
pub fn update(ctx: Context<Update>) -> Result<()> {
    let account = &mut ctx.accounts.data_account.load_mut()?;
    account.data = [2; 10232];
    Ok(())
}
```

#### Read a zero-copy account

Use `load(){:rs}` for read-only access to the account data:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct ReadOnly<'info> {
    pub data_account: AccountLoader<'info, Data>,
}
```

```rust showLineNumbers=false {2}
pub fn read_only(ctx: Context<ReadOnly>) -> Result<()> {
    let account = &ctx.accounts.data_account.load()?;
    msg!("First 10 bytes: {:?}", &account.data[..10]);
    Ok(())
}
```

## Common patterns

### Nested zero-copy types

For types used inside zero-copy accounts, use `#[zero_copy]{:rs}` (without `account`):

```rust showLineNumbers=false {8}
#[account(zero_copy)]
pub struct OrderBook {
    pub market: Pubkey,
    pub bids: [Order; 1000],
    pub asks: [Order; 1000],
}

#[zero_copy]
pub struct Order {
    pub trader: Pubkey,
    pub price: u64,
    pub quantity: u64,
}
```

### Accessor methods for byte arrays

Zero-copy uses `#[repr(packed)]{:rs}`, which makes direct field references unsafe. The `#[accessor]{:rs}` attribute generates safe getter and setter methods:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {4}
#[account(zero_copy)]
pub struct Config {
    pub authority: Pubkey,
    #[accessor(Pubkey)]
    pub secondary_authority: [u8; 32],
}

// Usage:
let config = &mut ctx.accounts.config.load_mut()?;
let secondary = config.get_secondary_authority();
config.set_secondary_authority(&new_authority);
```

### Zero-copy with PDAs

Zero-copy accounts work seamlessly with program-derived addresses:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {5}
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct CreatePdaAccount<'info> {
    #[account(
        init,
        seeds = [b"data", authority.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
        payer = authority,
        space = 8 + std::mem::size_of::<Data>(),
    )]
    pub data_account: AccountLoader<'info, Data>,
    #[account(mut)]
    pub authority: Signer<'info>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}
```

### Separate types for RPC parameters

Zero-copy types cannot derive `AnchorSerialize{:rs}` or `AnchorDeserialize{:rs}`. Define separate types for instruction parameters:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {8}
// For zero-copy account
#[zero_copy]
pub struct Event {
    pub from: Pubkey,
    pub data: u64,
}

#[derive(AnchorSerialize, AnchorDeserialize)]
pub struct EventParams {
    pub from: Pubkey,
    pub data: u64,
}

impl From<EventParams> for Event {
    fn from(params: EventParams) -> Self {
        Event {
            from: params.from,
            data: params.data,
        }
    }
}
```

## Common pitfalls

### Forgetting the account discriminator

<Callout variant="danger" title="Always reserve 8 bytes for the discriminator">
  Skipping the 8-byte discriminator from a `space{:rs}` calculation produces an account that the Anchor runtime cannot validate, since the discriminator check expects the first 8 bytes to be the account-type marker. The bug usually surfaces only on first read, where the runtime returns a deserialization error that looks unrelated to the allocation site.
</Callout>

```rust showLineNumbers=false {5}
// Wrong - missing discriminator
space = std::mem::size_of::<Data>()

// Correct - includes discriminator
space = 8 + std::mem::size_of::<Data>()
```

### Using dynamic types

<Callout variant="danger" title="Zero-copy fields must be `Copy{:rs}`">
  Zero-copy requires every field to be a `Copy{:rs}` type. `Vec<T>{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, and other heap-backed collections store a pointer rather than the data itself, so reading them through a zero-copy cast points at memory the program does not own. The compiler rejects these fields outright; if a derive error mentions `Pod{:rs}` or `Copy{:rs}`, the fix is to switch to a fixed-size array.
</Callout>

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(zero_copy)]
pub struct InvalidData {
    pub items: Vec<u64>,  // Vec is not Copy
    pub name: String,     // String is not Copy
}

#[account(zero_copy)]
pub struct ValidData {
    pub items: [u64; 100], // Fixed-size array
    pub name: [u8; 32],    // Fixed-size bytes
}
```

### Choosing between `load_init(){:rs}` and `load_mut(){:rs}`

Call `load_init(){:rs}` for first-time initialization (which sets the discriminator), and `load_mut(){:rs}` for subsequent updates:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {3,10}
// First initialization
pub fn initialize(ctx: Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
    let account = &mut ctx.accounts.data_account.load_init()?;
    account.data = [1; 10232];
    Ok(())
}

// Subsequent updates
pub fn update(ctx: Context<Update>) -> Result<()> {
    let account = &mut ctx.accounts.data_account.load_mut()?;
    account.data = [2; 10232];
    Ok(())
}
```

### Not validating array indices

Validate array indices before use to prevent panics:

```rust showLineNumbers=false {4-7}
pub fn update_item(ctx: Context<Update>, index: u32, value: u64) -> Result<()> {
    let account = &mut ctx.accounts.data_account.load_mut()?;

    require!(
        (index as usize) < account.items.len(),
        ErrorCode::IndexOutOfBounds
    );

    account.items[index as usize] = value;
    Ok(())
}
```

## Real-world use cases

### Event queue pattern

<Callout variant="example" title="Event queue">
  Store large sequences of events efficiently in a single zero-copy account rather than spreading
  them across many small accounts. Trading protocols, audit logs, and messaging systems all use this
  pattern.
</Callout>

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(zero_copy)]
pub struct EventQueue {
    pub head: u64,
    pub count: u64,
    pub events: [Event; 10000],
}

#[zero_copy]
pub struct Event {
    pub timestamp: i64,
    pub user: Pubkey,
    pub event_type: u8,
    pub data: [u8; 32],
}
```

### Order book pattern

<Callout variant="example" title="Order book">
  Efficient storage for trading pairs. DEXs such as Serum and Mango, along with NFT marketplaces,
  use this layout to keep bid and ask sides resident in a single account.
</Callout>

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(zero_copy)]
pub struct OrderBook {
    pub market: Pubkey,
    pub bid_count: u32,
    pub ask_count: u32,
    pub bids: [Order; 1000],
    pub asks: [Order; 1000],
}

#[zero_copy]
pub struct Order {
    pub trader: Pubkey,
    pub price: u64,
    pub size: u64,
    pub timestamp: i64,
}
```

## Examples

The examples below show two approaches for initializing zero-copy accounts:

1. Using the `init{:rs}` constraint to initialize the account in a single instruction.
2. Using the `zero{:rs}` constraint to initialize an account with data greater than 10240 bytes.

### Zero copy

<Tabs items={['Program', 'Client']}>
<Tab>

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_lang::prelude::*;

declare_id!("8B7XpDXjPWodpDUWDSzv4q9k73jB5WdNQXZxNBj1hqw1");

#[program]
pub mod zero_copy {
    use super::*;
    pub fn initialize(ctx: Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
        let account = &mut ctx.accounts.data_account.load_init()?;
        account.data = [1; 10232];
        Ok(())
    }

    pub fn update(ctx: Context<Update>) -> Result<()> {
        let account = &mut ctx.accounts.data_account.load_mut()?;
        account.data = [2; 10232];
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize<'info> {
    #[account(
        init,
        // 10240 bytes is max space to allocate with init constraint
        space = 8 + 10232,
        payer = payer,
    )]
    pub data_account: AccountLoader<'info, Data>,
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer<'info>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Update<'info> {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub data_account: AccountLoader<'info, Data>,
}

#[account(zero_copy)]
pub struct Data {
    // 10240 bytes - 8 bytes account discriminator
    pub data: [u8; 10232],
}
```

```ts title="test.ts" showLineNumbers=false
import * as anchor from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { Program } from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { ZeroCopy } from '../target/types/zero_copy'

describe('zero-copy', () => {
  // Configure the client to use the local cluster.
  anchor.setProvider(anchor.AnchorProvider.env())

  const program = anchor.workspace.zeroCopy as Program<ZeroCopy>
  const dataAccount = anchor.web3.Keypair.generate()

  it('Is initialized!', async () => {
    const tx = await program.methods
      .initialize()
      .accounts({
        dataAccount: dataAccount.publicKey,
      })
      .signers([dataAccount])
      .rpc()
    console.log('Your transaction signature', tx)

    const account = await program.account.data.fetch(dataAccount.publicKey)
    console.log('Account', account)
  })

  it('Update!', async () => {
    const tx = await program.methods
      .update()
      .accounts({
        dataAccount: dataAccount.publicKey,
      })
      .rpc()
    console.log('Your transaction signature', tx)

    const account = await program.account.data.fetch(dataAccount.publicKey)
    console.log('Account', account)
  })
})
```

### Initialize a large account

When initializing an account that requires more than 10,240 bytes of space, split the initialization into two steps:

1. Create the account in a separate instruction invoking the System Program.
2. Initialize the account data in the program instruction.

The maximum Solana account size is 10MB (10_485_760 bytes), with 8 bytes reserved for the account discriminator.

<Tabs items={['Program', 'Client']}>
<Tab>

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_lang::prelude::*;

declare_id!("CZgWhy3FYPFgKE5v9atSGaiQzbSB7cM38ofwX1XxeCFH");

#[program]
pub mod zero_copy_two {
    use super::*;
    pub fn initialize(ctx: Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
        let account = &mut ctx.accounts.data_account.load_init()?;
        account.data = [1; 10_485_752];
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize<'info> {
    #[account(zero)]
    pub data_account: AccountLoader<'info, Data>,
}

#[account(zero_copy)]
pub struct Data {
    // 10240 bytes - 8 bytes account discriminator
    pub data: [u8; 10_485_752],
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

```ts title="test.ts" {15-21,24-29} showLineNumbers=false
import * as anchor from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { Program } from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { ZeroCopyTwo } from '../target/types/zero_copy_two'

describe('zero-copy-two', () => {
  // Configure the client to use the local cluster.
  anchor.setProvider(anchor.AnchorProvider.env())

  const program = anchor.workspace.zeroCopyTwo as Program<ZeroCopyTwo>
  const dataAccount = anchor.web3.Keypair.generate()

  it('Is initialized!', async () => {
    const space = 10_485_760 // 10MB max account size
    const lamports = await program.provider.connection.getMinimumBalanceForRentExemption(space)

    const createAccountInstruction = anchor.web3.SystemProgram.createAccount({
      fromPubkey: program.provider.publicKey,
      newAccountPubkey: dataAccount.publicKey,
      space,
      lamports,
      programId: program.programId,
    })

    const initializeInstruction = await program.methods
      .initialize()
      .accounts({
        dataAccount: dataAccount.publicKey,
      })
      .instruction()

    const transaction = new anchor.web3.Transaction().add(
      createAccountInstruction,
      initializeInstruction,
    )

    const tx = await program.provider.sendAndConfirm(transaction, [dataAccount])

    console.log('Your transaction signature', tx)

    const account = await program.account.data.fetch(dataAccount.publicKey)
    console.log('Account', account)
  })
})
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>
