# index.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/clients/index.mdx

title: Clients and IDL
description: Build instructions from generated Rust account structs and the alpha IDL/TypeScript surface.
autoCards: false

A client is the code that builds instructions for your program. It picks an instruction, serializes its arguments, orders the accounts, then signs and sends the transaction to a cluster or test VM.

Anchor clients are built around the IDL and the generated helper structs that the program crate emits. The Rust path is the most complete in alpha because it has typed instruction structs, account-meta builders, resolved account helpers, and LiteSVM test integration.

TypeScript support exists through the current IDL and the `@anchor-lang/core` scaffold. The stable v2 npm surface is not published yet, so use TypeScript for integration and inspection while the package settles, and rely on Rust tests for exact instruction construction.

For a new v2 program, start with Rust tests. Once the transaction shape is proven there, use the generated IDL and TypeScript type output for app integration.

<CardGrid>

<Card title="Rust" href="/docs/v2/clients/rust/">
Use `InstructionData{:rs}`, `ToAccountMetas{:rs}`, full accounts structs, and `Resolved{:rs}` helpers in tests and Rust clients.
</Card>

<Card title="TypeScript" href="/docs/v2/clients/typescript/">
  Understand the current TypeScript package status and how to use generated IDLs.
</Card>

</CardGrid>

## What to use today

| Task | Recommended path |
| --- | --- |
| Integration tests | Rust tests with `anchor-v2-testing` and `anchor_v2_testing::svm(){:rs}`. |
| Instruction construction | Generated `program::instruction::*{:rs}` and `program::accounts::*{:rs}` modules. |
| PDA derivation | Generated `find_<account>_address(){:rs}` helpers or `Resolved{:rs}` account structs. |
| Profiling and debugger | Rust tests that call `anchor_v2_testing::svm(){:rs}`. |
| TypeScript integration | Generated IDL and TypeScript IDL type output, with alpha package caveats. |

---

# rust.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/clients/rust.mdx

title: Rust
description: Build instructions in Rust with generated instruction, account, and resolved account structs.

Rust is the primary client and test surface while the TypeScript package is still alpha. An Anchor program crate generates typed modules that Rust tests and other Rust clients can use directly, without reading an IDL at runtime.

The generated Rust surface is useful even when you do not plan to ship a Rust client. It gives tests a strongly typed way to build the exact instruction bytes and account metas the program expects.

In the default LiteSVM scaffold, the Rust client is an integration test next to the program crate:

<FileTree>
  <Dir name="programs">
    <Dir name="counter">
      <Dir name="tests">
        <File name="test_initialize.rs" comment="Builds and sends instructions" />
      </Dir>
      <Dir name="src">
        <File name="lib.rs" comment="Program crate that emits generated modules" />
      </Dir>
    </Dir>
  </Dir>
</FileTree>

The generated modules mirror the shape Anchor users expect:

- `program::instruction::*{:rs}` structs encode instruction discriminators and arguments.
- `program::accounts::*{:rs}` structs build full account metas.
- `program::accounts::*Resolved{:rs}` structs fill in derivable PDAs and well-known programs when possible.
- PDA helper methods such as `find_counter_address(){:rs}` derive addresses from the same seed metadata used by validation.

## Generated instruction data

Every handler gets an instruction struct under `program::instruction{:rs}`. The struct implements `InstructionData{:rs}`, so calling `data(){:rs}` returns the discriminator plus serialized arguments:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_lang_v2::InstructionData;

let data = vault::instruction::Deposit { amount: 1_000_000 }.data();
```

By default, instruction discriminators are the first 8 bytes of `sha256("global:" + handler_name){:rs}`. Programs that opt into compact byte discriminators with `#[discrim = N]{:rs}` still use the same `InstructionData{:rs}` trait.

## Account builders

<Tabs items={['Full accounts', 'Resolved accounts', 'to_instruction(){:rs}']}>
<Tab>

Full account structs include every account the instruction expects. This is the most explicit form and works for every account shape:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
use {
    anchor_lang_v2::{solana_program::instruction::Instruction, InstructionData, ToAccountMetas},
    anchor_lang_v2::programs::System,
};

let ix = Instruction::new_with_bytes(
    counter::id(),
    &counter::instruction::Initialize {}.data(),
    counter::accounts::Initialize {
        payer: payer.pubkey(),
        counter: counter.pubkey(),
        system_program: System::id(),
    }
    .to_account_metas(None),
);
```

Use this form when every address is already known, when an account cannot be derived from IDL seed metadata, or when a test should be explicit about the exact transaction shape.

</Tab>
<Tab>

When the derive can infer account addresses, Anchor also emits a `Resolved{:rs}` struct. The resolved form asks only for accounts the caller must supply and fills in the rest:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_lang_v2::ToAccountMetas;

let metas = multisig_v2::accounts::CreateResolved {
    creator: creator.pubkey(),
}
.to_account_metas(None);
```

Resolved structs derive PDAs whose seeds are visible to the macro, and insert well-known program accounts such as System or Token when the account wrapper determines the address.

</Tab>
<Tab>

The instruction struct also has a convenience `to_instruction(){:rs}` method:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
let ix = multisig_v2::instruction::Create {
    threshold: 2,
}
.to_instruction(multisig_v2::accounts::CreateResolved {
    creator: creator.pubkey(),
});
```

Several bench tests use this shape because it keeps the test focused on the accounts the caller actually controls.

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## PDA helpers

For PDA fields, the generated accounts module includes helper methods named from the account field:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
let (counter, bump) = counter::accounts::Initialize::find_counter_address(
    payer.pubkey().as_ref(),
);
```

When seeds have no runtime inputs, the helper has no arguments:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
let (config, bump) = nested_v2::accounts::Initialize::find_config_address();
```

Prefer these helpers in Rust tests when available. They keep client-side derivation locked to the program's account declaration.

## LiteSVM tests

The default scaffold uses Rust integration tests with LiteSVM through `anchor-v2-testing`:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_v2_testing::{Keypair, LiteSVM, Message, Signer, VersionedMessage, VersionedTransaction};
use anchor_lang_v2::{
    solana_program::instruction::Instruction,
    InstructionData,
    ToAccountMetas,
};

let mut svm: LiteSVM = anchor_v2_testing::svm();
let payer = Keypair::new();
let counter_account = Keypair::new();
svm.airdrop(&payer.pubkey(), 1_000_000_000).unwrap();

let bytes = include_bytes!("../../../target/deploy/counter.so");
svm.add_program(counter::id(), bytes).unwrap();

let ix = Instruction::new_with_bytes(
    counter::id(),
    &counter::instruction::Initialize {}.data(),
    counter::accounts::Initialize {
        payer: payer.pubkey(),
        counter: counter_account.pubkey(),
        system_program: anchor_lang_v2::programs::System::id(),
    }
    .to_account_metas(None),
);

let blockhash = svm.latest_blockhash();
let msg = Message::new_with_blockhash(&[ix], Some(&payer.pubkey()), &blockhash);
let tx = VersionedTransaction::try_new(
    VersionedMessage::Legacy(msg),
    &[&payer, &counter_account],
)
.unwrap();
let result = svm.send_transaction(tx);
assert!(result.is_ok());
```

Use `anchor_v2_testing::svm(){:rs}` instead of calling `LiteSVM::new(){:rs}` directly. The wrapper turns into a trace-recording VM when the crate is built with the generated `profile = ["anchor-v2-testing/profile"]{:toml}` feature, which powers `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test <dim>--profile</dim>`, `$ <blue>anchor</blue> debugger`, and `$ <blue>anchor</blue> coverage`.

## When to use Rust first

Use the Rust generated surface for:

- instruction tests that need to run against LiteSVM
- profiler, debugger, and coverage workflows
- client code that wants compile-time checking against the program crate
- account resolution features that TypeScript clients do not fully mirror yet

The IDL still matters for cross-language clients, but Rust is the most complete client surface during alpha.

## Standalone Rust clients

The in-crate generated modules above are the common path because integration tests share the program crate. For a Rust client that ships in a separate crate, `$ <blue>anchor</blue> codama generate <dim>-l</dim> rust` renders a standalone Rust crate from the IDL using the `@codama/renderers-rust` package:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> codama generate <dim>-l</dim> rust <dim>-p</dim> clients target/idl/counter.json
```

This is useful for off-chain services, SDKs, or downstream Rust apps that consume an Anchor program without depending on its program crate. See [CLI reference: `anchor codama`](/docs/v2/reference/cli/#anchor-codama) for renderer details.

---

# typescript.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/clients/typescript.mdx

title: TypeScript
description: Use generated IDLs and TypeScript type output from Anchor programs.

The TypeScript surface is an alpha integration path. The CLI builds IDL JSON and emits TypeScript type files. Current scaffolds use `@anchor-lang/core` `^1.0.0` while the stable v2 npm surface is still settling.

This page covers connecting an app, script, or frontend to a v2 program. The examples show the familiar Anchor client flow, but the alpha package is less authoritative than the generated Rust helpers.

<Callout variant="warning" title="Alpha package surface">
  Current scaffolds are pinned to `@anchor-lang/core` `^1.0.0` until a stable v2 package is
  published. Treat TypeScript codegen as active development, and use Rust tests as the source of
  truth for exact instruction construction.
</Callout>

During alpha, use TypeScript for application integration and IDL inspection. Prove exact instruction data, account ordering, PDA resolution, and optional-account behavior with generated Rust helpers and LiteSVM tests.

## Generated artifacts

`$ <blue>anchor</blue> build` writes the client-facing artifacts under `target/{:dir}`:

| Artifact | Path | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IDL JSON | `target/idl/<program>.json{:file}` | The canonical cross-language description of the program. |
| TypeScript IDL type | `target/types/<program>.ts{:file}` | Useful for typed client experiments and app code. |
| Rust generated helpers | Program crate modules | The source of truth for instruction builders today. |
| JavaScript client package | `@anchor-lang/core` `^1.0.0` | Usable for IDL-backed experiments while the stable v2 package is settling. |

Regenerate the IDL artifacts with:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> build
```

The generated IDL includes instruction names, discriminators, args, accounts, account types, events, constants, errors, optional account markers, and PDA seed metadata when the macro can inspect the seed list.

## Codama clients

Anchor also ships a Codama integration for projects that prefer the [Codama](https://github.com/codama-idl/codama) toolchain over `@anchor-lang/core`. `$ <blue>anchor</blue> codama generate` converts the IDL in-process, then renders client libraries through `@codama/cli`:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> codama generate <dim>-l</dim> js <dim>-p</dim> clients target/idl/counter.json
```

The JavaScript renderer pairs naturally with `@solana/kit`, and the same command supports `js-umi`, `rust`, and `go` outputs. See [CLI reference: `anchor codama`](/docs/v2/reference/cli/#anchor-codama) for the full flag set.

A typical app or script imports the generated files from the Anchor workspace:

<FileTree>
  <Dir name="target">
    <Dir name="idl">
      <File name="counter.json" comment="IDL JSON" />
    </Dir>
    <Dir name="types">
      <File name="counter.ts" comment="TypeScript IDL type" />
    </Dir>
  </Dir>
  <Dir name="app">
    <Dir name="src">
      <File name="program.ts" comment="Constructs the Program client" />
    </Dir>
  </Dir>
</FileTree>

## Client program

A `Program{:ts}` is built from an IDL and a provider. Read-only flows can use any provider-shaped object with a `connection{:ts}`. Calls that send transactions need an `AnchorProvider{:ts}` or another provider that implements `sendAndConfirm{:ts}`.

<Tabs items={['Frontend provider', 'Read-only connection']}>
<Tab>

In a frontend, wire the connection and wallet adapter into an Anchor provider before constructing the program:

```ts showLineNumbers=false
import { AnchorProvider, Program, setProvider } from '@anchor-lang/core'
import { useAnchorWallet, useConnection } from '@solana/wallet-adapter-react'
import type { Counter } from '../target/types/counter'
import idl from '../target/idl/counter.json'

const { connection } = useConnection()
const wallet = useAnchorWallet()

if (!wallet) {
  throw new Error('Wallet not connected')
}

const provider = new AnchorProvider(connection, wallet, {
  commitment: 'confirmed',
})
setProvider(provider)

export const program = new Program(idl as Counter, provider)
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

A read-only script can construct a program from a connection without a wallet.

```ts showLineNumbers=false
import { clusterApiUrl, Connection } from '@solana/web3.js'
import { Program } from '@anchor-lang/core'
import type { Counter } from '../target/types/counter'
import idl from '../target/idl/counter.json'

const connection = new Connection(clusterApiUrl('devnet'), 'confirmed')

export const program = new Program(idl as Counter, {
  connection,
})
```

This is useful for account queries, IDL-backed name lookup, and early integration tests that do not sign transactions.

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Invoke instructions

The methods builder is the entry point for TypeScript clients. The builder chain has these pieces:

| Step                        | Purpose                                                            |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `program.methods{:ts}`      | Starts an instruction call from the IDL namespace.                 |
| `.initialize(...args){:ts}` | Selects the instruction and passes serialized args.                |
| `.accounts({...}){:ts}`     | Supplies accounts the client must provide.                         |
| `.signers([...]){:ts}`      | Adds keypairs beyond the provider wallet when using `.rpc(){:ts}`. |
| `.rpc(){:ts}`               | Builds, signs, sends, and confirms a transaction.                  |
| `.transaction(){:ts}`       | Builds a transaction without sending it.                           |
| `.instruction(){:ts}`       | Builds one instruction for manual transaction composition.         |

The basic chain looks like this:

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const signature = await program.methods
  .increment()
  .accounts({
    counter,
    authority: wallet.publicKey,
  })
  .rpc()
```

Start at `program.methods{:ts}` and call the instruction by name with its args. Supply accounts with `.accounts(){:ts}`, add extra keypair signers via `.signers(){:ts}` when needed, then pick a terminal method.

<Tabs items={['.rpc(){:ts}', '.transaction(){:ts}', '.instruction(){:ts}']}>
<Tab>

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const signature = await program.methods
  .increment()
  .accounts({
    counter,
    authority: wallet.publicKey,
  })
  .rpc()
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const transaction = await program.methods
  .increment()
  .accounts({
    counter,
    authority: wallet.publicKey,
  })
  .transaction()
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const ix = await program.methods
  .increment()
  .accounts({
    counter,
    authority: wallet.publicKey,
  })
  .instruction()
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

During alpha, compare important TypeScript-built transactions against the generated Rust helper for the same instruction. The Rust helper is the most reliable reference for account ordering, PDA metadata, and any instruction shape that depends on code generated inside the program crate.

## PDA seed metadata

Generated clients can only auto-derive PDAs when the IDL contains enough seed metadata. Array-form seeds are the best shape:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(seeds = [b"vault", authority.address().as_ref()], bump)]
pub vault: Account<Vault>,
```

Opaque expression seeds still validate at runtime, but clients may not know how to reproduce them:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(seeds = Vault::seeds(authority.address()), bump)]
pub vault: Account<Vault>,
```

For public client-facing instructions, prefer array-form seeds whenever generated TypeScript clients should derive addresses automatically.

## Account fetching

Account clients are exposed under `program.account{:ts}`:

<Tabs items={['.fetch(){:ts}', '.fetchMultiple(){:ts}', '.all(){:ts}', 'memcmp{:ts}']}>
<Tab>

Fetch and deserialize one account by address:

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const counterAccount = await program.account.counter.fetch(counter)
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

Fetch multiple accounts by address:

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const manyCounters = await program.account.counter.fetchMultiple([counterA, counterB])
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

Fetch all accounts of a given account type:

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const allCounters = await program.account.counter.all()
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

Filter accounts by matching bytes at an offset:

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const counters = await program.account.counter.all([
  {
    memcmp: {
      offset: 16,
      bytes: authority.toBase58(),
    },
  },
])
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

Use the account wrapper to choose the right decoding and filter offsets. Not every account starts with an Anchor discriminator followed by a borsh payload.

| Account wrapper | Client decoding note |
| --- | --- |
| `Account<T>{:rs}` | Zero-copy and Pod-backed by default. Fixed offsets come from the `#[repr(C)]{:rs}` layout after the Anchor discriminator. |
| `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` | Variable-length borsh account data. |
| `Account<Mint>{:rs}` | SPL mint layout owned by the Token Program, with no Anchor discriminator. |
| `Account<TokenAccount>{:rs}` | SPL token-account layout owned by the Token Program, with no Anchor discriminator. |
| `InterfaceAccount<T>{:rs}` | Accepts Token or Token-2022 ownership. Token-2022 accounts may have TLV extension bytes after the base layout. |

For memcmp filters, calculate offsets from the actual wrapper layout. SPL token accounts start at byte offset `0`, while Anchor-discriminated program accounts start after the discriminator.

## Recommended workflow

Keep Rust integration tests as the execution harness:

<Steps>
<Step title="Define the program surface">

Define the instruction and accounts in Rust.

</Step>
<Step title="Regenerate IDL artifacts">

Run `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build` and inspect `target/idl/{:dir}` plus `target/types/{:dir}`.

</Step>
<Step title="Prove the transaction shape">

Write or update a LiteSVM test using the generated Rust helper.

</Step>
<Step title="Integrate TypeScript">

Build the app integration against the same IDL and keep TypeScript assumptions small until the alpha package lands.

</Step>
</Steps>

App developers get a usable IDL and type file, and the TypeScript package isn't forced to carry guarantees the alpha code hasn't earned yet.

## Current limitations

Some surfaces are still worth testing carefully in downstream clients:

- account-resolution paths that rely on generated PDA metadata
- generated CPI metadata
- opaque seed expressions
- Pod-backed account decoding conventions
- SPL and Token-2022 interface-account surfaces

Use the IDL for integration planning and early experiments, but keep Rust tests and generated account builders as the reference until the TypeScript package catches up.

# account-validation.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/fundamentals/account-validation.mdx

title: Account validation
description: 'How `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` loads accounts, runs constraints, and rejects duplicate mutable aliases.'

`#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` is where Anchor validation happens. It describes the accounts an instruction expects and the checks Anchor should run before the handler starts.

It is also what keeps handler code small. Instead of opening `AccountInfo{:rs}` values by hand and checking owners, signers, PDAs, and account data manually, you write those requirements on fields:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Create {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer,
    #[account(init, payer = payer, seeds = [b"config", payer.address().as_ref()], bump)]
    pub config: Account<Config>,
    pub system_program: Program<System>,
}
```

For each accounts struct, the macro emits:

- a `TryAccounts{:rs}` impl that walks account views and loads wrappers
- typed bumps
- a `MUT_MASK{:rs}` for duplicate mutable account detection
- account-meta builders for clients and tests
- IDL account metadata under `idl-build{:toml}`

Field order matters. Clients build the instruction in the order declared, and Anchor validates fields in that same order, stores PDA bumps in `ctx.bumps{:rs}`, then calls the handler with the loaded account struct. If a constraint expression references a sibling field, put that sibling earlier in the struct so it is already loaded.

## Built-in constraints

Common constraints include:

| Constraint | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `mut{:rs}` | Requires the account to be writable before loading it mutably. |
| `signer{:rs}` | Requires `is_signer{:rs}`. Usually prefer the `Signer{:rs}` wrapper. |
| `init{:rs}` | Creates and initializes the account. Requires `payer{:rs}`. |
| `init_if_needed{:rs}` | Creates only when the account is absent. |
| `payer = account{:rs}` | Funds `init{:rs}` or `init_if_needed{:rs}`. |
| `space = expr{:rs}` | Size to allocate for account creation. |
| `seeds = [...]{:rs}`, `bump{:rs}` | Verifies a PDA and records the bump. |
| `bump = expr{:rs}` | Verifies with an explicit stored bump. |
| `address = expr{:rs}` | Requires the account address to equal an expression. |
| `owner = expr{:rs}` | Requires the account owner to equal an expression. |
| `close = dest{:rs}` | Transfers lamports and zeros data on successful exit. |
| `realloc = expr{:rs}` | Resizes account data when `account-resize{:toml}` is enabled. |

`has_one{:rs}` is still accepted but deprecated. Put `address = parent.field{:rs}` on the sibling account instead.

## Custom constraints

Namespaced constraints are dispatched through `AccountConstraint<A>{:rs}`. A downstream crate can implement a marker such as `token::mint{:rs}` or `my_ns::min_value{:rs}` without changing the core derive.

The lifecycle has four hooks:

| Hook          | When it runs                                    |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `init{:rs}`   | After account creation.                         |
| `check{:rs}`  | During normal validation.                       |
| `update{:rs}` | Inside an `update(...){:rs}` constraint clause. |
| `exit{:rs}`   | During successful account exit.                 |

See [Extensibility](/docs/v2/programs/extensibility/) and [Account constraints](/docs/v2/reference/account-constraints/) for the trait shape.

## Duplicate mutable protection

Anchor rejects duplicate mutable account aliases by default. The derive generates a 256-bit mutable-field mask and combines it with a runtime bitvec as accounts are loaded. If two mutable fields point at the same address, validation returns `ConstraintDuplicateMutableAccount{:rs}`.

Opt out with `unsafe(dup){:rs}` only when the handler is written so it never holds conflicting mutable references:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct TouchTwice {
    #[account(mut, unsafe(dup))]
    pub first: Account<Data>,
    #[account(mut, unsafe(dup))]
    pub second: Account<Data>,
}
```

The opt-out must be deliberate because aliasing mutable account data is a common source of handler bugs.

# accounts-and-context.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/fundamentals/accounts-and-context.mdx

title: Accounts and context
description: '`Context<T>{:rs}`, typed bumps, remaining accounts, and account wrapper access.'

Handlers do not receive raw Solana accounts directly. Anchor first loads the account list into the struct named in `Context<T>{:rs}`. If validation succeeds, the handler receives that typed context and can use fields by name.

Every handler receives a mutable context:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
pub fn initialize(ctx: &mut Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
    ctx.accounts.counter.bump = ctx.bumps.counter;
    Ok(())
}
```

The mutable reference lets validation hooks and account-exit logic share state with the handler. Account wrappers load from pinocchio account views that are scoped at the handler boundary.

In the example above, `Initialize{:rs}` is the `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` struct for the instruction. `ctx.accounts.counter{:rs}` is already loaded as an `Account<Counter>{:rs}`, so the handler can update `count{:rs}` without manually checking the owner, discriminator, or writable bit.

## Context fields

`Context<T>{:rs}` gives the handler:

| Field or method                 | What it contains                                     |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `ctx.program_id{:rs}`           | The program id passed to the entrypoint.             |
| `ctx.accounts{:rs}`             | The validated `T{:rs}` accounts struct.              |
| `ctx.bumps{:rs}`                | A typed bumps struct generated from PDA fields.      |
| `ctx.remaining_accounts(){:rs}` | Lazily materialized extra `AccountView{:rs}` values. |

PDA bumps are generated as typed fields:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
let bump = ctx.bumps.vault;
```

Optional accounts produce optional bumps:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct MaybeProfile {
    pub user: Signer,
    #[account(seeds = [b"profile", user.address().as_ref()], bump)]
    pub profile: Option<Account<Profile>>,
}

pub fn handle(ctx: &mut Context<MaybeProfile>) -> Result<()> {
    if let Some(bump) = ctx.bumps.profile {
        msg!("profile present");
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

## Remaining accounts

`ctx.remaining_accounts(){:rs}` returns a `Vec<AccountView>{:rs}`. It walks the cursor only on first access and caches the result for later calls in the same instruction.

Use remaining accounts for variable-length account lists, such as multisig signers. Prefer declared fields whenever the list length is fixed, because declared fields get generated IDL metadata, account resolution, and duplicate-mut checks.

Remaining accounts are intentionally less structured. Reach for them when the number of accounts is part of the instruction data or when the list is truly open-ended. If a client can know the account at build time, make it a named field instead.

## Address access

Most wrappers expose `address(){:rs}` directly:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
let signer = ctx.accounts.authority.address();
```

For raw pinocchio views, use `account().address(){:rs}`:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
let account = ctx.accounts.data.account();
let address = account.address();
```

Use wrapper accessors when possible so code stays tied to the validated account type.

---

# cpi.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/fundamentals/cpi.mdx

title: Cross-program invocation
description: 'Learn how to make CPIs with `CpiContext{:rs}`, `CpiHandle{:rs}`, generated CPI wrappers, and PDA signer seeds.'

A Cross Program Invocation (CPI) is one program calling an instruction on another program. Composability on Solana is built on CPI. Token transfers, account creation through the System Program, and calls into another Anchor program all use it.

A CPI is constructed from the same three pieces as any Solana instruction:

1. The program ID of the program being called.
2. The accounts required by the instruction.
3. Any instruction data required as arguments.

Anchor's v2 CPI path keeps those pieces typed. `CpiContext<T>{:rs}` bundles the target program address, typed CPI accounts, signer seeds, and remaining accounts. `CpiHandle<'a>{:rs}` carries account handles into the CPI without exposing the raw account view for accidental re-borrows.

## System program CPI

`anchor_lang_v2::system_program` provides typed wrappers for every System Program instruction. The wrappers take a `CpiContext{:rs}` whose accounts struct holds `CpiHandle<'a>{:rs}` values, so the call stays inside Anchor's borrow-tracked model.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_lang_v2::system_program;

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Deposit {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer,
    #[account(mut)]
    pub vault: SystemAccount,
    pub system_program: Program<System>,
}

pub fn deposit(ctx: &mut Context<Deposit>, lamports: u64) -> Result<()> {
    let cpi = CpiContext::new(
        ctx.accounts.system_program.address(),
        system_program::Transfer {
            from: ctx.accounts.payer.cpi_handle_mut(),
            to: ctx.accounts.vault.cpi_handle_mut(),
        },
    );
    system_program::transfer(cpi, lamports)
}
```

The module exposes typed wrappers for the System Program instructions:

| Wrappers | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| `transfer{:rs}`, `create_account{:rs}`, `allocate{:rs}`, `assign{:rs}` | Ordinary signed account creation and lamport movement. |
| `*_with_seed{:rs}` variants of each | Cases where the base address is owned by another program and the resulting account address is derived deterministically. |
| The nonce-account family | Nonce account creation, withdrawal, authorization, and advance. |

## SPL token CPI

`anchor-spl-v2` exposes account structs and helper functions for common SPL Token instructions. The example below transfers tokens with `transfer_checked{:rs}`.

The instruction needs a source token account, mint, destination token account, authority, and token program:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct TransferTokens {
    pub mint: Account<Mint>,
    #[account(
        mut,
        token::mint = mint,
        token::authority = authority,
    )]
    pub from: Account<TokenAccount>,
    #[account(mut, token::mint = mint)]
    pub to: Account<TokenAccount>,
    pub authority: Signer,
    pub token_program: Program<Token>,
}
```

The handler builds the CPI accounts, wraps them in `CpiContext{:rs}`, then calls the SPL helper:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_spl_v2::token::{self, cpi as token_cpi};

pub fn transfer_tokens(
    ctx: &mut Context<TransferTokens>,
    amount: u64,
    decimals: u8,
) -> Result<()> {
    let accounts = token_cpi::accounts::TransferChecked {
        from: ctx.accounts.from.cpi_handle_mut(),
        mint: ctx.accounts.mint.cpi_handle(),
        to: ctx.accounts.to.cpi_handle_mut(),
        authority: ctx.accounts.authority.cpi_handle(),
    };

    let cpi = CpiContext::new(ctx.accounts.token_program.address(), accounts);
    token_cpi::transfer_checked(cpi, amount, decimals)
}
```

The account constraints protect the CPI from mismatched accounts before the Token Program runs. `token::mint = mint{:rs}` ensures both token accounts belong to the expected mint, and `token::authority = authority{:rs}` ensures the signer controls the source account.

## Generated Anchor CPI

When one Anchor program calls another Anchor program, the callee can expose generated CPI wrappers behind the `cpi{:toml}` feature. A caller can then use the callee's `program::cpi::accounts::*{:rs}` structs and wrapper functions.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
let cpi_accounts = callee::cpi::accounts::SetData {
    data: ctx.accounts.callee_data.cpi_handle_mut(),
    authority: ctx.accounts.authority.cpi_handle(),
};

let cpi_ctx = CpiContext::new(ctx.accounts.callee_program.address(), cpi_accounts);
callee::cpi::set_data(cpi_ctx, value)?;
```

The generated CPI account structs contain one `CpiHandle<'a>{:rs}` per account and implement `ToCpiAccounts<'a>{:rs}`. Wrapper functions pack instruction args and call `CpiContext::invoke{:rs}`.

<Callout variant="note" title="Current caveat">
  Generated CPI account wrappers currently skip accounts structs that contain `Option<_>{:rs}` or `Nested<_>{:rs}`. Those shapes need extra flattening and fallback logic. Runtime validation still supports them. This caveat is only about generated CPI wrappers.
</Callout>

## PDA signer seeds

A program can sign a CPI for a PDA derived from its own program ID. Program-owned vaults, authorities, and other accounts with no private key rely on this.

Attach signer seeds with `with_signer(){:rs}` when a PDA authorizes the CPI:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
let signer_seeds: &[&[&[u8]]] = &[&[
    b"vault-authority",
    ctx.accounts.mint.address().as_ref(),
    &[ctx.bumps.vault_authority],
]];

let cpi = CpiContext::new(ctx.accounts.token_program.address(), accounts)
    .with_signer(signer_seeds);
```

The outer slice can hold multiple signer PDAs. Each inner slice is the ordered seed list for one PDA, including its bump.

## `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` re-entry

If a CPI mutates an account that the current handler holds as `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}`, release and reacquire the borrow around the call:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
ctx.accounts.profile.release_borrow()?;
some_program::cpi::update_profile(cpi_ctx)?;
ctx.accounts.profile.reacquire_borrow_mut(ctx.program_id)?;
```

`Account<T>{:rs}` does not need this because its zero-copy fields read from the underlying buffer directly.

## `CpiHandle<'a>{:rs}`

`CpiHandle<'a>{:rs}` is intentionally narrow:

- `account.cpi_handle(){:rs}` creates a read-only handle
- `account.cpi_handle_mut(){:rs}` creates a writable handle and requires the account to be marked `mut{:rs}`
- `handle.address(){:rs}` returns the account address
- the handle does not deref to `AccountView{:rs}`

That missing `Deref{:rs}` is intentional. It prevents accidental use with checked pinocchio CPI builders that would re-borrow the same account views.

`CpiContext::invoke(data){:rs}` uses pinocchio's `invoke_signed_unchecked{:rs}`. The path stays safe for ordinary typed CPI because CPI account structs hold `CpiHandle<'a>{:rs}` values that borrow the typed account wrappers for the duration of the call.

Two layers catch aliasing:

- Rust rejects concurrent typed mutable access at compile time.
- pinocchio's account borrow state catches stale raw-borrow cases after the CPI returns.

---

# idl.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/fundamentals/idl.mdx

title: IDL
description: Learn how Anchor emits IDL metadata for instructions, accounts, types, events, constants, and account resolution.

An Interface Description Language (IDL) file for an Anchor program is a standardized JSON file describing the program's instructions, accounts, types, events, constants, and errors. Client code generators consume it to produce typed bindings without reading the Rust source.

<Callout variant="tip" title="Where to find the IDL">
  The `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build` command writes the IDL to `target/idl/<program-name>.json{:file}` and the generated TypeScript type file to `target/types/<program-name>.ts{:file}`.
</Callout>

Anchor builds the IDL from the same Rust items used by the program. The emission path is trait-driven. Account wrappers and type wrappers expose metadata through `IdlAccountType{:rs}` and `IdlType{:rs}` under the `idl-build{:toml}` feature.

`idl-build{:toml}` pulls in IDL assembly machinery and should not be shipped in production SBF binaries.

## Program instructions

The `instructions` array in the IDL maps directly to the public functions inside the `#[program]{:rs}` module. Each entry records the accounts and arguments the instruction requires.

<Tabs items={['Program', 'IDL', 'Client']}>
<Tab>

The program exposes an `initialize(){:rs}` instruction with one argument and an `Initialize{:rs}` accounts struct:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[program]
pub mod counter {
    use super::*;

    pub fn initialize(ctx: &mut Context<Initialize>, start: u64) -> Result<()> {
        ctx.accounts.counter.count = start;
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer,
    #[account(init, payer = payer)]
    pub counter: Account<Counter>,
    pub system_program: Program<System>,
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

The IDL captures the instruction name, discriminator, account list, and argument list:

```json showLineNumbers=false
{
  "name": "initialize",
  "discriminator": [175, 175, 109, 31, 13, 152, 155, 237],
  "accounts": [
    { "name": "payer", "writable": true, "signer": true },
    { "name": "counter", "writable": true },
    { "name": "systemProgram", "address": "11111111111111111111111111111111" }
  ],
  "args": [{ "name": "start", "type": "u64" }]
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

A generated client uses the IDL to build the transaction. The instruction name, args, and accounts in the builder mirror the IDL fields:

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const signature = await program.methods
  .initialize(new BN(42))
  .accounts({
    payer: wallet.publicKey,
    counter: counter.publicKey,
  })
  .signers([counter])
  .rpc()
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Program accounts

The `accounts` array in the IDL maps to structs annotated with `#[account]{:rs}`. These structs define account data created and owned by the program.

<Tabs items={['Program', 'IDL', 'Client']}>
<Tab>

The program defines a fixed-size `Counter{:rs}` account:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account]
pub struct Counter {
    pub count: u64,
    pub authority: Address,
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

The IDL records the account name and discriminator under `accounts`, and its field layout under `types`:

```json showLineNumbers=false
{
  "accounts": [
    {
      "name": "Counter",
      "discriminator": [255, 176, 4, 245, 188, 253, 124, 25]
    }
  ],
  "types": [
    {
      "name": "Counter",
      "type": {
        "kind": "struct",
        "fields": [
          { "name": "count", "type": "u64" },
          { "name": "authority", "type": "pubkey" }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

The TypeScript client can fetch the account by public key and decode it using the IDL:

```ts showLineNumbers=false
const counterAccount = await program.account.counter.fetch(counter)
console.log(counterAccount.count.toString())
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Discriminators

Anchor assigns a discriminator to every instruction and every Anchor account type. These bytes act as runtime identifiers so the program can dispatch the right instruction handler and so deserialization can verify the right account type.

By default, instruction discriminators are the first 8 bytes of `sha256("global:" + instruction_name){:rs}`. Account discriminators are the first 8 bytes of `sha256("account:" + struct_name){:rs}`.

CU-sensitive programs can opt into compact one-byte instruction discriminators with `#[discrim = N]{:rs}`:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[program]
pub mod vault {
    use super::*;

    #[discrim = 0]
    pub fn deposit(ctx: &mut Context<Deposit>, amount: u64) -> Result<()> {
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

You will not normally interact with discriminators directly. Anchor inserts them on the wire and verifies them on read. The discriminator fields in the generated JSON come from these rules.

## Account wrappers and IDL

Core wrappers such as `Signer{:rs}`, `Program<T>{:rs}`, `SystemAccount{:rs}`, `UncheckedAccount{:rs}`, and `Sysvar<T>{:rs}` surface account metadata through trait impls. SPL wrappers in `anchor-spl-v2` do the same from the downstream crate.

Custom wrappers should implement the IDL traits so the generated account list remains meaningful to clients.

## PDA seed metadata

PDA seeds defined in `seeds{:rs}` constraints can be included in the IDL. This lets generated clients auto-resolve accounts when the seed list is inspectable.

Array-form seeds get the richest output:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(seeds = [b"vault", authority.address().as_ref()], bump)]
pub vault: Account<Vault>,
```

Opaque expression seeds still work at runtime, but the IDL cannot always describe how a client should reproduce them:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(seeds = Vault::seeds(authority.address()), bump)]
pub vault: Account<Vault>,
```

Prefer array-form seeds for public instructions where generated clients should auto-derive PDAs.

## TypeScript status

The CLI builds IDL and TypeScript type files, but the TypeScript package is still alpha. Current scaffolds are pinned to `@anchor-lang/core` `^1.0.0` until a stable v2 package is published. Generated TypeScript client surfaces are active development, not a stable npm contract.

# pdas-and-resolution.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/fundamentals/pdas-and-resolution.mdx

title: PDAs and resolution
description: Learn how to use Program Derived Addresses, PDA constraints, generated bumps, resolved accounts, and IDL seed metadata.

<Callout variant="definition" title="Program Derived Address">
  A Program Derived Address (PDA) is a Solana account address derived deterministically from a list
  of seeds and a program ID. PDAs are off the Ed25519 curve, so they have no associated private key.
  The owning program can sign for them through CPI signer seeds.
</Callout>

Program Derived Addresses give programs a way to create accounts whose addresses are predictable from program-defined inputs. Anchor expresses PDA derivation through account constraints.

## Anchor PDA constraints

The `seeds{:rs}` constraint lists the values used to derive the PDA. Seeds can be static byte strings, account addresses, account data, or instruction arguments. The `bump{:rs}` constraint finds the bump seed that pushes the address off the Ed25519 curve.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer,
    #[account(init, payer = payer, seeds = [b"counter", payer.address().as_ref()], bump)]
    pub counter: Account<Counter>,
    pub system_program: Program<System>,
}
```

<Callout variant="note">
  The `seeds{:rs}` and `bump{:rs}` constraints are used together for normal PDA validation.
</Callout>

The generated bumps struct stores the canonical bump as a typed field:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
ctx.accounts.counter.bump = ctx.bumps.counter;
```

## Seed examples

Use an empty array to define a PDA without optional seeds:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct ReadGlobal {
    #[account(seeds = [], bump)]
    pub global: Account<Global>,
}
```

Pass a single byte literal to derive a PDA from a fixed value:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct ReadConfig {
    #[account(seeds = [b"config"], bump)]
    pub config: Account<Config>,
}
```

Use multiple seeds when the PDA should depend on a user, mint, market, or instruction-specific value:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct ReadProfile {
    pub user: Signer,
    #[account(seeds = [b"profile", user.address().as_ref()], bump)]
    pub profile: Account<Profile>,
}
```

The example above uses both a static seed (`b"profile"{:rs}`) and a dynamic seed (the user's address).

If all seeds are byte literals, Anchor can run PDA discovery at macro expansion time and bake the result into generated code:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(seeds = [b"global-config"], bump)]
pub config: Account<Config>,
```

Seeds that depend on runtime accounts or instruction arguments still use the runtime path.

## Explicit bumps

When `bump{:rs}` is used without a value, Anchor finds the canonical bump during validation. That is the simplest form and is the right default while creating an account.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(seeds = [b"counter", payer.address().as_ref()], bump)]
pub counter: Account<Counter>,
```

An account can also store its bump and use that value later:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(seeds = [b"counter"], bump = counter.bump)]
pub counter: Account<Counter>,
```

By storing the bump value in account data, the program avoids a runtime search when reloading the account.

## PDA creation

The `init{:rs}` constraint is commonly used with `seeds{:rs}` and `bump{:rs}` to create a new account whose address is a PDA. Under the hood, `init{:rs}` invokes the System Program to create the account.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct CreateProfile {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer,
    #[account(init, payer = payer, seeds = [b"profile", payer.address().as_ref()], bump)]
    pub profile: Account<Profile>,
    pub system_program: Program<System>,
}
```

`payer{:rs}` specifies who funds the account creation. For fixed-size `Account<T>{:rs}` data, v2 can derive the allocation size from the account wrapper's `Space{:rs}` implementation.

## `seeds::program{:rs}`

The `seeds::program{:rs}` constraint derives a PDA against another program ID. Use it when an instruction needs to validate PDA accounts created by another program.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct ReadExternal {
    #[account(
        seeds = [b"external"],
        bump,
        seeds::program = other_program.address(),
    )]
    pub external: UncheckedAccount,
    pub other_program: Program<OtherProgram>,
}
```

## Resolved account structs

For client and test code, `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` emits account-meta builders. Full structs include every account. Resolved structs include only fields the caller must provide while PDAs and well-known programs are derived or filled in.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
let metas = multisig_v2::accounts::CreateResolved {
    creator: creator.pubkey(),
}
.to_account_metas(None);
```

If `Create{:rs}` contains a `config{:rs}` PDA derived from `creator{:rs}` and a `system_program{:rs}`, the resolved form supplies only `creator{:rs}`. The builder derives `config{:rs}` and inserts the System Program account in the right position.

## PDA seeds in the IDL

Anchor emits PDA metadata into the IDL when it can inspect the seed list. Array-form seeds get the richest output:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(seeds = [b"profile", user.address().as_ref(), slug.as_ref()], bump)]
pub profile: Account<Profile>,
```

For array-form seeds, the macro can classify literals as const seeds, sibling accounts as account seeds, and instruction args as arg seeds. Const-evaluable expressions such as constant paths are rendered through the IDL build helper when they implement `AsRef<[u8]>{:rs}`.

Opaque expression seeds are valid for runtime validation, but client-side auto-derivation has less information:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(seeds = Profile::seeds(user.address()), bump)]
pub profile: Account<Profile>,
```

Use array-form seeds for accounts that generated clients should auto-resolve. Use expression-form seeds when the runtime abstraction matters more than generated client metadata.

---

# program-structure.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/fundamentals/program-structure.mdx

title: Program structure
description: 'Learn about the structure of Anchor programs, including `declare_id!(){:rs}`, `#[program]{:rs}`, `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}`, and `#[account]{:rs}`.'

The Anchor framework uses Rust macros to reduce boilerplate and enforce the checks every Solana program needs. Four macros do most of the work.

- `declare_id!(){:rs}` sets the program's on-chain address.
- `#[program]{:rs}` annotates the module containing the program's instruction handlers.
- `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` declares the accounts an instruction requires.
- `#[account]{:rs}` defines a custom account data type owned by the program.

The default scaffold splits these pieces across a few files:

<FileTree>
  <Dir name="programs">
    <Dir name="counter">
      <Dir name="src">
        <Dir name="instructions" comment="One file per instruction">
          <File name="initialize.rs" />
        </Dir>
        <File name="constants.rs" />
        <File name="error.rs" />
        <File name="instructions.rs" comment="Re-exports instruction modules" />
        <File name="lib.rs" comment="Declares the program module" highlight />
        <File name="state.rs" comment="Program-owned account data" />
      </Dir>
    </Dir>
  </Dir>
</FileTree>

For a small program, the pieces read more clearly as a single file. The example below exposes one `initialize(){:rs}` instruction that creates a counter account and stores an authority in it.

```rust title="programs/counter/src/lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_lang_v2::prelude::*;

declare_id!("3ynNB373Q3VAzKp7m4x238po36hjAGFXFJB4ybN2iTyg");

#[program]
pub mod counter {
    use super::*;

    pub fn initialize(ctx: &mut Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
        ctx.accounts.counter.count = 0;
        ctx.accounts.counter.authority = *ctx.accounts.payer.address();
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer,
    #[account(init, payer = payer)]
    pub counter: Account<Counter>,
    pub system_program: Program<System>,
}

#[account]
pub struct Counter {
    pub count: u64,
    pub authority: Address,
}
```

From those ordinary Rust items, the framework produces the Solana entrypoint, account parser, IDL metadata, and client-facing instruction builders.

## `declare_id!(){:rs}`

The `declare_id!(){:rs}` macro embeds the program's on-chain address, known as the program ID, into the compiled binary.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
declare_id!("3ynNB373Q3VAzKp7m4x238po36hjAGFXFJB4ybN2iTyg");
```

By default, the program ID is the public key of the keypair at `target/deploy/<program_name>-keypair.json{:file}`. To rewrite the `declare_id!(){:rs}` string to match the on-disk keypair, run:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> keys sync
```

<Callout variant="tip" title="When to run `$ anchor keys sync`">
  Run `$ <blue>anchor</blue> keys sync` after cloning a repository or regenerating a program
  keypair. Syncing prevents a mismatch between the declared ID and the program keypair used during
  deployment.
</Callout>

## `#[program]{:rs}`

The `#[program]{:rs}` attribute annotates the module that contains the program's instruction handlers. Every public function inside this module becomes an instruction callable from clients.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[program]
pub mod counter {
    use super::*;

    pub fn initialize(ctx: &mut Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
        ctx.accounts.counter.count = 0;
        ctx.accounts.counter.authority = *ctx.accounts.payer.address();
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

The first parameter of every instruction handler is a `Context<T>{:rs}`, where `T{:rs}` is a struct that implements account loading and validation. Any additional parameters become instruction arguments supplied by the client.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
pub fn set_count(ctx: &mut Context<SetCount>, count: u64) -> Result<()> {
    ctx.accounts.counter.count = count;
    Ok(())
}
```

`#[program]{:rs}` also generates the instruction dispatcher. By default, each handler gets the first 8 bytes of `sha256("global:" + handler_name){:rs}` as its discriminator. CU-sensitive programs can use compact one-byte discriminators:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[program]
pub mod vault {
    use super::*;

    #[discrim = 0]
    pub fn deposit(ctx: &mut Context<Deposit>, amount: u64) -> Result<()> {
        Ok(())
    }

    #[discrim = 1]
    pub fn withdraw(ctx: &mut Context<Withdraw>, amount: u64) -> Result<()> {
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

If one handler in the module uses `#[discrim = N]{:rs}`, every handler in that module must declare a unique byte discriminator.

## `Context<T>{:rs}`

`Context<T>{:rs}` exposes everything the handler needs from the runtime beyond its own instruction arguments.

| Field or method                 | What it contains                                     |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `ctx.program_id{:rs}`           | The program id passed to the entrypoint.             |
| `ctx.accounts{:rs}`             | The validated `T{:rs}` accounts struct.              |
| `ctx.bumps{:rs}`                | A typed bumps struct generated from PDA fields.      |
| `ctx.remaining_accounts(){:rs}` | Lazily materialized extra `AccountView{:rs}` values. |

Access each account through `ctx.accounts.<field_name>{:rs}`. The field has already been loaded and validated before the handler starts.

## `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}`

The `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` macro generates account loading and validation for an instruction.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer,
    #[account(init, payer = payer)]
    pub counter: Account<Counter>,
    pub system_program: Program<System>,
}
```

Each field maps to one account the instruction requires. Field names are arbitrary, but they should describe the role the account plays in the instruction.

Account validation is the first line of defense against malicious input. Anchor enforces two complementary mechanisms that are usually used together.

- [Account constraints](/docs/v2/reference/account-constraints/) declared in the `#[account(...)]{:rs}` attribute enforce runtime conditions on each account. Common constraints include `init{:rs}`, `mut{:rs}`, `seeds{:rs}`, `bump{:rs}`, and `constraint{:rs}`.
- [Account types](/docs/v2/programs/account-types/) specified in the field's type enforce static expectations about what kind of account the client must pass. Examples include `Account<T>{:rs}`, `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}`, `Signer{:rs}`, `Program<T>{:rs}`, and `UncheckedAccount{:rs}`.

Once validation succeeds, the handler accesses accounts through `ctx.accounts.<field_name>{:rs}`.

## `#[account]{:rs}`

The `#[account]{:rs}` attribute turns a plain struct into an Anchor-managed account type.

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account]
pub struct Counter {
    pub count: u64,
    pub authority: Address,
}
```

In v2, the default account form is fixed-size and zero-copy. `#[account]{:rs}` gives `Counter{:rs}` a stable `#[repr(C)]{:rs}` layout, derives the required Pod traits, adds an Anchor discriminator, and implements ownership metadata for the declaring program.

For a normal program-owned account, the on-chain layout is:

```text showLineNumbers=false
[8-byte discriminator][repr(C) Counter]
```

Use `Account<T>{:rs}` for fixed-size Pod-backed state. Use `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` when the account needs variable-length fields such as `Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, or payload enums.

<Callout variant="important" title="Choosing the account model">
  `Account<T>{:rs}` is zero-copy and Pod-backed by default. For variable-length data, mark the type with `#[account(borsh)]{:rs}` and use `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` in the accounts struct.
</Callout>

## Generated modules

The program macro emits generated surfaces that clients and tests rely on:

- `program::instruction::*{:rs}` structs that implement `InstructionData{:rs}`
- `program::accounts::*{:rs}` structs that implement `ToAccountMetas{:rs}`
- typed `Bumps{:rs}` for each accounts struct
- IDL print hooks behind `idl-build{:toml}`
- `program::cpi::*{:rs}` wrappers behind the `cpi{:toml}` feature

These modules are compile-time output from the macros, not source files checked into the program. Tests and CPI callers can still import them as normal Rust modules because the macro expands them into the crate.

## `#![no_std]{:rs}` by default

`anchor-lang-v2` is `#![no_std]{:rs}`. The default `alloc{:toml}` feature is on, so user programs can still use `Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, and any generated macro code that needs allocation. Disabling `alloc{:toml}` is possible, but most programs should keep the default feature set.

---

# first-program.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/get-started/first-program.mdx

title: First program
description: Scaffold, build, and test an Anchor program with the LiteSVM template.

The quickest path is the default `$ <blue>anchor</blue> init` template. It creates a workspace, a multi-file Rust program, and a LiteSVM integration test under `programs/<name>/tests/{:dir}`.

This walkthrough uses a tiny counter program so the generated files are easy to inspect. What matters is the shape of the project. Anchor writes the entrypoint, account validation, tests, IDL, and build artifacts into predictable places.

<Steps>
<Step title="Scaffold the workspace">

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> init <dim>--no-install</dim> counter
$ <blue>cd</blue> counter
```

`<dim>--no-install</dim>` skips the JavaScript package install. The default test template is Rust + LiteSVM, so the program can build and test without Node.

The new workspace has this shape:

<FileTree>
  <Dir name="app" comment="Frontend code, empty by default" />
  <Dir name="migrations" comment="Optional deploy scripts">
    <File name="deploy.ts" />
  </Dir>
  <Dir name="programs" comment="On-chain programs">
    <Dir name="counter">
      <Dir name="src">
        <Dir name="instructions" comment="Instruction handlers">
          <File name="initialize.rs" />
        </Dir>
        <File name="constants.rs" comment="Program constants" />
        <File name="error.rs" comment="Custom errors" />
        <File name="instructions.rs" comment="Instruction module root" />
        <File name="lib.rs" comment="Program entrypoint" highlight />
        <File name="state.rs" comment="Account data types" />
      </Dir>
      <Dir name="tests" comment="LiteSVM integration tests">
        <File name="test_initialize.rs" />
      </Dir>
      <File name="Cargo.toml" comment="Program crate manifest" />
    </Dir>
  </Dir>
  <File name="Anchor.toml" comment="Workspace config" />
  <File name="Cargo.toml" comment="Rust workspace manifest" />
  <File name="package.json" comment="TypeScript package metadata" />
  <File name="rust-toolchain.toml" comment="Rust toolchain pin" />
  <File name="tsconfig.json" comment="TypeScript config" />
</FileTree>

</Step>
<Step title="Inspect the generated program">

Start with `programs/counter/src/lib.rs{:file}`. It declares the modules, the program id, and the instruction entrypoints. The default multi-file template keeps the handler body in `instructions/initialize.rs{:file}`, then the `#[program]{:rs}` module forwards to it.

```rust title="programs/counter/src/lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
pub mod constants;
pub mod error;
pub mod instructions;
pub mod state;

use anchor_lang_v2::prelude::*;

pub use instructions::*;

declare_id!("3ynNB373Q3VAzKp7m4x238po36hjAGFXFJB4ybN2iTyg");

#[program]
pub mod counter {
    use super::*;

    pub fn initialize(ctx: &mut Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
        initialize::handler(ctx)
    }
}
```

Your generated `declare_id!(){:rs}` value will be different. Anchor creates it from the program keypair under `target/deploy/{:dir}`.

The first real instruction is in `programs/counter/src/instructions/initialize.rs{:file}`. It uses `anchor_lang_v2::prelude::*{:rs}`, `&mut Context<T>{:rs}`, and account wrappers without `<'info>{:rs}` lifetimes:

```rust title="programs/counter/src/instructions/initialize.rs" showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_lang_v2::prelude::*;

use crate::state::Counter;

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer,
    #[account(init, payer = payer)]
    pub counter: Account<Counter>,
    pub system_program: Program<System>,
}

pub fn handler(ctx: &mut Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
    ctx.accounts.counter.count = 0;
    ctx.accounts.counter.authority = *ctx.accounts.payer.address();
    msg!("Counter initialized");
    Ok(())
}
```

The account data is fixed-size, so it uses the default zero-copy account form:

```rust title="programs/counter/src/state.rs" showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_lang_v2::prelude::*;

#[account]
pub struct Counter {
    pub count: u64,
    pub authority: Address,
}
```

`#[account]{:rs}` makes `Counter{:rs}` Pod-backed and gives `Account<Counter>{:rs}` the layout `[8-byte discriminator][Counter bytes]`. Use [`BorshAccount<T>{:rs}`](/docs/v2/programs/borsh-accounts-and-realloc/) instead when the account contains `Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, or payload enums.

The `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` struct is the checklist Anchor runs before the handler. Here, `payer{:rs}` must be writable, `counter{:rs}` is created and paid for by `payer{:rs}`, and `system_program{:rs}` is the well-known program field the scaffold expects.

</Step>
<Step title="Build and test">

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> build
$ <blue>anchor</blue> test
```

`$ <blue>anchor</blue> build` compiles the program and writes the SBF binary to `target/deploy/counter.so{:file}`. It also writes client-facing artifacts such as `target/idl/counter.json{:file}` and `target/types/counter.ts{:file}`.

`$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` runs the script in `Anchor.toml{:file}`. For the default LiteSVM template, that script is `$ cargo test`, and the workspace is configured to skip starting a local validator.

The LiteSVM test adds the deployed SBF program to an in-process VM, builds an instruction using generated account structs, and sends a signed transaction:

```rust title="programs/counter/tests/test_initialize.rs" showLineNumbers=false
use {
    anchor_lang_v2::{
        accounts::Account, bytemuck, programs::System,
        solana_program::instruction::Instruction, Id, InstructionData, Space, ToAccountMetas,
    },
    anchor_v2_testing::{Keypair, LiteSVM, Message, Signer, VersionedMessage, VersionedTransaction},
};

#[test]
fn test_initialize() {
    let program_id = counter::id();
    let payer = Keypair::new();
    let counter = Keypair::new();
    let mut svm = anchor_v2_testing::svm();

    svm.add_program(program_id, include_bytes!("../../../target/deploy/counter.so")).unwrap();
    svm.airdrop(&payer.pubkey(), 1_000_000_000).unwrap();

    let instruction = Instruction::new_with_bytes(
        program_id,
        &counter::instruction::Initialize {}.data(),
        counter::accounts::Initialize {
            payer: payer.pubkey(),
            counter: counter.pubkey(),
            system_program: System::id(),
        }
        .to_account_metas(None),
    );

    let blockhash = svm.latest_blockhash();
    let msg = Message::new_with_blockhash(&[instruction], Some(&payer.pubkey()), &blockhash);
    let tx = VersionedTransaction::try_new(
        VersionedMessage::Legacy(msg),
        &[&payer, &counter],
    )
    .unwrap();

    let res = svm.send_transaction(tx);
    assert!(res.is_ok(), "send_transaction failed: {:?}", res);

    let account = svm.get_account(&counter.pubkey()).expect("counter account");
    assert_eq!(account.data.len(), <Account<counter::state::Counter> as Space>::INIT_SPACE);
    let counter_state: &counter::state::Counter = bytemuck::from_bytes(&account.data[8..]);
    assert_eq!(counter_state.count, 0);
    assert_eq!(counter_state.authority, payer.pubkey());
}
```

</Step>
<Step title="Profile and debug">

The generated `profile = ["anchor-v2-testing/profile"]{:toml}` feature lets the same tests feed the profiler and debugger. Run either tool directly. Each tool records traces on demand if they are not already present.

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> test <dim>--profile</dim>     <dim># renders flamegraph SVGs</dim>
$ <blue>anchor</blue> debugger              <dim># opens the instruction-stepper TUI</dim>
```

The trace-backed tooling is covered in [Profiling and debugger](/docs/v2/testing/profiling-and-debugger/).

</Step>
</Steps>

# installation.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/get-started/installation.mdx

title: Installation
description: Install the Anchor CLI and depend on the alpha crates from the anchor-next branch.

Anchor v2 installs from source while the alpha is branch-only. The normal Solana program toolchain is a prerequisite, so make sure Rust, Cargo, and the Solana CLI are already on your `PATH`:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ rustc <dim>--version</dim>
$ cargo <dim>--version</dim>
$ solana <dim>--version</dim>
```

If you are setting up a machine from scratch, install Rust with [rustup](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install) and install the Solana CLI from the [Agave install docs](https://docs.anza.xyz/cli/install). On Windows, run the Solana and Anchor commands inside WSL rather than PowerShell.

The v2 alpha crates have not been published to `crates.io` yet, so install the CLI directly from the [`anchor-next`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/tree/anchor-next) branch:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>cargo</blue> install <dim>--git</dim> https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor.git <dim>--branch</dim> anchor-next anchor-cli <dim>--locked</dim> <dim>--force</dim>
```

<Callout variant="warning" title="Overwrites the anchor binary">
  `$ <blue>cargo</blue> install` overwrites the `anchor` binary on your `PATH`. To keep another
  Anchor install available, run this binary from a source checkout instead of putting it first on
  `PATH`.
</Callout>

AVM tracks published Anchor releases. Until v2 has published releases, use `$ <blue>cargo</blue> install <dim>--git</dim> ... <dim>--branch</dim> anchor-next` for the CLI you use with these docs.

On macOS, the final link can fail with an error like `ld: could not parse bitcode object file ... Unknown attribute kind`. If that happens, disable LTO for this install:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=off <blue>cargo</blue> install <dim>--git</dim> https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor.git <dim>--branch</dim> anchor-next anchor-cli <dim>--locked</dim> <dim>--force</dim>
```

## Local checkout

A local checkout is useful for inspecting internals, patching the CLI, or running the debugger against the checked-in bench programs:

<Steps>
<Step title="Clone the repository">

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>git</blue> clone https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor.git
$ <blue>cd</blue> anchor
$ <blue>git</blue> checkout anchor-next
```

</Step>
<Step title="Install the CLI from source">

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>cargo</blue> install <dim>--path</dim> cli <dim>--force</dim>
```

Prepend `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=off` on macOS if you hit the LTO error above.

</Step>
</Steps>

## Program dependencies

New workspaces created by `$ <blue>anchor</blue> init` already include the git dependency for `anchor-lang-v2`. Add `anchor-spl-v2` when the program uses SPL token helpers or Token-2022 interfaces:

```toml title="Cargo.toml" showLineNumbers=false
[dependencies]
anchor-lang-v2 = { git = "https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor.git", branch = "anchor-next" }
anchor-spl-v2 = { git = "https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor.git", branch = "anchor-next" }
```

Add these to the program crate at `programs/<program-name>/Cargo.toml{:file}`, not the workspace root `Cargo.toml{:file}`.

The default `anchor-lang-v2` feature set is `alloc{:toml}`, `guardrails{:toml}`, and `account-resize{:toml}`. Optional features include `const-rent{:toml}`, `compat{:toml}`, and `testing{:toml}`. See [Feature flags](/docs/v2/reference/feature-flags/) for the tradeoffs.

## Test dependencies

The default scaffold uses Rust tests with `anchor-v2-testing`. Add the dev dependency to the same `programs/<program-name>/Cargo.toml{:file}`:

```toml title="Cargo.toml" showLineNumbers=false
[dev-dependencies]
anchor-v2-testing = { git = "https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor.git", branch = "anchor-next" }

[features]
profile = ["anchor-v2-testing/profile"]
```

That `profile{:toml}` feature is what `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test <dim>--profile</dim>`, `$ <blue>anchor</blue> debugger`, and `$ <blue>anchor</blue> coverage` use to record SBF register traces.

---

# migrating-from-v1.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/get-started/migrating-from-v1.mdx

title: Migrating from v1
description: Port a v1 program to v2 with the main rename and account-model changes.

Most v1 programs port to v2 with mechanical renames plus one account-model decision. Fixed-size state goes through zero-copy `Account<T>{:rs}`. Variable-length state goes through `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}`.

This page is for existing programs. If you are learning Anchor for the first time, start with [First program](/docs/v2/get-started/first-program/) and come back here when you need to compare old code to new code.

<Steps>
<Step title="Apply the mechanical renames">

Update the crate name, handler signatures, wrapper lifetimes, and key type names using the table below.

</Step>
<Step title="Choose the account model">

Move fixed-size state to `Account<T>{:rs}` and move variable-length state to `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}`.

</Step>
<Step title="Refresh constraints">

Replace deprecated `has_one{:rs}` checks with explicit `address{:rs}` checks where possible, then verify PDA seeds and bumps compile.

</Step>
<Step title="Rebuild the test harness">

Use LiteSVM tests through `anchor_v2_testing::svm(){:rs}` so the same tests can feed profiling, debugger, and coverage tooling.

</Step>
</Steps>

## Rename table

| v1 | v2 |
| --- | --- |
| `use anchor_lang::prelude::*{:rs}` | `use anchor_lang_v2::prelude::*{:rs}` |
| `solana_program{:rs}` | `pinocchio{:rs}` or v2 re-exports |
| `std{:rs}` required | `#![no_std]{:rs}` compatible, with `alloc{:toml}` on by default |
| `<'info>{:rs}` lifetimes on wrappers | removed |
| `Context<T>{:rs}` handlers | `&mut Context<T>{:rs}` handlers |
| `Pubkey{:rs}` | `Address{:rs}` |
| `Account<'info, T>{:rs}` for fixed-size data | `Account<T>{:rs}` with `T: Pod{:rs}` |
| `Account<'info, T>{:rs}` for `Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, payload enums | `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` |
| `AccountLoader<'info, T>{:rs}` zero-copy | `Account<T>{:rs}` |
| `ctx.bumps.get("name"){:rs}` | `ctx.bumps.name{:rs}` |
| `has_one = field{:rs}` | `address = parent.field{:rs}` on the sibling account |

<Callout variant="note" title="AccountLoader means something else in v2">
  v2 still has a type named `AccountLoader{:rs}`, but it is the sequential account cursor used internally by generated validation code. It is not the v1 user-facing zero-copy wrapper.
</Callout>

## Account data choice

`Account<T>{:rs}` is now zero-copy by default. The account bytes are cast directly into `T{:rs}`, so `T{:rs}` must be fixed-size and Pod-compatible:

<Tabs items={['Account<T>{:rs}', 'BorshAccount<T>{:rs}']}>
<Tab>

```rust title="v2 fixed-size state" showLineNumbers=false
#[account]
pub struct Counter {
    pub count: u64,
    pub authority: Address,
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Increment {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub counter: Account<Counter>,
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

For variable-length data, use `#[account(borsh)]{:rs}`:

```rust title="v2 variable-length state" showLineNumbers=false
#[account(borsh)]
pub struct Profile {
    pub owner: Address,
    pub name: String,
    pub friends: Vec<Address>,
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct EditProfile {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub profile: BorshAccount<Profile>,
}
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Constraint changes

The v1 `has_one{:rs}` constraint still parses, but v2 emits a deprecation warning. Prefer moving the check onto the sibling account with `address{:rs}`:

<Tabs items={['has_one{:rs}', 'address{:rs}']}>
<Tab>

```rust title="v1 style" del={3} showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Withdraw {
    #[account(has_one = creator)]
    pub config: Account<Config>,
    pub creator: UncheckedAccount,
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab>

```rust title="v2 style" add={5} showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Withdraw {
    pub config: Account<Config>,
    #[account(address = config.creator)]
    pub creator: UncheckedAccount,
}
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

`address{:rs}` is more general. The right-hand side can be any expression, not only a field with the same name as a sibling account.

## Compat feature

The `compat{:toml}` feature re-exposes a small set of v1-shaped helpers so existing call sites compile without rewrites:

```toml title="Cargo.toml" showLineNumbers=false
[dependencies]
anchor-lang-v2 = { git = "https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor.git", branch = "anchor-next", features = ["compat"] }
```

| v1 helper | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `debug!{:rs}` | Logging macro that accepts any Rust format string by routing through `alloc::format!{:rs}`. |
| `error!{:rs}`, `err!{:rs}` | Convert an error code into a `ProgramError{:rs}` (and an `Err(...){:rs}` wrapper). |
| `pubkey!{:rs}` | Compile-time base58 decode that yields an `Address{:rs}`. |
| `Pubkey{:rs}` | Type alias for `Address{:rs}` under `anchor_lang_v2::solana_program::pubkey{:rs}`. |
| `AccountViewCompat{:rs}` | Extension trait that exposes v1-style accessors on pinocchio's `AccountView{:rs}`. |

`error!{:rs}` is implemented as a thin shim in v2, not a proc-macro, so it does not allocate a rich `AnchorError{:rs}` with source and message metadata the way v1 did. v2 keeps runtime errors as `ProgramError{:rs}` and routes error text through the IDL.

Keep `compat{:toml}` off in production unless one of these shims is on a hot path. `debug!{:rs}` in particular allocates and is more expensive than v2's native `msg!{:rs}`.

The `Lamports{:rs}` trait, which gives accounts v1-style `get_lamports{:rs}`, `add_lamports{:rs}`, and `sub_lamports{:rs}` methods, is in the prelude unconditionally and does not require the `compat{:toml}` feature.

## Still alpha

Some surfaces are intentionally incomplete while v2 is alpha. Less-common `anchor-spl` constraints, parts of the TypeScript publishing pipeline, and some client-codegen shapes are still settling. See [Alpha limitations](/docs/v2/reference/alpha-limitations/) before porting a large production program.

---

# index.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/index.mdx

title: Anchor v2
description: Alpha docs for anchor-lang-v2, the pinocchio-based Anchor runtime.
autoCards: false

Anchor is a framework for Solana programs. It provides a Rust eDSL for writing programs, an IDL format for describing them, generated client surfaces, and a CLI for the workspace loop.

`anchor-lang-v2` is the alpha runtime for this version of Anchor. It is pinocchio-based, `#![no_std]{:rs}`, zero-copy by default for fixed-size accounts, and organized around traits so account wrappers, constraints, CPI helpers, and IDL metadata can be extended from downstream crates.

If you are new to Anchor, read the getting started pages first and keep the generated counter project open while reading the fundamentals. Most pages refer back to the same few pieces of the model, including a handler, a `Context<T>{:rs}`, an accounts struct, account data, and generated client helpers.

<Callout variant="warning" title="Alpha">
  This version is alpha software. It has not been audited, is not published on `crates.io`, and APIs
  may break between commits. Depend on it from git on the
  [`anchor-next`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/tree/anchor-next) branch.
</Callout>

## Design

Anchor programs are written as Rust handlers plus account validation structs. The runtime loads accounts, verifies constraints, derives PDAs, emits IDL metadata, and dispatches instructions into your handlers.

The default account model is fixed-size and zero-copy. Use `Account<T>{:rs}` for Pod-backed account state, and use `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` when an account needs variable-length fields such as `Vec{:rs}` or `String{:rs}`. CPI uses borrow-tracked `CpiHandle<'a>{:rs}` values so typed account access and cross-program calls share the same safety model.

## Bench numbers

<Callout variant="example" title="Bench programs">
  You can see worked programs at
  [`bench/programs/`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/tree/anchor-next/bench/programs). Binary
  sizes and CU ranges below are from the current Anchor programs on this branch.
</Callout>

| Program | Description | Binary | CU range | Bin down | CU down |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `helloworld` | Single-instruction counter | 6.5 KB | 1,395 | 19.2x | 4.2x |
| `prop-amm` | Oracle feed with asm fast-path | 8.3 KB | 26-1,379 | 16.8x | 3.1-50.4x |
| `vault` | Single-depositor SOL vault | 5.4 KB | 393-1,905 | 19.8x | 3.0-6.3x |
| `nested` | Shared validation via `Nested<T>{:rs}` | 13.3 KB | 476-2,872 | 11.9x | 6.9-10.0x |
| `multisig` | Four-instruction SOL multisig | 31.2 KB | 475-3,039 | 5.4x | 3.0-9.1x |
