# account-data-model.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/programs/account-data-model.mdx

title: Account data model
description: 'How Anchor stores account data and why `Account<T>{:rs}` is zero-copy by default.'

Solana accounts are byte arrays with an owner. Anchor's account wrappers decide how those bytes are checked and interpreted before your handler uses them.

`Account<T>{:rs}` is the default wrapper for fixed-size program state. It is zero-copy, so it views account bytes as `T{:rs}` instead of deserializing into an owned value.

For a normal program-owned account, the on-chain layout is:

```text showLineNumbers=false
[8-byte discriminator][repr(C) T]
```

Loading `Account<T>{:rs}` validates the owner, discriminator, and minimum data length, then casts the raw account bytes into `T{:rs}`. Exit is a no-op because mutations already happened in the account buffer.

The main decision is whether the account has a fixed layout. Fixed-size structs use `Account<T>{:rs}`. Accounts with `Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, or other variable-length payloads use `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}`.

## Fixed-size state

Use `Account<T>{:rs}` for fixed-size state:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account]
pub struct Position {
    pub owner: Address,
    pub size: PodU64,
    pub open: PodBool,
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Update {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub position: Account<Position>,
}
```

`#[account]{:rs}` enforces the pieces zero-copy needs:

- `#[repr(C)]{:rs}` layout
- `T: bytemuck::Pod{:rs}`
- no padding holes
- an Anchor discriminator
- an `Owner{:rs}` impl for the declaring program

The no-padding assertion is intentionally strict. Padding bytes are untyped state, so the macro turns that whole class of bug into a compile error.

## Variable-length state

Use `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` when the data cannot be a fixed-size Pod type:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(borsh)]
pub struct Profile {
    pub owner: Address,
    pub name: String,
    pub friends: Vec<Address>,
}
```

`BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` deserializes on load, keeps a borrow guard, and serializes on successful exit. That costs more than zero-copy, but it is the right model for `Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, and payload enums.

## Dynamic tails

`Slab<H, Item>{:rs}` is the built-in zero-copy dynamic-tail primitive. It stores a fixed header plus a length-prefixed tail of Pod items:

```text showLineNumbers=false
[disc:8][H][len:u32][tail padding][Item; capacity]
```

`Account<T>{:rs}` is implemented as a specialization of `Slab<T, HeaderOnly>{:rs}`.

## External accounts

SPL token state is not Anchor-discriminated. `anchor-spl-v2` models those accounts with `SlabSchema{:rs}` implementations whose data starts at offset `0`, so `Account<Mint>{:rs}` and `Account<TokenAccount>{:rs}` can zero-copy over SPL-owned account data.

---

# account-types.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/programs/account-types.mdx

title: Account types
description: Account wrappers and when to use each one.

Account wrappers load from pinocchio `AccountView{:rs}` values and implement the shared `AnchorAccount{:rs}` trait. The wrapper you choose determines the account's ownership checks, data layout, borrow behavior, and exit behavior.

For most program-owned state, the choice is between `Account<T>{:rs}` and `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}`. The rest of the wrappers describe signers, programs, sysvars, optional slots, and the intentional escape hatch.

| Type                    | Use for                                                                |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Account<T>{:rs}`       | Program-owned fixed-size data. Zero-copy, Pod-backed.                  |
| `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}`  | Variable-length data with `Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, or payload enums. |
| `Slab<H, Item>{:rs}`    | Header plus dynamic Pod item tail.                                     |
| `Option<A>{:rs}`        | Optional account slot, with the program id as the absent sentinel.     |
| `Nested<T>{:rs}`        | Inline composition of another `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` struct.       |
| `Box<A>{:rs}`           | Heap-boxed wrapper for large account structs.                          |
| `Signer{:rs}`           | An account that must have signed the transaction.                      |
| `Program<T: Id>{:rs}`   | A CPI target or well-known executable program.                         |
| `SystemAccount{:rs}`    | System-owned account with no typed payload.                            |
| `UncheckedAccount{:rs}` | Escape hatch with no validation.                                       |
| `Sysvar<T>{:rs}`        | Account-form sysvar access when a handler requires a sysvar account.   |

## `Account<T>{:rs}`

`Account<T>{:rs}` is the default wrapper for your own fixed-size state. It requires `T: Pod{:rs}` and uses `[disc][repr(C) T]{:text}` layout:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account]
pub struct Counter {
    pub count: u64,
    pub authority: Address,
}
```

For zero-copy details, see [Account data model](/docs/v2/programs/account-data-model/).

## `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}`

Use `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` for state that cannot be Pod:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(borsh)]
pub struct Profile {
    pub owner: Address,
    pub name: String,
}
```

It serializes on successful exit and provides `release_borrow(){:rs}` / `reacquire_borrow_mut(){:rs}` for CPI or realloc paths that need to mutate the same account through another route.

## `Slab<H, Item>{:rs}`

`Slab<H, Item>{:rs}` stores a Pod header followed by a dynamic item tail. It is useful for account-local ledgers, order books, ring buffers, and other bounded collections that should stay zero-copy.

The wrapper exposes vector-style methods such as `try_push{:rs}`, `pop{:rs}`, `iter{:rs}`, indexing, and resize helpers behind the `account-resize{:toml}` feature.

## `Option<A>{:rs}`

`Option<A>{:rs}` makes an account slot optional. When absent, clients pass the program id as a sentinel address. PDA bumps become `Option<u8>{:rs}` so handlers can distinguish present from absent:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct MaybeProfile {
    pub user: Signer,
    #[account(seeds = [b"profile", user.address().as_ref()], bump)]
    pub profile: Option<Account<Profile>>,
}
```

## `Nested<T>{:rs}`

`Nested<T>{:rs}` lets multiple instructions share a validation block:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct AdminGate {
    pub admin: Signer,
    #[account(address = config.admin)]
    pub config: Account<Config>,
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Reset {
    pub gate: Nested<AdminGate>,
    #[account(mut)]
    pub counter: Account<Counter>,
}
```

The nested fields are flattened into the outer account list. `Nested<T>{:rs}` does not consume an extra account slot.

## Utility wrappers

`Signer{:rs}`, `Program<T>{:rs}`, `SystemAccount{:rs}`, `UncheckedAccount{:rs}`, and `Sysvar<T>{:rs}` keep ordinary Anchor code readable. `UncheckedAccount{:rs}` performs no validation, so pair it with explicit constraints or handler checks before trusting it.

`Sysvar<T>{:rs}` accepts the pinocchio sysvar types whose payload can be read directly into a typed value. The supported types are `Clock{:rs}`, `Rent{:rs}`, and `Instructions{:rs}`.

`SlotHashes{:rs}` deliberately does not implement `SysvarId{:rs}`, so `Sysvar<SlotHashes>{:rs}` fails to compile with a missing-trait diagnostic. Programs that need slot-hash data should call the partial-read syscall directly through pinocchio.

## Trait surface

All wrappers implement `AnchorAccount{:rs}`. Third-party crates can add new wrappers by implementing that trait. See [Extensibility](/docs/v2/programs/extensibility/).

---

# borsh-accounts-and-realloc.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/programs/borsh-accounts-and-realloc.mdx

title: Borsh accounts and realloc
description: 'Variable-length account data, `InitSpace{:rs}`, realloc constraints, and borrow release.'

Use `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` when account data is naturally variable-length. This is the account model for state that needs `Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, or enum payloads that cannot fit into a fixed Pod layout:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(borsh)]
#[derive(InitSpace)]
pub struct Profile {
    pub owner: Address,
    #[max_len(64)]
    pub name: String,
    #[max_len(16)]
    pub friends: Vec<Address>,
}
```

The `#[account(borsh)]{:rs}` attribute derives borsh serialization for the account type. `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` deserializes on load and serializes on successful exit.

## Sizing new accounts

`#[derive(InitSpace)]{:rs}` computes the maximum serialized size from `#[max_len(...)]{:rs}` annotations:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct CreateProfile {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer,
    #[account(init, payer = payer, space = 8 + Profile::INIT_SPACE)]
    pub profile: BorshAccount<Profile>,
    pub system_program: Program<System>,
}
```

The extra `8` is the Anchor discriminator.

## Realloc

The derive supports realloc constraints for accounts that need to grow or shrink. This example follows the v2 realloc fixture and keeps the size formula tied to one variable-length field:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(borsh)]
pub struct DynData {
    pub items: Vec<u8>,
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
#[instruction(new_items: Vec<u8>)]
pub struct Grow {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer,
    #[account(
        mut,
        realloc = 8 + 4 + new_items.len(),
        realloc_payer = payer,
        realloc_zero = false,
    )]
    pub data: BorshAccount<DynData>,
    pub system_program: Program<System>,
}
```

The `8` is the Anchor discriminator. The `4` is the borsh length prefix for `Vec<u8>{:rs}`.

The `account-resize{:toml}` feature is on by default because realloc needs pinocchio's account-resize hook. Do not disable that feature while the program still uses realloc helpers.

## CPI re-entry

`BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` holds a borrow guard. If a CPI will mutate the same account, release the borrow before the CPI and reacquire it after:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
ctx.accounts.profile.release_borrow()?;
other_program::cpi::update_profile(cpi_ctx)?;
ctx.accounts.profile.reacquire_borrow_mut(ctx.program_id)?;
```

`release_borrow(){:rs}` commits in-memory changes first, so the CPI sees the latest state. `reacquire_borrow_mut(){:rs}` reruns owner, discriminator, and size checks before deserializing the post-CPI bytes.

`Account<T>{:rs}` does not need this pattern because it reads zero-copy from the account buffer.

---

# errors-and-require.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/programs/errors-and-require.mdx

title: Errors and require
description: 'Custom errors and `#![no_std]{:rs}` require macros.'

Use `#[error_code]{:rs}` to name custom program errors and `require!{:rs}` helpers to return them from validation checks. Custom error names and messages are IDL metadata. The program returns `ProgramError::Custom(code){:rs}` on chain.

## Custom errors

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[error_code]
pub enum VaultError {
    #[msg("The requested amount is zero")]
    ZeroAmount,
    #[msg("The caller is not the vault authority")]
    BadAuthority,
}
```

By default, variants start at the standard Anchor custom-error offset. Override the offset when a program needs to preserve an existing error-code range:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[error_code(offset = 7000)]
pub enum MarketError {
    InvalidPrice,
}
```

## Require macros

Anchor exports no_std-friendly require macros:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
require!(amount > 0, VaultError::ZeroAmount);
require_keys_eq!(ctx.accounts.authority.address(), &ctx.accounts.vault.authority);
require_gte!(available, amount);
```

Available helpers include:

- `require!{:rs}`
- `require_eq!{:rs}`
- `require_neq!{:rs}`
- `require_keys_eq!{:rs}`
- `require_keys_neq!{:rs}`
- `require_gt!{:rs}`
- `require_gte!{:rs}`

The key-specific helpers handle `Address{:rs}` comparisons, while the ordinary helpers cover numeric or other displayable values.

## No runtime AnchorError

The runtime does not allocate an `AnchorError{:rs}` structure with file, line, name, and message fields. That data is useful to clients through the IDL, but keeping it out of the SBF runtime avoids heap allocation and formatting cost in the error path.

---

# events.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/programs/events.mdx

title: Events
description: 'Emit program events with `wincode{:rs}` or `bytemuck{:rs}` encoding.'

Events are structured log records emitted by a program. Clients and indexers can read them from transaction logs instead of trying to infer every state change from account data.

Events are declared with `#[event]{:rs}` and emitted with `emit!{:rs}`. The default encoder is wincode configured to match borsh wire layout for Anchor-supported shapes.

## Default events

Use default events when the payload includes variable-length fields:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[event]
pub struct OrderFilled {
    pub maker: Address,
    pub taker: Address,
    pub size: u64,
    pub memo: String,
}

emit!(OrderFilled {
    maker: *ctx.accounts.maker.address(),
    taker: *ctx.accounts.taker.address(),
    size,
    memo,
});
```

The default encoding supports `Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, `Option{:rs}`, and enums while staying cheaper than borsh on SBF.

## Bytemuck events

When every field is fixed-size and Pod-compatible, use `#[event(bytemuck)]{:rs}`:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[event(bytemuck)]
#[repr(C)]
pub struct PriceUpdate {
    pub price: PodU64,
    pub slot: PodU64,
}
```

This emits the discriminator and then copies the body bytes directly. It is the cheapest event path, but it is only correct for fixed-size Pod payloads.

## Choosing an event form

Default `#[event]{:rs}` is the right pick for expressive Rust data. `#[event(bytemuck)]{:rs}` is the cheaper option for compact telemetry records with stable fixed-size fields.

## Self-CPI events

Transaction logs can be truncated by RPC providers, which makes log-only events unreliable for indexers that need to replay program history. The self-CPI event pattern emits an event as instruction data on a no-op CPI back to the program, so indexers can recover it from instruction history instead of logs.

Opt in by enabling the `event-cpi{:toml}` feature on `anchor-lang-v2`, then mark the handler's accounts struct with `#[event_cpi]{:rs}` and emit with `emit_cpi!{:rs}`:

```toml title="Cargo.toml" showLineNumbers=false
[dependencies]
anchor-lang-v2 = { git = "...", branch = "anchor-next", features = ["event-cpi"] }
```

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[event_cpi]
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct EmitOnce {
    #[account(mut, seeds = [COUNTER_SEED], bump)]
    pub counter: Account<Counter>,
}

pub fn emit_once(ctx: &mut Context<EmitOnce>, value: u64) -> Result<()> {
    ctx.accounts.counter.value = value;
    emit_cpi!(EventCpiObserved { value, marker: 7 });
    Ok(())
}
```

`#[event_cpi]{:rs}` injects an `event_authority{:rs}` PDA derived from `[b"__event_authority"]{:rs}` plus a `program{:rs}` field into the accounts struct. `emit_cpi!{:rs}` issues a self-CPI tagged with a reserved 8-byte discriminator. The `#[program]{:rs}` dispatcher checks for that tag before normal instruction dispatch and short-circuits the call after verifying the signer PDA, so the CPI never reaches a user handler.

Use self-CPI events when downstream indexers need replay guarantees stronger than log retention provides. The default `emit!{:rs}` path remains the right choice for ordinary telemetry that consumers read from logs.

---

# extensibility.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/programs/extensibility.mdx

title: Extensibility
description: How to write your own account primitives and constraint markers without forking the Anchor macro.

Anchor moves account loading, constraint checks, program identities, and discriminator behavior behind traits. That lets downstream crates ship new account primitives, constraint markers, or program-ID identities without changing the derive macro.

The core trait surface that extensions implement is intentionally small:

| Trait | What it adds |
| --- | --- |
| `AnchorAccount{:rs}` | A new account wrapper (load/exit lifecycle, owner/disc validation) |
| `AccountConstraint<A>{:rs}` | A new namespaced constraint (`#[account(my_namespace::key = value)]{:rs}`) |
| `Id{:rs}` | A new well-known program for `Program<T: Id>{:rs}` |
| `Discriminator{:rs}` | A custom 8-byte discriminator on an account or instruction |

## `AnchorAccount{:rs}`

Implementing `AnchorAccount{:rs}` on a wrapper type is what makes it usable as a field in `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}`. The trait extends `Deref<Target = Self::Data>{:rs}`, so consumers can reach the inner data directly through `&*account{:rs}`. The required methods are `load{:rs}`, `account{:rs}`, and (optionally) `load_mut{:rs}`, `exit{:rs}`, and `close{:rs}`. `cpi_handle{:rs}` and `cpi_handle_mut{:rs}` come with default impls:

```rust title="my_wrapper.rs" showLineNumbers=false
use anchor_lang_v2::prelude::*;
use core::ops::Deref;

pub struct MyWrapper<T: Pod> {
    view: AccountView,
    data: T,
}

impl<T: Pod> Deref for MyWrapper<T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T { &self.data }
}

impl<T: Pod + Discriminator + Owner> AnchorAccount for MyWrapper<T> {
    type Data = T;
    const MIN_DATA_LEN: usize = 8 + core::mem::size_of::<T>();

    fn load(view: AccountView, program_id: &Address) -> Result<Self, ProgramError> {
        // Validate owner, discriminator, size, then pointer-cast bytes into `T`.
        unimplemented!()
    }

    unsafe fn load_mut(view: AccountView, program_id: &Address) -> Result<Self, ProgramError> {
        // Same as load, plus an `is_writable` check and the mutable borrow flag.
        unimplemented!()
    }

    fn account(&self) -> &AccountView { &self.view }

    fn exit(&mut self) -> ProgramResult {
        // Persist any in-memory mutations back to the account buffer.
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

The trait defaults `MIN_DATA_LEN{:rs}` to `0{:rs}`, which forces the on-curve check. Wrappers that require non-empty account data can override it with a non-zero structural minimum so the verifier can fall back to a hash-and-compare.

<Callout variant="intuition" title="What `MIN_DATA_LEN{:rs}` actually buys">
  A wrapper that requires a non-empty account is one that must have been created via signed CPI, and `invoke_signed{:rs}` already ran the on-curve check at creation. Setting `MIN_DATA_LEN{:rs}` to a non-zero value tells the PDA verifier "this account was provably created through a signed path", which is the condition under which the curve re-check can be skipped.
</Callout>

Once implemented, `MyWrapper<T>{:rs}` is a first-class field type:

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct UseMine {
    pub data: MyWrapper<MyData>,
}
```

<Callout variant="example" title="A third-party wrapper in the wild">
  [`anchor-dynamic-account`](https://github.com/chen-robert/anchor-dynamic-account) adds zero-copy accounts with auto-reallocating `Vec<T>{:rs}` and `String{:rs}` tails. The whole wrapper is a third-party crate, with no changes required to the core runtime.
</Callout>

## `AccountConstraint<A>{:rs}`

To add a new namespaced constraint, implement `AccountConstraint<A>{:rs}` on a marker type. The trait's four methods correspond to the phases of a constraint's lifecycle:

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
pub trait AccountConstraint<A> {
    type Value;
    fn init(account: &mut A, value: &Self::Value) -> Result<()>;
    fn check(account: &A, value: &Self::Value) -> Result<()>;
    fn update(account: &mut A, value: &Self::Value) -> Result<()>;
    fn exit(account: &mut A, value: &Self::Value) -> Result<()>;
}
```

- `init{:rs}` runs after account creation (under `init{:rs}` or the create-branch of `init_if_needed{:rs}`)
- `check{:rs}` runs on existing accounts and on non-init fields
- `update{:rs}` runs inside an `update(...){:rs}` constraint clause
- `exit{:rs}` always runs during the account exit phase

Once the impl is in scope, a constraint marker named `my_namespace::key{:rs}` becomes available as `#[account(my_namespace::key = value)]{:rs}` on any account field.

The `anchor-spl-v2` crate is built on this pattern. It implements `token::*{:rs}` and `mint::*{:rs}` as a downstream crate rather than baking them into the core derive. Its `associated_token{:rs}` module currently exposes associated token address derivation helpers.

## `Id{:rs}` for `Program<T: Id>{:rs}`

To add a new well-known program type that works with `Program<T: Id>{:rs}`, implement `Id{:rs}` on a unit marker struct. The trait's single method returns the program's canonical address:

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
pub struct MyProgram;
impl Id for MyProgram {
    fn id() -> Address {
        Address::new_from_array([/* 32 bytes */])
    }
}

#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct UseMine {
    pub my_program: Program<MyProgram>,
}
```

At load time, `Program<MyProgram>{:rs}` validates that the account's address matches `MyProgram::id(){:rs}`, and (under the default `guardrails{:toml}` feature) that the account is `executable{:rs}`.

## Why this works

The core derive shrinks materially because the generated code now goes through trait calls like `<MyType as AnchorAccount>::load(view, program_id){:rs}` rather than inlining all of the validation logic per field. Adding a new account wrapper or constraint becomes a trait implementation in a downstream crate, not a fork of the macro itself.

For the full trait surface, see [`lang-v2/src/traits.rs`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/blob/anchor-next/lang-v2/src/traits.rs) on the `anchor-next` branch.

---

# index.mdx

title: Program development
description: Build program state, errors, events, and extension points.
autoCards: false

Program development starts with the account data model. A Solana program mostly reads accounts, checks they are the right accounts, mutates account data, and sometimes calls other programs.

In v2, fixed-size state is zero-copy by default, variable-length state opts into borsh, and account or constraint behavior can be extended from downstream crates. If you are not sure where to start, read Account data model first, then Account types.

# pod-types.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/programs/pod-types.mdx

title: Pod types
description: The alignment-1 integer wrappers, `PodVec<T, MAX>{:rs}`, and the `#[pod_wrapper]{:rs}` macro for safe enum-to-Pod conversion.

<Callout variant="definition" title="Pod">
  Pod (plain old data) means the type is fixed-size, has `#[repr(C)]{:rs}` layout, and contains no padding holes. `Account<T>{:rs}` requires `T: Pod{:rs}` so it can pointer-cast directly from the account's raw bytes without a deserialize step.
</Callout>

To make `T: Pod{:rs}` easy to satisfy, Anchor ships a small set of alignment-1 wrappers that let most user data lay out cleanly without any manual padding.

## Integer wrappers

The unsigned wrappers are `PodU16{:rs}`, `PodU32{:rs}`, `PodU64{:rs}`, and `PodU128{:rs}`. The signed wrappers are `PodI16{:rs}`, `PodI32{:rs}`, `PodI64{:rs}`, and `PodI128{:rs}`. Each stores an integer as `[u8; N]{:rs}` with native little-endian encoding.

Alignment 1 means no padding around the field, so wide integer fields sit flush against their neighbors in a `#[repr(C)]{:rs}` struct.

`PodU8{:rs}` and `PodI8{:rs}` are type aliases for native `u8{:rs}` and `i8{:rs}`. The primitives are already alignment 1, so no wrapper is needed:

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
#[account]
pub struct Position {
    pub owner: Address,
    pub size: PodU64,
    pub entry_price: PodI128,
    pub leverage: PodU16,
}
```

Methods on each wrapper:

- `.get(){:rs}` reads the wrapped integer
- `From<native>{:rs}` constructs from a native integer
- `.checked_add{:rs}`, `.checked_sub{:rs}`, `.checked_mul{:rs}`, `.checked_div{:rs}` return `Option<Self>{:rs}`
- `.saturating_add{:rs}`, `.saturating_sub{:rs}`, etc. saturate at the type's bounds
- `.is_zero(){:rs}` short-circuit zero check
- `.neg(){:rs}` on signed types

## `PodBool{:rs}`

`PodBool{:rs}` is a single-byte boolean wrapper where any non-zero byte counts as `true{:rs}` and a zero byte counts as `false{:rs}`. Use it for flag fields in zero-copy structs to side-step the `bool{:rs}` validity-bit pitfall, where Rust treats it as undefined behavior to read a `bool{:rs}` whose underlying byte is anything other than `0` or `1{:rs}`:

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
#[account]
pub struct Listing {
    pub seller: Address,
    pub active: PodBool,
    pub closed: PodBool,
    pub _pad: [u8; 6],
}
```

## `PodVec<T, MAX>{:rs}`

`PodVec<T, MAX>{:rs}` is a fixed-capacity vector with a `u16{:rs}` length prefix, stored inline in the account rather than behind a heap pointer. The on-disk layout is `[len:u16][T; MAX]{:rs}` with no padding.

`T{:rs}` must itself be alignment-1 so the surrounding `#[account]{:rs}` struct can be `Pod{:rs}`. `MAX{:rs}` is baked into the type so the compiler knows the exact size at every call site:

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
#[account]
pub struct MultisigConfig {
    pub creator: Address,
    pub threshold: u8,
    pub bump: u8,
    pub label: PodVec<u8, 32>,
    pub signers: PodVec<Address, 10>,
}
```

Methods fall into four groups:

| Group | Methods | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Panicking mutators | `.push{:rs}`, `.extend_from_slice{:rs}`, `.set_from_slice{:rs}` | Panic on overflow. |
| Fallible mutators | `.try_push{:rs}`, `.try_extend_from_slice{:rs}` | Return `Result<(), CapacityError>{:rs}`. |
| Indexing accessors | `.as_slice{:rs}`, `.iter{:rs}`, `.get{:rs}`, `.pop{:rs}` | Panic when the stored length prefix exceeds `MAX{:rs}`. Pair with `.try_as_slice{:rs}`, `.try_get{:rs}`, `.try_pop{:rs}`. |
| Length-only helpers | `.len{:rs}`, `.is_empty{:rs}`, `.capacity{:rs}`, `.clear{:rs}`, `.truncate{:rs}` | Never index into `data{:rs}`. Always safe. |

The indexing-accessor panic can fire when a `PodVec{:rs}` is cast from attacker-controlled bytes whose length prefix exceeds `MAX{:rs}`. Either use the fallible variants at the call site or call `.validate(){:rs}` once at load time to reject bad bytes up front.

Reach for `PodVec{:rs}` when the upper bound is small and known ahead of time. For genuinely open-ended data, use `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` with a regular `Vec<T>{:rs}` instead.

## `#[pod_wrapper]{:rs}` for enums

Plain Rust enums are not `Pod{:rs}` because the discriminant has bit patterns that the type system considers invalid. The `#[pod_wrapper]{:rs}` attribute solves this by deriving a transparent `u8{:rs}`-backed wrapper that validates the discriminant against the declared variants whenever the value is compared or converted:

```rust title="lib.rs" showLineNumbers=false
#[pod_wrapper]
#[repr(u8)]
pub enum OrderSide {
    Bid = 0,
    Ask = 1,
}

#[account]
pub struct Order {
    pub price: PodU64,
    pub side: PodOrderSide,
}
```

`PodOrderSide{:rs}` is the generated wrapper. The operations `=={:rs}`, `!={:rs}`, and `.into(){:rs}` each validate the underlying byte against the declared variants. A stale or corrupted byte panics rather than returning an invalid value, which catches account-data tampering at the wrapper boundary before an invalid discriminant can reach program logic.

When unvalidated access is the right choice, the raw `.0{:rs}` field is still available. Useful for migrating an older variant set without panicking on values that pre-date the current declaration.

---

# account-constraints.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/reference/account-constraints.mdx

title: Account constraints
description: Built-in and namespaced account constraints.

Account constraints are declared on fields inside a `#[derive(Accounts)]{:rs}` struct. They run before the handler and cover account-metadata checks, PDA derivation, account creation and resizing, account closing, and extension-specific checks.

| Constraint | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `mut{:rs}` | Requires writable account metadata and loads the wrapper mutably. |
| `signer{:rs}` | Requires `is_signer{:rs}`. Prefer `Signer{:rs}` for ordinary signers. |
| `init{:rs}` | Creates and initializes the account. Requires `payer{:rs}`. |
| `init_if_needed{:rs}` | Creates on the absent branch, otherwise validates existing data. |
| `payer = field{:rs}` | Pays rent for init paths. |
| `space = expr{:rs}` | Allocation size for init. |
| `seeds = [...]{:rs}` | PDA seeds. Array form gives the best IDL metadata. |
| `bump{:rs}` | Finds and records the canonical bump. |
| `bump = expr{:rs}` | Verifies with an explicit bump. |
| `seeds::program = expr{:rs}` | Derives against another program id. |
| `address = expr{:rs}` | Checks the account address against an expression. Accepts any `T: Into<Address>{:rs}` on the right. |
| `owner = expr{:rs}` | Checks the owner address. |
| `executable{:rs}` | Requires the account's executable flag. |
| `constraint = expr{:rs}` | Runs a custom boolean expression. Repeatable. |
| `constraint(expr [@ err]){:rs}` | Parenthesized form of `constraint{:rs}`. Repeatable. |
| `has_one = field{:rs}` | Deprecated relation check. Prefer `address = parent.field{:rs}` on the sibling account. |
| `zeroed{:rs}` | Initializes an allocated account whose discriminator is still all zero bytes. |
| `close = dest{:rs}` | Closes account on successful exit. |
| `realloc = expr{:rs}` | Resizes account data when enabled. |
| `realloc_payer = field{:rs}` | Pays for realloc growth. |
| `realloc_zero = bool{:rs}` | Controls zeroing for new bytes. |
| `unsafe(dup){:rs}` | Opts out of duplicate mutable account rejection for this field. |

Prefer `address = parent.field{:rs}` when a sibling account must match an address stored in another account.

## Namespaced constraints

Namespaced constraints are implemented by marker types that satisfy `AccountConstraint<A>{:rs}`:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(token::mint = mint, token::authority = owner)]
pub vault: Account<TokenAccount>,
```

The derive routes each marker through lifecycle hooks:

| Syntax | Hook |
| --- | --- |
| `ns::key = value{:rs}` | `check{:rs}` |
| `init, ns::key = value{:rs}` | `init{:rs}` during creation for runtime-only markers. Built-in namespace markers are handled by init params. |
| `init_if_needed, ns::key = value{:rs}` | `init{:rs}` then `check{:rs}` on create, `check{:rs}` on existing |
| `update(ns::key = value){:rs}` | `update{:rs}` |
| any successful path | `exit{:rs}` during account exit |

The `anchor-spl-v2` crate uses this extension point for `token::*{:rs}` and `mint::*{:rs}` constraints.

## Custom constraints

`constraint{:rs}` runs an arbitrary boolean expression and accepts either the equals form or a parenthesized form. Both spellings can appear multiple times in one `#[account(...)]{:rs}`, and the checks fire in source order:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(
    mut,
    constraint = pool.is_open,
    constraint(amount > 0 @ MyError::AmountTooSmall),
    constraint(pool.cap >= pool.total + amount),
)]
pub pool: Account<Pool>,
```

A bare failure raises `ErrorCode::ConstraintRaw{:rs}`. Append `@ err{:rs}` to use a custom error. `constraint(a, b){:rs}` is a parse error rather than two checks: chain checks by writing separate entries.

## `address{:rs}` expressions

The right-hand side of `address = expr{:rs}` is converted through `Into<Address>{:rs}`, so wrappers, byte arrays, and references all flow through the same constraint:

```rust showLineNumbers=false
#[account(address = pool.authority)]
pub authority: UncheckedAccount,

#[account(address = MY_AUTHORITY_BYTES)]
pub admin: UncheckedAccount,
```

Use this when an account address comes from a sibling account's field, a constant, or a domain-specific newtype that implements `Into<Address>{:rs}`.

# account-types.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/reference/account-types.mdx

title: Account types
description: Quick reference for Anchor account wrappers.

| Wrapper | Validates | Data model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Account<T>{:rs}` | owner, discriminator, minimum data length | zero-copy Pod data |
| `BorshAccount<T>{:rs}` | owner, discriminator, minimum data length | borsh deserialize on load, serialize on exit |
| `Slab<H, Item>{:rs}` | owner, discriminator, tail layout | zero-copy header plus item tail |
| `Option<A>{:rs}` | absent sentinel or inner wrapper | optional account slot |
| `Nested<T>{:rs}` | inner accounts struct | inline account composition |
| `Box<A>{:rs}` | inner wrapper | heap-boxed wrapper |
| `Signer{:rs}` | `is_signer{:rs}` | no account data |
| `Program<T>{:rs}` | `T::id(){:rs}`, plus executable under `guardrails{:toml}` | no account data |
| `SystemAccount{:rs}` | system owner | no typed data |
| `UncheckedAccount{:rs}` | nothing | raw account view |
| `Sysvar<T>{:rs}` | sysvar id | syscall-loaded sysvar value |

Use [Program account types](/docs/v2/programs/account-types/) for examples and guidance.

# alpha-limitations.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/reference/alpha-limitations.mdx

title: Alpha limitations
description: Known caveats and incomplete surfaces while v2 is alpha.

This version is alpha. It is not audited, not on `crates.io`, and APIs may break between commits.

Keep these limitations in mind while depending on the `anchor-next` branch:

- Rust crates are consumed from git on `anchor-next`.
- no stable v2 TypeScript package has been published yet. Current scaffolds remain pinned to `@anchor-lang/core` `^1.0.0`.
- `anchor-spl-v2` covers core token, mint, interface account, and several Token-2022 extension paths. Less-common SPL surfaces, especially metadata-oriented constraints, may not be covered yet.
- generated `program::cpi::*{:rs}` wrappers are available for supported account structs, but account structs containing `Option<_>{:rs}` or `Nested<_>{:rs}` are currently skipped by CPI wrapper generation.
- runtime PDA validation supports both array-form seeds and opaque seed expressions. Client-side derivation and rich IDL seed metadata work best for array-form seeds that the macro can inspect.

Do not treat the safety defaults as an audit. Review, fuzz, and test before depending on this version for production funds.

---

# anchor-toml.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/reference/anchor-toml.mdx

title: '`Anchor.toml{:toml}` configuration'
description: "Reference for the fields available in an Anchor workspace's `Anchor.toml{:toml}` file."

`Anchor.toml{:file}` is the workspace configuration file used by the Anchor CLI. The CLI discovers it by walking up from the current directory, and reads it for program paths, the active provider, scripts, test infrastructure, and toolchain settings.

The scaffold from `$ <blue>anchor</blue> init` is the best starting point:

```toml title="Anchor.toml" showLineNumbers=false
[toolchain]
package_manager = "yarn"

[features]
resolution = true
skip-lint = false

[programs.localnet]
counter = "..."

[provider]
cluster = "localnet"
wallet = "~/.config/solana/id.json"

[scripts]
test = "cargo test"

skip_local_validator = true
```

## `[provider]{:toml}`

The provider sets the default cluster and wallet for CLI commands:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[provider]
cluster = "localnet"
wallet = "~/.config/solana/id.json"
```

`cluster` can be a named cluster such as `localnet`, `devnet`, `testnet`, or `mainnet`, or a custom URL. `wallet` is the keypair used for commands that need a signer.

You can override either value on a command with global flags:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> build <dim>--provider.cluster</dim> devnet <dim>--provider.wallet</dim> ~/.config/solana/devnet.json
```

## `[programs.<cluster>]{:toml}`

Program sections map program names to declared program IDs for a cluster:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[programs.localnet]
counter = "Counter111111111111111111111111111111111111"

[programs.devnet]
counter = "DevCounter11111111111111111111111111111111"
```

The program name should match the Rust crate name after Anchor normalizes it to snake case. Commands such as `$ <blue>anchor</blue> keys list`, `$ <blue>anchor</blue> keys sync`, `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build`, `$ <blue>anchor</blue> program deploy`, and `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` use this map to connect source crates, keypair files, IDLs, and deployed program addresses.

The CLI also accepts object-form program entries when a command needs a custom deployment path or IDL path:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[programs.localnet]
counter = { address = "Counter111111111111111111111111111111111111", path = "target/deploy/counter.so", idl = "target/idl/counter.json" }
```

## `[scripts]{:toml}`

Scripts are named shell commands. Run a script with `$ <blue>anchor</blue> run <dim><script-name></dim>`:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[scripts]
test = "cargo test"
lint = "cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets"
```

`$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` runs the `test` script after the build and deployment setup. The generated LiteSVM workspace uses `$ <blue>cargo</blue> test` because the tests run in process rather than through an RPC validator.

## `skip_local_validator{:toml}`

Set `skip_local_validator = true{:toml}` when the test harness does not need a local RPC validator:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
skip_local_validator = true
```

The LiteSVM scaffold sets this because the test VM runs inside the Rust process. Use the same setting for other in-process Rust harnesses that do not need an RPC validator. If the flag is absent and the provider cluster is localnet, `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` can start a local validator before running the test script.

## `[features]{:toml}`

Workspace features configure CLI behavior:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[features]
resolution = true
skip-lint = false
```

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `resolution{:toml}` | `true{:toml}` | Emit and use IDL account-resolution metadata where available. |
| `skip-lint{:toml}` | `false{:toml}` | Skip safety-comment lint checks during IDL generation. |

## `[workspace]{:toml}`

The workspace section controls which Rust program crates the CLI builds and where generated TypeScript IDL types are copied:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[workspace]
members = ["programs/*"]
exclude = ["programs/experimental"]
types = "app/src/idl"
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `members{:toml}` | Program manifest paths relative to `Anchor.toml{:file}`. When omitted, the CLI looks under `programs/*{:dir}`. |
| `exclude{:toml}` | Paths to skip after resolving `members{:toml}`. |
| `types{:toml}` | Directory where generated TypeScript IDL type files are copied. |

## `[toolchain]{:toml}`

Toolchain settings choose versions and JavaScript package tooling:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[toolchain]
anchor_version = "1.0.1"
solana_version = "3.1.10"
package_manager = "pnpm"
```

`package_manager` accepts `npm`, `yarn`, `pnpm`, or `bun`. When the field is omitted, Anchor resolves an available package manager from the local environment.

`anchor_version` is used by workflows that delegate version management to AVM. Git-installed alpha builds are usually run directly from the checkout or from the installed `anchor` binary on `PATH`.

## `[hooks]{:toml}`

Hooks run shell commands before or after major CLI stages:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[hooks]
pre-build = "cargo fmt --check"
post-build = "cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets"
pre-test = ["cargo test --workspace --no-run", "cargo nextest list"]
post-test = "echo done"
```

Supported hook names are `pre-build`, `post-build`, `pre-test`, `post-test`, `pre-deploy`, and `post-deploy`. Snake-case aliases such as `pre_build` also parse. A hook can be a single command string or a list of command strings. Nonzero exit codes stop the CLI command.

## `[test]{:toml}`

The test section configures validator-backed test runs:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[test]
startup_wait = 10000
shutdown_wait = 2000
upgradeable = true
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `startup_wait{:toml}` | Milliseconds to wait for the validator to start. |
| `shutdown_wait{:toml}` | Milliseconds to wait during validator shutdown. |
| `upgradeable{:toml}` | Deploy the program under test as upgradeable, with the provider wallet as initial upgrade authority. |

`[[test.genesis]]` preloads programs at genesis:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[[test.genesis]]
address = "Dex111111111111111111111111111111111111111"
program = "fixtures/dex.so"
upgradeable = true
```

## `[test.validator]{:toml}`

`[test.validator]` forwards settings to `$ <blue>solana-test-validator</blue>` for validator-backed tests:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[test.validator]
url = "https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com"
warp_slot = 100
slots_per_epoch = "32"
rpc_port = 8899
ledger = "test-ledger"
limit_ledger_size = "10000"
```

Common nested entries include cloned accounts, account JSON files, account directories, and deactivated features:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[[test.validator.clone]]
address = "metaqbxxUerdq28cj1RbAWkYQm3ybzjb6a8bt518x1s"

[[test.validator.account]]
address = "Ev8WSPQsGb4wfjybqff5eZNcS3n6HaMsBkMk9suAiuM"
filename = "fixtures/account.json"

[[test.validator.account_dir]]
directory = "fixtures/accounts"

[test.validator]
deactivate_feature = [
  "Feat111111111111111111111111111111111111111",
]
```

Use `$ <blue>solana-test-validator</blue> <dim>--help</dim>` for the full set of validator flags. The fields in `Anchor.toml{:file}` intentionally mirror those options where practical.

## `[surfpool]{:toml}`

Surfpool is the default local network backend for supported CLI flows. Configure it with `[surfpool]`:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[surfpool]
startup_wait = 5000
shutdown_wait = 2000
rpc_port = 8899
ws_port = 8900
host = "127.0.0.1"
online = true
datasource_rpc_url = "https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com"
```

Additional Surfpool fields include `airdrop_addresses`, `manifest_file_path`, `runbooks`, `slot_time`, `log_level`, and `block_production_mode`.

## `Test.toml{:toml}`

Large workspaces can put suite-specific test config in `Test.toml{:file}` files. The CLI discovers them under the workspace and merges them with optional base files:

```toml title="tests/token/Test.toml" showLineNumbers=false
extends = ["../Test.base.toml"]

[scripts]
test = "cargo test -p token-tests"

[test]
startup_wait = 15000
```

`Test.toml{:file}` supports the same `test` and `scripts` shapes used by `Anchor.toml{:file}`. Relative paths inside test validator config are resolved from the `Test.toml{:file}` file that declares them.

# cli.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/reference/cli.mdx

title: Anchor CLI
description: CLI reference for project scaffolding, builds, tests, profiling, debugger, coverage, IDL, and workspace commands.

The Anchor CLI is the workspace toolchain. It scaffolds projects, builds programs, runs tests, generates IDLs, deploys, and drives the trace tooling.

This alpha is installed from git:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>cargo</blue> install <dim>--git</dim> https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor.git <dim>--branch</dim> anchor-next anchor-cli <dim>--locked</dim> <dim>--force</dim>
```

<Callout variant="warning" title="Overwrites `anchor` on PATH">
  `$ <blue>cargo</blue> install` overwrites the `anchor` binary on your `PATH`, including one
  managed by AVM. To keep another Anchor install available, run this binary from a source checkout.
</Callout>

Run `$ <blue>anchor</blue> <dim>--help</dim>` or `$ <blue>anchor</blue> <dim><command></dim> <dim>--help</dim>` for the exact flags supported by your checkout.

## Common commands

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> init` | Create a new workspace. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> new` | Add a program to an existing workspace. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build` | Build workspace programs and emit IDLs. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` | Build, deploy when needed, and run tests. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test <dim>--profile</dim>` | Run tests with register tracing and flamegraphs. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> debugger` | Open the instruction-level debugger. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> coverage` | Generate LCOV from SBF register traces. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl` | Build, fetch, initialize, and manage IDLs. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> codama` | Convert IDLs to Codama and render client libraries. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> account` | Deserialize an account using an IDL type. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> keys` | Inspect and sync program keypairs. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> program` | Deploy and manage programs. |

## `<blue>anchor</blue> init`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> init counter <dim>--no-install</dim>
```

Initializes a new workspace. The default program template is the modular Rust template, and the default test template is LiteSVM.

The generated workspace includes:

<FileTree>
  <Dir name="programs" comment="Solana program crates" />
  <Dir name="migrations" comment="Deploy scripts" />
  <Dir name="tests" comment="Workspace-level tests when selected" />
  <File name="Anchor.toml" comment="Anchor workspace config" />
  <File name="Cargo.toml" comment="Rust workspace config" />
  <File name="package.json" comment="JavaScript dependencies when installed" />
</FileTree>

Useful flags:

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `<dim>--no-install</dim>` | Skip JavaScript dependency installation. |
| `<dim>--no-git</dim>` | Skip git initialization. |
| `<dim>--template</dim> <dim>multiple</dim>` | Use the modular Rust program layout. This is the default. |
| `<dim>--template</dim> <dim>single</dim>` | Use a single `lib.rs{:file}` program layout. |
| `<dim>--test-template</dim> <dim>litesvm</dim>` | Generate Rust LiteSVM tests. This is the default. |
| `<dim>--test-template</dim> <dim>mollusk</dim>` | Generate Mollusk Rust tests. |
| `<dim>--javascript</dim>` | Use JavaScript instead of TypeScript for JS templates. |
| `<dim>--package-manager</dim> <dim>pnpm</dim>` | Choose a package manager instead of auto-detecting. |

The LiteSVM template sets `skip_local_validator = true{:toml}` in `Anchor.toml{:file}` and adds this feature to the program crate:

```toml showLineNumbers=false
[features]
profile = ["anchor-v2-testing/profile"]
```

That feature is what powers `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test <dim>--profile</dim>`, `$ <blue>anchor</blue> debugger`, and `$ <blue>anchor</blue> coverage`.

## `<blue>anchor</blue> new`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> new escrow
```

Creates a new program under `programs/{:dir}` in an existing workspace. It uses the modular template by default:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> new escrow <dim>--template</dim> multiple
$ <blue>anchor</blue> new prototype <dim>--template</dim> single
```

`$ <blue>anchor</blue> new` does not create the workspace-level test harness. Use `$ <blue>anchor</blue> init` when starting a new project from scratch.

## `<blue>anchor</blue> build`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> build
```

Builds the workspace programs through `$ <blue>cargo</blue> build-sbf`, writes deploy artifacts under `target/deploy/{:dir}`, and emits IDLs under `target/idl/{:dir}`.

Useful flags:

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `<dim>--program-name</dim> <dim><name></dim>` | Build a single program. |
| `<dim>--no-idl</dim>` | Build the SBF program without emitting IDL. |
| `<dim>--idl</dim> <dim><dir></dim>` | Write IDL JSON to a custom directory. |
| `<dim>--idl-ts</dim> <dim><dir></dim>` | Write TypeScript IDL types to a custom directory. |
| `<dim>--ignore-keys</dim>` | Skip the program-keypair and `declare_id!{:rs}` mismatch check. |
| `<dim>--verifiable</dim>` | Build in a deterministic Docker environment. |
| `<dim>--no-docs</dim>` | Suppress doc strings in IDL output. |

Forward arguments to `$ <blue>cargo</blue> build-sbf` after `<dim>--</dim>`:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> build <dim>--</dim> <dim>--features</dim> my-feature
```

## `<blue>anchor</blue> test`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> test
```

Builds the workspace, deploys programs when needed, and runs the configured test script.

In LiteSVM workspaces, the scaffolded `skip_local_validator = true{:toml}` setting means `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test` runs Rust tests without starting a validator. If the setting is absent and the configured cluster is localnet, the CLI can still start a local validator unless `<dim>--skip-local-validator</dim>` is passed.

Useful flags:

| Flag                                          | Description                                  |
| --------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `<dim>--program-name</dim> <dim><name></dim>` | Build and test one program.                  |
| `<dim>--skip-build</dim>`                     | Reuse existing build artifacts.              |
| `<dim>--skip-deploy</dim>`                    | Run tests against already deployed programs. |
| `<dim>--skip-local-validator</dim>`           | Do not start a local validator.              |
| `<dim>--no-idl</dim>`                         | Skip IDL generation.                         |
| `<dim>--run</dim> <dim><path></dim>`          | Run tests under a specific path.             |
| `<dim>--validator</dim> <dim>surfpool</dim>`  | Use Surfpool as the local network backend.   |
| `<dim>--validator</dim> <dim>legacy</dim>`    | Use `$ <blue>solana-test-validator</blue>`.  |

### Profiling

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> test <dim>--profile</dim>
```

Records per-test SBF register traces and renders flamegraph SVGs under `target/anchor-v2-profile/{:dir}`. This requires Rust tests that call `anchor_v2_testing::svm(){:rs}` and a crate feature that forwards to `anchor-v2-testing/profile`.

## `<blue>anchor</blue> debugger`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> debugger
$ <blue>anchor</blue> debugger initialize
$ <blue>anchor</blue> debugger <dim>--skip-run</dim>
```

Runs the same trace-producing path as `$ <blue>anchor</blue> test <dim>--profile</dim>`, then opens a TUI over captured instructions. The optional positional argument filters captured traces to tests whose name contains that substring.

Useful flags:

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `<dim>--skip-run</dim>` | Open the TUI over existing traces in `target/anchor-v2-profile/{:dir}`. |
| `<dim>--skip-build</dim>` | Skip `$ <blue>cargo</blue> build-sbf` when the deploy artifact is fresh. |
| `<dim>--skip-lint</dim>` | Forwarded to the underlying test invocation. |
| `<dim>--gdb</dim>` | Capture traces through the sbpf gdb-stub path. This is much slower. |

The debugger only works with trace-producing Rust tests. If no traces are found, check that the tests call `anchor_v2_testing::svm(){:rs}` and that the program crate has `profile = ["anchor-v2-testing/profile"]{:toml}`.

## `<blue>anchor</blue> coverage`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> coverage
```

Builds programs with DWARF info, runs LiteSVM tests with register tracing, maps executed program counters back to Rust source lines, and writes LCOV.

Useful flags:

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `<dim>--skip-run</dim>` | Generate coverage from existing traces. |
| `<dim>--skip-build</dim>` | Skip `$ <blue>cargo</blue> build-sbf` when artifacts are fresh. |
| `<dim>--output</dim> <dim><path></dim>` | Write LCOV somewhere other than `target/coverage/sbf.lcov{:file}`. |
| `<dim>--trace-dir</dim> <dim><dir></dim>` | Read or write traces from a custom directory. |

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> coverage <dim>--output</dim> target/coverage/sbf.lcov
$ <blue>anchor</blue> coverage <dim>--skip-run</dim> <dim>--trace-dir</dim> target/coverage/traces
```

## `<blue>anchor</blue> idl`

The `idl` subcommand builds local IDL files and manages on-chain IDL metadata accounts.

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl build
```

Builds the IDL for the current program. Use `<dim>-o</dim>` to write JSON to a file and `<dim>-t</dim>` to write the generated TypeScript IDL type:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl build <dim>--program-name</dim> counter <dim>-o</dim> target/idl/counter.json <dim>-t</dim> target/types/counter.ts
```

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl init <dim>-f</dim> target/idl/counter.json <dim><program-id></dim>
```

Creates an on-chain IDL account for the given program and writes the IDL file into it.

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl fetch <dim>-o</dim> counter.json <dim><program-id></dim>
```

Fetches an on-chain IDL.

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl upgrade <dim>-f</dim> target/idl/counter.json <dim><program-id></dim>
```

Upgrades an existing on-chain IDL metadata account.

Other useful IDL commands:

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl type <dim><path/to/idl.json></dim>` | Generate a TypeScript type from an IDL file. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl convert <dim><legacy-idl.json></dim>` | Convert a legacy IDL to the newer IDL spec. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl create-buffer <dim>-f</dim> <dim><path/to/idl.json></dim>` | Create a buffer metadata account. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl set-buffer-authority <dim><buffer></dim> <dim>-n</dim> <dim><new-authority></dim>` | Set a new authority on a buffer account. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl write-buffer <dim><program-id></dim> <dim>--buffer</dim> <dim><buffer></dim>` | Write metadata from a buffer account. |
| `$ <blue>anchor</blue> idl close <dim><program-id></dim>` | Close a metadata account and recover rent. |

Use on-chain IDLs carefully while this version is alpha because IDL shapes may change between commits.

## `<blue>anchor</blue> codama`

The `codama` subcommand converts an Anchor IDL to a Codama IDL tree and renders client libraries through the `@codama/cli` toolchain. It is the path for generating cross-language clients from a single program description.

### Convert

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> codama convert target/idl/counter.json <dim>-o</dim> target/codama-counter.json
```

`convert{:bash}` translates an Anchor IDL JSON file into a Codama IDL JSON tree rooted at a `rootNode`. The conversion runs in-process and mirrors the reference TypeScript implementation in `@codama/nodes-from-anchor`, so the output is stable against the JavaScript toolchain.

### Generate

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> codama generate <dim>-l</dim> js,rust <dim>-p</dim> clients target/idl/counter.json
```

`generate{:bash}` runs the same conversion in-process, then hands the result to `@codama/cli` (run via `npx --yes codama` by default) to render clients in one or more languages. Each language is written under `<path>/<language>/{:dir}` and uses the matching `@codama/renderers-*` package:

| Language | Renderer package           |
| -------- | -------------------------- |
| `js`     | `@codama/renderers-js`     |
| `js-umi` | `@codama/renderers-js-umi` |
| `rust`   | `@codama/renderers-rust`   |
| `go`     | `@codama/renderers-go`     |

### Flags

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `<dim>-l</dim> <dim><language></dim>` | Languages to generate. Repeat or comma-separate: `<dim>-l</dim> <dim>js,go</dim> <dim>-l</dim> <dim>rust</dim>`. |
| `<dim>-p</dim> <dim><path></dim>` | Base output directory. Default: `clients{:dir}`. |
| `<dim>-o</dim> <dim><file></dim>` | (Convert only) Write Codama IDL JSON to a file instead of stdout. |

<Callout variant="note" title="Operational notes">
  `generate{:bash}` shells out to `npx{:bash}`, so the host needs a Node.js toolchain on `PATH`. The Codama IDL is versioned independently from the Anchor IDL, so rendered clients depend on the `@codama/nodes` version stamped into `rootNode.version`.
</Callout>

## `<blue>anchor</blue> account`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> account <dim><program-name></dim>.<dim><AccountTypeName></dim> <dim><account-pubkey></dim>
$ <blue>anchor</blue> account <dim><program-name></dim>.<dim><AccountTypeName></dim> <dim><account-pubkey></dim> <dim>--idl</dim> <dim><path/to/idl.json></dim>
```

Fetches an account and deserializes it to JSON using an IDL type. Not every account wrapper is a borsh account with an Anchor discriminator. SPL accounts and Pod-backed zero-copy accounts have different layouts.

## Workspace utilities

### `<blue>anchor</blue> keys`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> keys list
$ <blue>anchor</blue> keys sync
```

Lists program keypairs and syncs each program's `declare_id!(){:rs}` value with the keypair file.

### `<blue>anchor</blue> cluster`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> cluster list
```

Lists configured cluster endpoints.

### `<blue>anchor</blue> run`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> run <dim><script-name></dim>
```

Runs a script declared in the workspace's `Anchor.toml{:file}`.

### `<blue>anchor</blue> shell`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> shell
```

Starts a Node.js shell with an Anchor client configured from the local workspace. This workflow is most useful for IDL inspection and client experiments while TypeScript package support is alpha.

### `<blue>anchor</blue> clean`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> clean
```

Removes generated artifacts except program keypairs.

### `<blue>anchor</blue> verify`

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>anchor</blue> verify <dim><program-id></dim>
```

Verifies that on-chain bytecode matches a locally compiled artifact. Use `$ <blue>anchor</blue> build <dim>--verifiable</dim>` for deterministic builds.

# examples-and-benchmarks.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/reference/examples-and-benchmarks.mdx

title: Examples and benchmarks
description: Checked-in example programs, benchmark families, and current size and compute numbers.

Examples are checked into the repository rather than published as a separate examples package. The most important worked programs are under [`bench/programs/`](https://github.com/otter-sec/anchor/tree/anchor-next/bench/programs).

These examples do three things:

- They show complete Anchor programs in realistic shapes.
- They provide repeatable benchmark fixtures for binary size and compute units.
- They act as source material for docs, since they compile with the current branch.

If you are learning the framework, read `helloworld` first, then `vault`, then `multisig`. That path moves from one instruction, to PDA-owned state, to a larger program with multiple handlers and shared validation.

## Benchmark programs

| Program | Path | What it demonstrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `helloworld` | `bench/programs/helloworld/anchor-v2{:dir}` | Minimal counter-style init path and baseline framework overhead. |
| `vault` | `bench/programs/vault/anchor-v2{:dir}` | SOL deposit and withdraw flows with PDA validation. |
| `nested` | `bench/programs/nested/anchor-v2{:dir}` | Shared account validation through `Nested<T>{:rs}`. |
| `multisig` | `bench/programs/multisig/anchor-v2{:dir}` | Multi-instruction SOL multisig with dynamic signer data. |
| `prop-amm` | `bench/programs/prop-amm/anchor-v2{:dir}` | Oracle feed with a small assembly fast path. |
| `humidifi` | `bench/programs/humidifi/anchor-v2{:dir}` | Standalone benchmark program checked in with a built artifact. |

The benchmark harness is the `anchor-bench` crate under `bench/{:dir}`. It builds each program, loads the resulting `.so{:file}` into LiteSVM, runs the relevant instruction cases, records binary sizes, and measures compute units from the executed transaction metadata.

## Current headline numbers

The current overview numbers are directional, not a stability guarantee. This version is alpha and exact values can move as codegen, pinocchio, and tooling change.

| Program | Description | Binary | CU range | Bin down | CU down |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `helloworld` | Single-instruction counter | 6.5 KB | 1,395 | 19.2x | 4.2x |
| `prop-amm` | Oracle feed with asm fast path | 8.3 KB | 26-1,379 | 16.8x | 3.1-50.4x |
| `vault` | Single-depositor SOL vault | 5.4 KB | 393-1,905 | 19.8x | 3.0-6.3x |
| `nested` | Shared validation via `Nested<T>{:rs}` | 13.3 KB | 476-2,872 | 11.9x | 6.9-10.0x |
| `multisig` | Four-instruction SOL multisig | 31.2 KB | 475-3,039 | 5.4x | 3.0-9.1x |

`Binary` and `CU range` are from the current Anchor implementation in each family. `Bin down` and `CU down` compare against the older paired Anchor implementation used by the benchmark harness.

## What each family compares

The harness groups programs into families so the same instruction shape can be compared across implementations.

| Family | Compared variants | Instruction cases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hello_world` | Anchor, older Anchor, Quasar, Pinocchio, Steel | `init` |
| `vault` | Anchor, older Anchor, Quasar, Pinocchio, Steel | `deposit`, `withdraw` |
| `nested` | Anchor and older Anchor | `initialize`, `increment`, `reset` |
| `multisig` | Anchor and older Anchor | `create`, `deposit`, `set_label`, `execute_transfer` |
| `prop_amm` | Anchor plus asm fast path and older Anchor | `initialize`, `update`, `rotate_authority` |

The non-Anchor variants help calibrate the benchmark against lower-level frameworks. The Anchor rows are the rows used for the headline documentation table.

## Running benchmarks

From the repository root, run a specific benchmark integration test:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>cargo</blue> test <dim>-p</dim> anchor-bench helloworld_end_to_end <dim>--</dim> <dim>--nocapture</dim>
```

Other benchmark tests are:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>cargo</blue> test <dim>-p</dim> anchor-bench vault_end_to_end <dim>--</dim> <dim>--nocapture</dim>
$ <blue>cargo</blue> test <dim>-p</dim> anchor-bench nested_end_to_end <dim>--</dim> <dim>--nocapture</dim>
$ <blue>cargo</blue> test <dim>-p</dim> anchor-bench multisig_end_to_end <dim>--</dim> <dim>--nocapture</dim>
$ <blue>cargo</blue> test <dim>-p</dim> anchor-bench prop_amm_end_to_end <dim>--</dim> <dim>--nocapture</dim>
```

Set `BENCH_SKIP_BUILD=1` in your shell to reuse existing `.so{:file}` artifacts:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ BENCH_SKIP_BUILD=1 <blue>cargo</blue> test <dim>-p</dim> anchor-bench helloworld_end_to_end <dim>--</dim> <dim>--nocapture</dim>
```

Run the full benchmark test suite when updating all headline numbers:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>cargo</blue> test <dim>-p</dim> anchor-bench <dim>--tests</dim> <dim>--</dim> <dim>--nocapture</dim>
```

## Reading benchmark output

Each test asserts that every expected suite produced a nonzero binary size and a sane compute-unit measurement. With `--nocapture`, the tests also print comparison tables sorted by compute units.

The output table includes:

| Column    | Meaning                                              |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `rank`    | Position within the family for one instruction.      |
| `variant` | Human-readable implementation label.                 |
| `bytes`   | Size of the built deploy artifact.                   |
| `CU`      | Compute units consumed by the measured transaction.  |
| `vs best` | Difference from the lowest-CU variant in that table. |

## How comparisons stay fair

The paired programs are written to keep the business logic and addresses comparable:

- Anchor variants share program IDs within each benchmark family.
- PDA seeds are kept equivalent so bump differences do not skew results.
- The harness measures the same instruction cases for each variant.
- LiteSVM executes the transactions and reports compute units.
- Binary size comes from the built deploy artifact.
- The benchmark payer keypair is derived deterministically from a fixed label.

The suite table in `bench/src/lib.rs{:file}` is the source of truth for program IDs, manifest paths, instruction names, and case builders.

## Reading the examples

Use the examples as source material for real Anchor code:

| Example | Useful for |
| --- | --- |
| `helloworld/anchor-v2{:dir}` | Minimal `#[program]{:rs}`, PDA init, generated Rust instruction builders. |
| `vault/anchor-v2{:dir}` | Lamport movement, PDA resolution, and comparison with lower-level implementations. |
| `nested/anchor-v2{:dir}` | Reusing validation logic across instructions with `Nested<T>{:rs}`. |
| `multisig/anchor-v2{:dir}` | Fixed-size state, `PodVec<T, MAX>{:rs}`, dynamic signer validation, and resolved account builders. |
| `prop-amm/anchor-v2{:dir}` | Performance-oriented program structure and custom fast paths. |

For SPL token examples, also read `tests-v2/programs/spl/src/lib.rs{:file}`. That test program exercises `anchor-spl-v2` init constraints, CPI helpers, interface accounts, and Token-2022 extension readers.

## Updating the docs

When updating benchmark numbers, rerun the relevant `anchor-bench` tests and update both [Anchor overview](/docs/v2/) and this page together. The overview table is the summary. This page is the reference that explains where to find the examples, how the measurements are produced, and how to reproduce them.

Keep benchmark prose modest. The numbers are strong, but this version is still alpha, not audited, and not published on crates.io.

# feature-flags.mdx

Source: https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs-v2/src/content/docs/v2/reference/feature-flags.mdx

title: Feature flags
description: 'Reference for the `alloc{:toml}`, `guardrails{:toml}`, `account-resize{:toml}`, `const-rent{:toml}`, `compat{:toml}`, and `event-cpi{:toml}` feature flags on `anchor-lang-v2`.'

`anchor-lang-v2` ships seven feature flags, three of which are on by default and the other four opt-in. Most programs never need to touch them, but tuning the set is useful for trimming binary size and CU cost in production builds.

| Feature | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `alloc{:toml}` | on | Pulls in `extern crate alloc{:rs}` for `Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, `BTreeMap{:rs}`. |
| `guardrails{:toml}` | on | Runtime safety checks on dispatch and `load_mut{:rs}`. |
| `account-resize{:toml}` | on | Enables `realloc_account{:rs}` and pinocchio's resize hook. |
| `const-rent{:toml}` | off | Folds the rent formula to a compile-time constant. |
| `compat{:toml}` | off | Exposes v1-shaped helpers such as `debug!{:rs}`, `error!{:rs}`, and `pubkey!{:rs}`. |
| `event-cpi{:toml}` | off | Enables the `#[event_cpi]{:rs}` accounts attribute and the `emit_cpi!{:rs}` macro. |
| `testing{:toml}` | off | Enables `anchor_lang_v2::testing{:rs}` with mock account scaffolding. |

## `alloc{:toml}` (default)

The `alloc{:toml}` feature enables `extern crate alloc{:rs}` and re-exports the `alloc{:rs}` crate under `anchor_lang_v2::__alloc{:rs}`. Generated macro code reaches `Vec{:rs}`, `String{:rs}`, and other heap-allocated types through that re-export, so user crates do not have to import `alloc{:rs}` themselves.

<Callout variant="note" title="When to disable">
  Only embedded targets without a heap have a reason to turn `alloc{:toml}` off. The ergonomic cost is significant. Most realistic user code that touches `Vec{:rs}` or `String{:rs}` will not compile without it.
</Callout>

## `guardrails{:toml}` (default)

The `guardrails{:toml}` feature enables a small set of runtime checks that catch caller bugs the borrow checker cannot see statically:

- `check_program_id{:rs}` on dispatch rejects misrouted instructions
- `is_writable{:rs}` enforcement in data-account `load_mut{:rs}` paths returns an error when the account is not marked `mut{:rs}`
- executable checks on `Program<T>{:rs}` reject non-program accounts before CPI

Disabling the feature drops those guardrail-only emits, which saves roughly 300 bytes of binary and 1 to 2 CU per account:

```toml title="Cargo.toml" showLineNumbers=false
[dependencies]
anchor-lang-v2 = { git = "...", branch = "anchor-next", default-features = false, features = ["alloc", "account-resize"] }
```

<Callout variant="warning" title="Don't disable lightly">
  The runtime safety net is what catches accidental misuse during development. Only turn `guardrails{:toml}` off in production after the program has been thoroughly tested.
</Callout>

## `account-resize{:toml}` (default)

The `account-resize{:toml}` feature enables `realloc_account{:rs}` and adds a pinocchio entrypoint hook. The hook writes `data_len{:rs}` into `RuntimeAccount.padding{:rs}` for every non-duplicate account, which is what lets `AccountView::resize(){:rs}` enforce the `MAX_PERMITTED_DATA_INCREASE{:rs}` cap.

Disabling the feature saves roughly 300 bytes of binary and 2 CU per account, but only when the program never calls `realloc_account{:rs}` in the first place.

<Callout variant="danger" title="Don't disable while call sites exist">
  If `realloc_account{:rs}` could run without the resize hook, it would corrupt the stored `original_data_len{:rs}`. The function is feature-gated so this fails at compile time instead. Disable `account-resize{:rs}` only after removing every realloc path.
</Callout>

## `const-rent{:toml}` (off)

The `const-rent{:toml}` feature folds `rent_exempt_lamports{:rs}` to a compile-time constant by combining pinocchio's `DEFAULT_LAMPORTS_PER_BYTE{:rs}` and `ACCOUNT_STORAGE_OVERHEAD{:rs}`. With the constant in place, `create_account{:rs}` skips the `Rent::get(){:rs}` sysvar call entirely. The savings come out to roughly 90 CU per `create_account{:rs}` CPI.

<Callout variant="warning" title="Rent-formula drift">
  If Solana changes the rent formula in the future (for example, through a SIMD like SIMD-0194), programs built with `const-rent{:toml}` will compute stale values until they are rebuilt. The feature is off by default so programs pick up runtime formula changes transparently.
</Callout>

<Callout variant="tip" title="When to enable">
  Reach for `const-rent{:toml}` when 90 CU per `create_account{:rs}` matters more than rent-formula drift safety, and when the program is rebuilt and redeployed often enough that refreshing the constant is part of the normal release cycle.
</Callout>

## `compat{:toml}` (off)

The `compat{:toml}` feature exposes a small set of v1-shaped helpers for programs in the middle of porting. The most useful is `debug!(msg){:rs}`, a logging macro shaped like `msg!{:rs}` that accepts any Rust format string by routing through `alloc::format!{:rs}`. That covers `{:?}{:rs}`, `{:x}{:rs}`, and dynamic width specifiers, none of which native `msg!{:rs}` supports.

The remaining helpers re-expose v1 names so existing call sites compile without rewrites:

| Helper                                     | Form                                              |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `error!{:rs}`, `err!{:rs}`, `pubkey!{:rs}` | Macros                                            |
| `Pubkey{:rs}`                              | Type alias for `Address{:rs}`                     |
| `AccountViewCompat{:rs}`                   | Extension trait on pinocchio's `AccountView{:rs}` |

<Callout variant="warning" title="`debug!{:rs}` cost">
  `debug!{:rs}` is meaningfully more expensive than the native `msg!{:rs}` because of the heap allocation and fmt-trait dispatch. The feature is off by default to keep production binaries from accidentally shipping the heavier path.
</Callout>

## `event-cpi{:toml}` (off)

The `event-cpi{:toml}` feature wires the self-CPI event emit pattern through Anchor's derives. When enabled, it adds the `#[event_cpi]{:rs}` accounts attribute and the `emit_cpi!{:rs}` macro.

The `#[program]{:rs}` dispatcher then reserves an 8-byte tag at the top of instruction data. Indexers that cannot read transaction logs can recover emitted events from instruction history through that tag.

<Callout variant="note" title="Why off by default">
  The dispatcher would pay the 8-byte tag check on every instruction. Programs that do not use event CPIs avoid that cost by keeping `event-cpi{:toml}` off.
</Callout>

See [Events](/docs/v2/programs/events/) for the call shape.

## `testing{:toml}` (off)

The `testing{:toml}` feature exposes the `anchor_lang_v2::testing{:rs}` module, which provides stack-backed mock pinocchio types (such as `AccountView{:rs}` and the SBF input buffer) that the `lang-v2/tests/{:dir}` integration tests and Miri witnesses depend on. Enabling `testing{:toml}` also turns on `const-rent{:toml}` so host-side tests can exercise rent-dependent helpers without needing SVM sysvar support:

```console showLineNumbers=false
$ <blue>cargo</blue> test <dim>-p</dim> anchor-lang-v2 <dim>--features</dim> testing
```

<Callout variant="note" title="Why off by default">
  Production BPF binaries should never ship the test scaffold, so `testing{:toml}` stays opt-in.
</Callout>

## Recipe: minimal binary, prod profile

```toml title="Cargo.toml" showLineNumbers=false
[dependencies]
anchor-lang-v2 = { git = "...", branch = "anchor-next", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```

This profile drops both `guardrails{:toml}` and `account-resize{:toml}` for the smallest possible binary.

<Callout variant="danger" title="Verify before shipping">
  Only adopt this profile once the program has been thoroughly tested and you have verified that no instruction calls `realloc_account{:rs}`. The `guardrails{:toml}` net catches caller bugs the borrow checker cannot see statically. Ship without it only after fuzzing and review have closed those holes.
</Callout>

## Recipe: maximum CU savings

```toml title="Cargo.toml" showLineNumbers=false
[dependencies]
anchor-lang-v2 = { git = "...", branch = "anchor-next", default-features = false, features = ["alloc", "const-rent"] }
```

This profile adds rent-formula constant folding on top of the minimal recipe. Rebuild and redeploy whenever Solana changes the rent formula so the constants stay in sync.

---
